Born in Augusta, Georgia, in 1971, he emerged as a standout on the national scene and represented the United States at the 1992 Olympic Games before turning professional later that year. A rangy orthodox fighter with a commanding jab, sharp timing, and measured counterpunching, Forrest earned his breakthrough in 2002 when he twice defeated the previously unbeaten Shane Mosley, capturing the WBC and lineal welterweight championship and establishing himself among the elite of his era.

Forrest’s reign at welterweight was halted by Ricardo Mayorga, whose heavy-handed aggression handed him two defeats in 2003. Shoulder injuries and long layoffs followed, but Forrest rebuilt at super welterweight, highlighting his veteran craft with a series of methodical victories. In 2007 he outboxed former champion Carlos Baldomir to claim the WBC title at 154 pounds, a testament to his adaptability after years disrupted by surgery and inactivity. He briefly ceded that belt to Sergio Mora in 2008, then regained it convincingly in a direct rematch later that year, underscoring the poise and strategic adjustments that were hallmarks of his style. Across his prime campaigns, Forrest was noted as much for ring IQ as for power, using pressure in phases but most often controlling distance behind a disciplined lead hand.

Beyond boxing, Forrest was widely respected for philanthropy in the Atlanta area, where he founded a nonprofit organization dedicated to supporting young people and adults with developmental challenges. His life was cut short in July 2009 when he was fatally shot during an attempted robbery in Atlanta, a killing that led to multiple convictions. Tributes emphasized his sportsmanship, mentorship, and community leadership, and his championship triumphs—particularly the victories over Mosley—remain central to assessments of his legacy.

Hazbin Hotel is an American adult animated musical comedy series created by Vivienne “VivziePop” Medrano. Originating from a 2019 independently produced pilot released on YouTube, the project attracted a large online following for its stylized, high-energy animation, original songs, and irreverent, horror-inflected humor. In 2020 the property was picked up for television development by A24, with the serialized version premiering worldwide on Prime Video in January 2024. The narrative centers on Charlotte “Charlie” Morningstar, the optimistic princess of Hell, who founds a rehabilitation hotel for sinners in the hope of reducing the violent culls imposed by Heaven and proving that redemption is possible even for the damned. She is aided by her girlfriend and manager Vaggie and a chaotic ensemble of residents and staff; the arrival of the mysterious Alastor, a powerful “Radio Demon” with opaque motives, accelerates the hotel’s profile while complicating Charlie’s pacifist ideals. Across its first season, the show balances episodic musical set pieces with serialized arcs involving Hell’s media-obsessed overlords, organized vice, and the fraught personal histories of the hotel’s inhabitants.

Produced by A24 in association with Medrano’s studio SpindleHorse Toons, Hazbin Hotel blends Broadway-style numbers with contemporary pop production, integrating songs into character development and plot turns rather than treating them as standalone interludes. The series is noted for its saturated color palette, rapid-fire visual gags, and a mythology that interweaves biblical imagery with modern celebrity culture. It has drawn comparisons to other adult animation for its graphic violence and coarse humor, while its musical ambitions and redemption-focused premise distinguish it within the genre. Critical reception following the streaming debut was generally favorable, highlighting the vocal performances, soundtrack, and visual dynamism, with some reviewers questioning pacing and tonal whiplash between farce and melodrama. The franchise exists alongside Helluva Boss, a separate web series set in the same universe, and has generated substantial merchandising, fan art, and convention presence. A second season has been announced, with further exploration of the hotel’s mission and the politics of Hell anticipated.

Dealbreakers Talk Show No. 0001 is a fourth-season installment of the American sitcom 30 Rock that chronicles the chaotic launch of Liz Lemon’s in-universe talk show, spun out of her popular relationship-advice book. The episode follows Liz as she transitions from head writer to on-camera host, only to discover that the demands of high-definition television, branding mandates, and live audience expectations magnify her insecurities. As executive producer, Jack Donaghy marshals a small army of consultants and control-room specialists to shape the pilot, insisting on sleek graphics, sponsor integration, and a relentlessly upbeat tone. The production’s glossy surface quickly buckles under the pressure of real-time performance, and Liz’s carefully rehearsed persona unravels in a tangle of stage fright, technical miscues, and ill-advised last-minute tweaks.

The narrative uses the failed premiere to satirize the television industry’s impulse to engineer authenticity, lampooning everything from rigid format beats to the anxiety induced by studio lighting and camera-ready grooming. Cutaways to the control room highlight Jack’s belief that postproduction polish can rescue any on-air stumble, while backstage scenes depict writers and performers recalibrating their loyalties as they hedge bets on whether the spin-off will eclipse the sketch show that originally employed them. In keeping with the series’ meta-comedy, the episode nests a show within a show and then dissects its implosion in real time, turning technical jargon and network etiquette into comic set pieces.

Contemporary reviewers praised the episode’s brisk escalation of calamities and its portrait of performance anxiety as both personal and institutional, noting how Tina Fey’s physical comedy and Alec Baldwin’s managerial bravado complement each other. It is frequently cited as a pivot point in the season’s arc: the ordeal clarifies Liz’s ambivalence about celebrity, reaffirms the value of her behind-the-scenes role, and sharpens the series’ broader critique of corporate optimization masquerading as creative vision.

Alexander Gordon (1752–1799) was a Scottish physician whose lucid investigation of epidemic puerperal fever in Aberdeen made him an early, prescient voice for contagion and preventive practice in obstetrics. Trained at Aberdeen and seasoned by service as a naval surgeon before further study in London with leading accoucheurs, he returned to his native city in the late 1780s to practice midwifery. There he confronted a devastating series of puerperal fever cases between 1789 and 1792 and responded with meticulous record‑keeping, tracing the timing, geography, and personal links of each case. In his Treatise on the Epidemic Puerperal Fever of Aberdeen (1795) he set out evidence that the disease was not a mysterious atmospheric miasma but a specific contagion, frequently carried from patient to patient by physicians and midwives on their hands and clothing. He noted parallel outbreaks of erysipelas and sore throat among attendants and their contacts, reasoning that these conditions were related manifestations of the same infectious principle.

Gordon’s conclusions led to practical, testable recommendations: strict cleanliness, handwashing and a change of apparel between deliveries; prompt isolation of the ill; avoidance of attendance at births by anyone recently exposed to cases; and thorough cleansing and airing of rooms and linens. He even urged practitioners to suspend obstetric work for a period after encountering the fever, anticipating by decades the measures later associated with hospital hygiene and asepsis. The directness of his argument—naming chains of transmission and implicating professional practice—provoked resentment among contemporaries and limited the immediate influence of his treatise. Gordon died only a few years after its publication, before his insights gained wide acceptance. In the nineteenth century his work was rediscovered and praised, notably by Oliver Wendell Holmes, and is now regarded as a landmark in observational epidemiology and the control of puerperal sepsis, foreshadowing the later achievements of Semmelweis and the antiseptic reforms that transformed obstetric care.

IAUDIO is a line of portable digital audio players developed by the South Korean company Cowon Systems that gained prominence in the early and mid-2000s for emphasizing sound quality, broad format support, and flexible connectivity at a time when many rivals focused on closed ecosystems. Introduced as Cowon expanded from PC audio software and codecs into hardware, the earliest iAUDIO flash models established a reputation for solid build quality, user-replaceable or long-lasting batteries, and firmware features that appealed to enthusiasts. As the market shifted toward higher-capacity devices, the brand’s hard drive and advanced flash players, notably mid-decade models such as the X5, M3, and U- and G‑series variants, offered unusual capabilities including line-in and microphone recording, FM radio with scheduling, voice memo functions, and USB On-The-Go file transfer without a PC. IAUDIO devices were frequently praised for playing not only MP3 and WMA but also less common formats such as Ogg Vorbis and FLAC, alongside extensive equalization and effects settings later marketed under Cowon’s JetEffect and BBE enhancements.

The product family cultivated a loyal user base that valued its preference for open mass-storage USB modes, straightforward drag-and-drop file management, and tactile controls suited to pocket operation. Enthusiast communities produced guides, themes, and alternative firmware support on some models, further extending longevity beyond official updates. While the players competed in the same era as the iPod and offerings from iRiver, Creative, and Sony, IAUDIO positioned itself as a feature-forward, audio-centric alternative, often trading mainstream simplicity for granular control over playback and recording. Distribution expanded from South Korea to North America and Europe through specialized retailers and online channels, cementing a niche among portable audio hobbyists and field recordists.

As capacious flash memory, touch interfaces, and video playback reshaped the category, Cowon gradually shifted branding toward its own name for later devices, and the IAUDIO marque receded by the early 2010s. Its legacy persists in the company’s continued emphasis on codec breadth and sound customization, and in a secondary market sustained by durable hardware and a persistent community of users.

Napoleon Zervas (1891–1957) was a Greek army officer and resistance leader whose career spanned the turbulent decades from the Balkan Wars to the Greek Civil War. Born in Arta and educated as a professional soldier, he fought in the Balkan Wars, on the Macedonian Front in the First World War, and in the Asia Minor Campaign, rising through the ranks in staff and field postings. A staunch republican in the interwar period, he took part in the failed Venizelist coup of 1935 and was dismissed from the army, a rupture that shaped his subsequent opposition to the royalist establishment and to the authoritarian Metaxas regime.

During the Axis occupation he founded the National Republican Greek League (EDES) in 1941 with support from Britain’s Special Operations Executive. Operating primarily in Epirus, EDES grew into one of the principal resistance formations alongside the left-wing EAM/ELAS. Zervas’s forces cooperated with ELAS and British saboteurs in the destruction of the Gorgopotamos bridge in November 1942, a signature feat of the resistance. Relations soon deteriorated, however, and from late 1943 EDES and ELAS engaged in intermittent civil conflict that overshadowed operations against the occupiers. Scholars have long debated allegations that EDES units in Epirus reached local understandings with Axis forces in order to fend off ELAS, a charge Zervas denied while emphasizing his movement’s anti-Axis credentials. In 1944 EDES operations against the Cham Albanian population of Thesprotia culminated in expulsions and killings; contemporary reports and later research have accused EDES of atrocities, while Greek nationalist narratives framed the actions as reprisals in a zone of shifting wartime loyalties.

After liberation Zervas entered politics, founding a personal party and serving as a deputy and cabinet minister. As Minister of Public Order during the civil war years he advocated a hard line against the communist insurgency, a stance that helped secure British and later American backing but also deepened the polarization of Greek society. He died in Athens, leaving a legacy at once identified with republican resistance in Epirus and indelibly marked by the internecine violence of occupation and civil war.

The Phelps and Gorham Purchase was the first large-scale attempt to open western New York to American settlement after the Revolution, rooted in overlapping colonial charters that left New York and Massachusetts claiming the same interior. By the Treaty of Hartford in 1786, New York retained sovereignty while Massachusetts received the “preemption right” to purchase Indigenous title to roughly six million acres west of a line later called the Preemption Line. In 1788 Oliver Phelps and Nathaniel Gorham acquired those rights from Massachusetts, agreeing to pay in depreciated state securities, and immediately set about extinguishing Seneca title. At Buffalo Creek in 1788 they negotiated a cession of the lands east of the Genesee River and, on its west bank, a narrow strip known as the Mill Yard Tract that included valuable falls sites; in all, about 2.6 million acres were opened. From a base at Canandaigua they commissioned surveys into New England–style townships, established mills and roads, and promoted migration into the Finger Lakes region, founding communities such as Canandaigua and Geneva. The initial Preemption Line run to fix the Massachusetts claim proved inaccurate, producing the “Old” and later “New” lines and a tangle of boundary disputes that lingered for years around Seneca Lake and beyond.

Their financial structure unraveled almost as quickly as settlement advanced. When federal assumption of state debts raised the market value of the very securities they had pledged, the cost of the bargain soared beyond their reach. By 1790–1791 Phelps and Gorham surrendered their remaining unsold rights back to Massachusetts, retaining only portions they had conveyed east of the Genesee and along the mill tract. Massachusetts sold the balance to Robert Morris, who in turn conveyed most of it to the Holland Land Company, setting the stage for the systematic development of the far western counties. Despite their collapse, the purchase fixed survey frameworks, encouraged early infrastructure, and decisively redirected migration into what became Ontario, Steuben, Livingston, Monroe, and neighboring counties.

Insufflation is the act of introducing a gas, vapor, or finely divided powder into a cavity, vessel, or passage, typically by means of gentle pressure or blowing. The term derives from the Latin insufflare, “to blow into,” and it has long described techniques used for diagnostic, therapeutic, and symbolic purposes. In premodern medicine apothecaries and surgeons employed bellows, tubes, or hand bulbs to deliver medicaments to the ear, nose, or throat, and nineteenth‑century otologists popularized Eustachian tube inflation with devices such as the Politzer bag to equalize middle‑ear pressure.

In contemporary practice, insufflation is fundamental to endoscopic surgery. Carbon dioxide is introduced into the peritoneal cavity to establish a pneumoperitoneum for laparoscopy, creating space and improving visualization while remaining nonflammable and rapidly absorbed. Clinicians typically regulate flow and intra‑abdominal pressure with electronic insufflators to minimize physiologic disturbances; recognized complications include hypercarbia, reduced venous return, subcutaneous emphysema, and, rarely, gas embolism or pneumothorax. Gastrointestinal endoscopy similarly uses air or carbon dioxide to distend the lumen, with carbon dioxide favored for faster postprocedural comfort due to its quicker uptake. Beyond surgery, insufflation underlies several respiratory therapies: manual resuscitators and anesthesia circuits deliver lung inflation, while mechanical insufflation‑exsufflation devices alternate positive and negative pressures to augment cough in patients with neuromuscular weakness. Pharmaceutical delivery also employs insufflation; intranasal administration can target local nasal disorders or achieve systemic absorption of select agents, and research platforms use dry‑powder insufflators for vaccines and antibiotics where cold‑chain constraints or needle avoidance are priorities.

Outside medicine, insufflation has ritual and symbolic uses. Late antique and medieval Christian rites recorded the clerical breathing upon catechumens or the possessed as a sign of purification or the imparting of spirit, a practice variably retained, modified, or abolished across traditions. Related acts are attested in other religious and folk‑healing contexts. In laboratory and veterinary settings, specialized insufflators introduce aerosols or powders into animal airways for toxicology and pharmacology studies, providing controlled dosing without solvents.

Paola is a coastal town and comune in the province of Cosenza, in the Calabria region of southern Italy, set between the Tyrrhenian Sea and the steep, wooded slopes of the coastal Apennines. Its historic center climbs inland from the waterfront in a compact weave of lanes, stairways, and stone houses, while the marina and seafront quarters spread along the gulf below. The town is internationally known as the birthplace of Saint Francis of Paola, founder of the Minims, and the Sanctuary of San Francesco, with its church, cloisters, and fountains, has shaped Paola’s identity since the late fifteenth century. Pilgrimages peak in spring around the saint’s feast, when processions, illuminations, and a traditional blessing of the sea draw visitors from across Calabria and beyond.

Historically, Paola developed under Norman and later Angevin and Aragonese rule within the Kingdom of Naples, its fortunes tied to coastal trade, fishing, and the religious house that attracted patronage and artisans. Earthquakes and raids left their marks, but the core street plan and several palazzi preserve a stratified urban fabric. Today the local economy blends services and small commerce with fishing, olive groves, citrus, and growing seasonal tourism. Beaches and coves attract summer travelers, while religious and cultural tourism sustains activity in shoulder seasons.

Paola’s railway station sits on Italy’s main Tyrrhenian corridor linking Salerno with Reggio di Calabria and serves as a gateway to the interior via the line ascending to Cosenza through long tunnels beneath the range. The coastal state road parallels the sea, and a mountain highway connects quickly to the regional capital. The port facilities host a modest fishing fleet and leisure craft. The climate is typically Mediterranean, with mild, wetter winters and hot, dry summers tempered by sea breezes; the nearby heights channel cool air and increase rainfall, feeding short streams that mark the town’s valleys and contribute to a varied landscape within a compact territory.

Frank Elegar is an Antiguan professional basketball player whose career traces a steady ascent from NCAA development to a long tenure across prominent European competitions. Raised in the Caribbean basketball tradition and refined in the collegiate ranks at Drexel University, he evolved from a raw interior prospect into a reliable two-way big, earning conference recognition for his rebounding, rim protection, and increasingly polished post and face-up scoring. Going undrafted in 2008 steered him toward the international game, where he quickly established himself as a dependable frontcourt presence capable of adapting to varied systems and roles.

His professional path spans multiple countries and tiers of competition, with formative stops in Belgium and Turkey before a standout run in Estonia with Kalev/Cramo, where his athleticism and motor helped the club contend for and win domestic honors. Success in the Baltics opened doors to higher-profile stages, including the VTB United League and EuroCup, and later assignments in France and Eastern Europe. Throughout, coaches have prized his screen-setting, vertical spacing in the pick-and-roll, and second-chance creation on the offensive glass. Defensively, Elegar has been noted for timing as a shot-contester, comfort defending in space on hedges and switches, and the willingness to anchor a paint-oriented scheme when required.

Elegar has also been a fixture for Antigua and Barbuda’s national team, lending size and experience in Caribbean regional play and serving as a visible example for younger players from a small federation seeking pathways to higher levels. His professional reputation rests on durability, conditioning, and an ability to contribute without heavy play-calling—traits that made him a popular midseason addition for clubs looking to stabilize rotations or add veteran toughness for playoff pushes. While seldom a primary scorer, his efficiency around the rim, improved free-throw reliability, and consistent rebounding have underpinned a career defined by adaptability, persistence, and high-level team impact.

Divided by Night is a studio album by the American electronic duo the Crystal Method, issued in 2009 as the follow-up to their mid-2000s work and conceived amid a period of rapid change in digital production and distribution. The title gestures to a central preoccupation with nocturnal space—both the literal hours in which much of the material was composed and the figurative divide between private listening and public, club-facing spectacle. Working primarily in their Los Angeles studio, the producers combined analog synthesizers, guitar textures, and software-based sequencing to build arrangements that alternate between hard-edged rhythmic builds and more atmospheric interludes. The project emphasized collaboration with a range of guest vocalists and instrumentalists, a strategy intended to widen the palette beyond the duo’s established big beat and breakbeat foundations.

Production notes released around the album’s rollout highlighted an interest in contrasts: saturated bass and crisp percussion offset by spacious, reverb-heavy melodic lines; tightly quantized grooves set against humanized takes captured in single passes. Sequencing was treated as narrative, with transitions designed to emulate the arc of a late-night set, cresting and receding in intensity. The album appeared across multiple formats, including digital platforms that featured exclusive mixes or bonus tracks in select territories, reflecting the marketplace’s fragmentation at the time.

Critical reception was mixed to positive. Reviewers frequently praised the craftsmanship of the sound design and the integration of guest performances, while some argued that the stylistic breadth came at the expense of cohesion. Commercially, the record performed most strongly on specialized dance and electronic charts, buoyed by a lead single that received rotation in clubs and on alternative outlets. In retrospective appraisals, commentators often position Divided by Night as a hinge between the duo’s earlier, sample-forward era and the EDM-adjacent aesthetics that would dominate festival stages in the early 2010s, noting its role in bridging veteran big beat sensibilities with a more collaborative, song-oriented approach.

Jay Zeamer Jr. was a United States Army Air Forces pilot in the Southwest Pacific theater during the Second World War and a recipient of the Medal of Honor for extraordinary valor. Deployed early in the campaign against Japan, he developed a reputation as an aggressive, resourceful flier who gravitated to hazardous long-range missions. Finding it difficult at first to secure a regular crew, he eventually gathered a team of like‑minded volunteers and took charge of a weathered B‑17E, serial number 41‑2666, which they modified extensively for endurance and self‑defense. Nicknamed “Old 666,” the bomber carried extra guns, improvised armor, and specialized cameras, and was used for reconnaissance, mapping, and strike sorties deep into enemy-held airspace.

On June 16, 1943, Zeamer led a solo photographic mapping mission over Bougainville to obtain detailed imagery needed for future Allied operations. The task required a long, straight, and predictable flight path, inviting interception. After successfully beginning the mapping run, the B‑17 was attacked by a large force of Japanese fighters. In the opening passes, the nose compartment took heavy fire; the bombardier, Technical Sergeant Joseph R. Sarnoski, though mortally wounded, remained at his gun and continued to repel attackers. Zeamer, himself badly wounded by shrapnel and gunfire, kept the aircraft steady to complete the photography, then maneuvered to evade further attacks while his crew fought back from multiple stations. Despite severe structural damage and injuries throughout the crew, the bomber returned across open sea and landed safely at base in New Guinea with its critical reconnaissance imagery intact.

For their actions during the Bougainville mission, Zeamer and Sarnoski were each awarded the Medal of Honor, among the few times in the Pacific war that two members of the same aircrew received the nation’s highest decoration for the same engagement. The exploit of “Old 666” became emblematic of the perilous reconnaissance work that underpinned Allied planning in the theater.

A thyristor-switched capacitor is a shunt reactive power device in which discrete capacitor banks are connected to or disconnected from an alternating-current network by anti-parallel thyristor valves, providing rapid and wear-free switching. It is widely employed as a building block of static var compensators, often paired with a thyristor-controlled reactor to achieve both inductive and capacitive control, but it can also be used on its own where only leading vars are required. By injecting capacitive reactive power in steps, a thyristor-switched capacitor regulates bus voltage, improves power factor, increases transmission margins, and mitigates voltage flicker from fluctuating loads such as arc furnaces. Because each branch is either fully on or fully off, steady-state harmonic generation is minimal compared with phase-controlled reactors, and overall losses are low, limited chiefly to thyristor conduction drop and dielectric losses.

Switching is synchronized to the network to minimize transients. The control system measures the instantaneous system voltage and the capacitor’s residual voltage and issues a gate command at the moment these are equal in magnitude and polarity, resulting in near-zero switching current. A small series reactor in each branch further limits di/dt and inrush, and snubber networks protect the valves. Capacitor units include discharge resistors and unbalance detection to manage trapped charge and insulation failures. Typical response times are on the order of a half to a few cycles, much faster than mechanically switched capacitor banks and sufficient for dynamic voltage support in transmission and industrial distribution systems. Multiple banks are commonly sized in binary or uniform steps to approximate a continuous droop characteristic for voltage control while avoiding overcompensation.

Design and application considerations include coordination with network resonance, provision of harmonic filters if nearby non-linear equipment dictates, thermal management of the valves, and control interaction with co-located reactors or power electronics. Compared with alternative technologies, thyristor-switched capacitors offer a robust, economical means of fast capacitive var support, with the principal limitation being their inherently discrete step resolution.

Australian rules football has been played on the Gold Coast since the mid-twentieth century, gaining a foothold through service personnel, interstate migrants and holiday workers who brought the Victorian code to a region long identified with rugby league. By the early 1960s a local competition had coalesced, bridging the Queensland–New South Wales border and producing enduring community clubs such as Southport, Surfers Paradise, Broadbeach, Labrador, Palm Beach Currumbin and Coolangatta-Tweed Heads. These sides established a suburban culture of Saturday football, junior programs and volunteer-led facilities that anchored the game to beacheside suburbs and growth corridors west of the highway.

From the 1980s the Gold Coast’s presence in Queensland’s senior pathways became more pronounced. Southport graduated from regional competition to the state league and quickly became one of Queensland football’s pre-eminent clubs, its professionalism and recruiting reach setting benchmarks for off-field administration and on-field success. The opening of Carrara Oval, and the decision to base the Brisbane Bears there in the late 1980s, brought top-level matches to the Coast for the first time, exposing local audiences to national-calibre football and providing aspirational pathways for teenagers emerging from school and club systems. Redevelopments at Carrara and an expanding schools and juniors network through the 1990s and 2000s consolidated the code’s infrastructure in a rapidly growing city.

AFL expansion delivered a permanent elite presence when the Gold Coast Suns were licensed and entered the national competition in 2011, playing at a rebuilt Carrara Stadium. The new club catalysed academies, coaching courses and talent identification across the Coast and northern New South Wales. In the same year the NEAFL linked local heavyweights, including Southport and the Suns’ reserves, into a broader second-tier competition; after its 2020 reorganisation both transitioned into an expanded VFL, where Southport swiftly became a contender. Women’s football advanced in parallel, with Gold Coast clubs prominent in Queensland’s state league and the Suns joining the AFLW in 2020. By the decade’s end, participation had diversified and grown, embedding Australian rules football as a visible strand of the Gold Coast’s sporting identity.

Asterias amurensis is a large asteriid sea star native to the cold temperate coasts of the northwest Pacific, including Japan, Korea, northern China and the Russian Far East. Typically five-armed, with a small central disc and long, tapering rays, it attains an arm span of 40 centimeters or more. The aboral surface is studded with short spines and pedicellariae, and coloration varies from pale yellow to orange or mottled purple, often providing effective camouflage on sand and rubble. Like other forcipulate asteroids, it moves on hundreds of tube feet arranged in rows, each tipped with a suction cup that grips rock, prey shells or wharf pilings. It is an opportunistic carnivore of bivalves, gastropods and other invertebrates, prying open shells with steady force and everting its stomach to digest tissues externally. Separate sexes broadcast spawn; females release millions of eggs, and larvae pass through planktonic bipinnaria and brachiolaria stages that can drift for weeks, facilitating dispersal.

In its native range A. amurensis occupies rocky reefs, soft sediments and estuaries from the intertidal to at least tens of meters depth, tolerating wide ranges of temperature and salinity. It has become a high-profile marine invader in southern Australia, most notably in Tasmania’s Derwent Estuary and Victoria’s Port Phillip Bay, where it likely arrived via ballast water and the movement of fouled aquaculture gear. There it reaches dense aggregations, preys heavily on scallops, mussels and oysters, and competes with native echinoderms, altering benthic community structure and affecting commercial shellfish operations. Management focuses on prevention, early detection and physical removal, including diver hand-collection and baited traps; strict biosecurity measures for shipping and aquaculture aim to reduce further spread. The species’ high fecundity, broad environmental tolerance and capacity to regenerate lost arms from portions of the central disc complicate control efforts. Ongoing research examines seasonal reproduction, larval ecology and habitat use to refine monitoring and mitigation in both native and invaded waters.

Migliorismo denotes a reformist current within the Italian left that privileged gradual, pragmatic improvement over maximalist or revolutionary aims. The term, derived from the Italian migliorare (“to improve”), has roots in early twentieth-century socialist debates pitting incremental reformers against massimalisti, but it acquired particular salience inside the Italian Communist Party (PCI) from the late 1970s through the 1980s. There it came to identify a moderate wing, associated with leaders such as Giorgio Napolitano and Gerardo Chiaromonte and often linked to the pragmatic culture of the Milan federation, which favored engagement with Italy’s economic establishment and institutions. Initially used by critics as a mildly pejorative label for right-leaning communists, it was later adopted more neutrally to describe a recognizable tendency of thought and practice.

Ideologically, migliorismo accepted a mixed economy and sought to reconcile social justice with competitiveness, efficiency and European integration. It emphasized reforms to modernize public administration, rationalize the welfare state and strengthen collective bargaining, aiming to deliver measurable gains in living standards and workplace rights. Internationally, it promoted a pro-European and Atlantic orientation for the Italian left, arguing that credibility within NATO and the European Community was compatible with advancing labor protections and industrial policy. Domestically, it advocated stable governing alliances and maintained an open, if often tense, dialogue with the Socialist Party, contending that reformism required cooperation across the center-left rather than moral condemnation or isolation.

Within the PCI’s plural culture, migliorismo sometimes clashed with currents inspired by Pietro Ingrao and with elements of Enrico Berlinguer’s legacy, particularly when the “moral question” was seen to preclude coalition-building. After the Cold War and the dissolution of the PCI in 1991, many of its positions influenced the Democratic Party of the Left and subsequent center-left formations, contributing to their evolution toward European social democracy. Supporters credit migliorismo with helping the Italian left transition into a governing force; detractors view it as an adaptive drift that diluted transformative ambition. In contemporary usage, the word can designate a broader disposition in Italian politics favoring incremental, negotiated change over sweeping rupture.

Ansei Uchima (1921–2000) was a Japanese American artist whose refined woodblock prints forged a distinctive bridge between the sōsaku-hanga ethos of self-carved, self-printed work and the language of postwar abstraction. Born in California to immigrant parents and educated for a time in Japan, he came of age within Tokyo’s lively circle of modern printmakers clustered around Onchi Kōshirō. There Uchima absorbed a belief in the artist’s total authorship—designing, carving, and printing—while also becoming an eloquent conduit to Western audiences who were beginning to look seriously at modern Japanese prints. He assisted visiting writers and collectors, notably helping to shape the conversations that introduced sōsaku-hanga to an international readership.

Uchima’s mature prints are immediately recognizable for their orchestration of translucent color and nuanced surface. He favored water-based pigments on handmade washi, using delicate bokashi gradations, careful overprinting, and subtle embossing to build luminous atmospheres. Within these veils of tone, calligraphic marks, floating rectangles, and understated grids create rhythmic scaffolds that feel at once architectural and poetic. The works rarely depict specific places; instead they evoke weather, memory, and intervals of silence, with titles that often allude to seasons, bells, or the moon. Mica, mineral whites, and occasionally collaged papers enhance the prints’ tactile presence without sacrificing their restraint. Though celebrated as a printmaker, Uchima also explored drawing, watercolor, and mixed media, extending his vocabulary while preserving the meditative clarity that defined his practice.

Relocating to New York in the late 1950s, Uchima exhibited widely and taught for many years, introducing generations of students to Japanese materials and baren-printing techniques. He married the artist Toshiko Uchima, and together they participated in a transpacific milieu of postwar art that valued exchange and experiment. His work entered major public collections in the United States, Europe, and Japan, including leading museums known for modern prints. Remembered for serenity without sentimentality, Uchima demonstrated how a centuries-old medium could speak with a contemporary voice, his prints distilling time, place, and perception into quietly radiant harmonies.

George Le Grand Jacob was a Bombay Army officer who became one of the most capable political agents in western India in the mid-nineteenth century, combining administrative acumen with a scholar’s curiosity. Entering service as a young infantry officer, he moved early into the political department and spent much of his career in Cutch and Kathiawar, where British influence rested on delicate negotiations with local rulers, mercantile elites, and pastoral communities. Jacob earned a reputation for firm but tactful management: he arbitrated succession disputes, pressed for the suppression of banditry and piracy along the peninsular coast, and promoted measures intended to stabilize revenue and open trade. His memoranda from this period display an attentive eye for local custom and law, and a willingness to record the perspectives of chiefs and town notables alongside those of colonial superiors.

Parallel to his official duties, Jacob pursued oriental studies with unusual range. He acquired fluency in Persian and several vernaculars of western India, contributed translations and historical notes to learned journals, and took an active interest in numismatics and inscriptions as aids to recovering regional histories. His papers often bridged the concerns of administrator and antiquary, using coins, chronicles, and temple records to trace dynastic lines and commercial networks across the Gulf of Kachchh and Kathiawar.

During the uprising of 1857–58 he played a coordinating role in the defense and administration of western districts, working to keep the loyalty of allied states and to secure transport routes and coastal towns. Honors followed in the reorganization of the Indian empire, and his long service was recognized with high rank and orders of knighthood. In retirement he arranged his correspondence and reports into a reflective narrative of policy and practice in the West, published after his death as a study of the region before and during the mutinies. The work remains a frequently cited source for the political and intellectual world he helped to shape.

Malaysia Federal Route 1 is the historic north–south backbone of Peninsular Malaysia’s road network, predating the era of modern expressways and binding together a chain of market towns, regional hubs, and state capitals along the peninsula’s western corridor. Administered by the Public Works Department (JKR), it traditionally begins at Kilometre Zero in Johor Bahru and runs to the Thai frontier at Bukit Kayu Hitam in Kedah, where it links with Thailand Route 4. Along its course it serves or provides access to major centres such as Batu Pahat, Segamat, Seremban, Kuala Lumpur, Ipoh, Taiping, Butterworth, Sungai Petani, and Alor Setar, threading through older commercial districts that grew up around the road long before controlled-access highways existed. Many stretches have since been dualled, straightened, or accompanied by town bypasses, yet the route retains the character of a trunk arterial that stitches together diverse local economies.

Constructed in phases under British colonial administration and refined through the post-independence decades, the road played a pivotal role in administrative integration, commerce, and, during the Second World War, the movement of military forces in the Malayan campaign. With the completion of the North–South Expressway in the 1980s and 1990s, long-haul traffic migrated to tolled, limited-access corridors, but Federal Route 1 remained essential: it is toll-free, functions as a strategic redundancy when the expressway is disrupted, and continues to handle dense commuter and intercity flows, particularly on urbanized sections such as Jalan Ipoh and Jalan Kuching in the Kuala Lumpur area and the Skudai corridor in Johor.

Engineering on the route is varied, reflecting its incremental evolution. Older two-lane segments penetrate town centres, while newer links provide four-lane divided carriageways and safer geometry; numerous bridges and river crossings mark state boundaries and floodplains. Speed limits follow standard federal-road practice, and continuous kilometre posts, at-grade junctions, and frequent intersections with other federal and state routes create a fine-grained network that supports roadside commerce. As both a piece of living transport heritage and a practical artery, Federal Route 1 remains embedded in Malaysia’s social and economic landscape.

Reagan v. Farmers’ Loan & Trust Co., decided by the United States Supreme Court in 1894, arose from a challenge to rate schedules promulgated by the Texas Railroad Commission shortly after its creation. A trust company representing railroad bondholders sought to enjoin the commissioners from enforcing maximum freight and passenger rates that, it alleged, were so low as to be confiscatory. Because Texas attached severe penalties to violations, the challengers argued that carriers could not safely test the legality of the schedules without first obtaining equitable relief. The Court held that federal courts had authority to restrain state officers from enforcing unconstitutional regulations, notwithstanding the Eleventh Amendment, when those officers sought to act beyond the limits of valid state power. While the State itself could not be sued, an in personam decree against the commissioners was proper to prevent irreparable injury and to preserve an opportunity for judicial review.

On the merits, the Court affirmed the broad police power of states to regulate common carriers, including the setting of maximum rates, but emphasized constitutional boundaries. A rate that deprives a carrier of a fair return on the value of the property devoted to public use violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The judiciary, therefore, may inquire into the reasonableness of rates fixed by an administrative body, not to substitute its own economic judgments wholesale, but to ensure that the agency has not imposed a schedule that is arbitrary or confiscatory. The decision signaled that due process in rate-making is satisfied if affected parties have meaningful access to courts to test reasonableness, even when the administrative process itself lacks trial-type procedures. Reagan became an important precursor to later doctrines governing suits against state officials and the substantive standards for reviewing public-utility and railroad rates, anticipating both the fair-return approach elaborated in subsequent cases and the enforcement-limiting principle more fully articulated in Ex parte Young.

Animal agriculture affects the environment through the rearing of livestock and the production of their feed. The scale and nature of these effects vary with the species, production system, and local conditions. Grazing occupies large areas of land, some of which are unsuitable for growing crops, while intensive pig and poultry operations rely heavily on cultivated feed. Where forests, savannas, or other natural habitats are converted to pasture or cropland, the resulting loss of habitat can reduce biodiversity and release carbon stored in vegetation and soils. Grazing can also help maintain some open habitats, although heavy grazing may compact soil, increase erosion, and alter plant communities.

Greenhouse gas emissions arise from several stages of livestock production. Cattle, sheep, and other ruminants produce methane as microorganisms digest feed in their digestive systems. Stored manure can emit methane, while manure and fertilizers applied to soils can release nitrous oxide. Carbon dioxide emissions come from land-use change and from energy used in producing feed, operating farms, and processing products. Beef and lamb generally have higher greenhouse gas emissions per unit of protein than pork or poultry, although estimates vary among producers and depend partly on how land-use change and other sources are accounted for.

Water use is associated mainly with feed production, particularly where crops are irrigated. Its local impact depends on how much water is available and whether production competes with other users or with the needs of aquatic ecosystems. Runoff from fertilized fields and livestock operations can carry nitrogen and phosphorus into waterways, promoting algal blooms and depleting dissolved oxygen as the algae decompose. Measures such as matching manure applications to crop nutrient needs and maintaining vegetated buffers along waterways can reduce these losses. Measures aimed at one impact do not necessarily reduce others: raising more animals on less land, for example, can concentrate manure in areas with too little cropland to absorb its nutrients.

Ziapelta is a genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of the San Juan Basin in northwestern New Mexico, United States. The type and only named species, Ziapelta sanjuanensis, was described in 2014 from fossils recovered in the De-na-zin Member of the Kirtland Formation, a sequence of fluvial mudstones and sandstones deposited during the late Campanian. Its generic name references the Zia sun symbol of New Mexico combined with the Latin pelta, “small shield,” alluding to the animal’s armor, while the species epithet honors San Juan County, where the remains were discovered. The holotype includes a well-preserved skull and associated armor elements, providing rare detail on cranial ornamentation in a southern Laramidian ankylosaurid.

As an ankylosaurine, Ziapelta was a low-slung, quadrupedal herbivore protected by a mosaic of bony osteoderms, including heavy plates across the neck and back. The skull is densely sheathed in fused dermal bones that form discrete polygonal tiles and pronounced horns at the rear corners, and it bears a distinctive pattern of sculpturing and grooves that separates it from contemporaneous ankylosaurids. Phylogenetic analyses place Ziapelta within Ankylosauridae and suggest close affinities to northern Laramidian taxa such as Euoplocephalus and Scolosaurus rather than to the geographically proximate Nodocephalosaurus, another ankylosaurid known from the Kirtland Formation. This unexpected relationship highlights the complex biogeography of armored dinosaurs on the western landmass of North America during the Campanian.

The De-na-zin Member records humid floodplain ecosystems along the western shore of the Western Interior Seaway, and Ziapelta lived among a diverse dinosaur fauna that included ceratopsians, hadrosaurids, and theropods. Its presence contributes to evidence for latitudinal faunal provinciality in Laramidia, with distinct northern and southern assemblages that nonetheless experienced episodic interchange. Ziapelta enriches the sparse ankylosaurid record of the American Southwest and provides anatomical data crucial for resolving ankylosaurine relationships, cranial evolution, and the timing and routes of dispersal across Campanian North America.

Martha Wadsworth Brewster was a New England poet active in the mid-eighteenth century whose Poems on Divers Subjects, issued in New London in 1757, stands among the earliest single-author volumes of poetry by a woman printed in British North America. Little is securely known about her life beyond the kinship networks and occasions her poems themselves document; the title page and dedications suggest a writer grounded in provincial social circles that connected clergy, merchants, and extended families, and the verse repeatedly situates her within the moral and devotional rhythms of Congregational New England. The collection ranges widely in form and topic—elegies, epithalamia, scriptural paraphrases, panegyrics, and brief meditative pieces—often written to mark specific local events such as deaths, marriages, and public fasts. Brewster frequently deploys acrostics that encode the names of addressees, a fashionable device in colonial occasional verse that at once personalizes her poems and hints at the patronage economy surrounding their circulation.

The prefatory matter and several poems engage the paradoxes of female authorship in a culture that prized modesty, rehearsing the conventional disclaimers of unlearnedness even as they claim a public, printed voice. Brewster’s lines blend neoclassical couplets and emblematic imagery with the cadences of devotional prose, and they exhibit the mnemonic clarity of hymnody while also venturing into topical commentary shaped by providentialist reading of news and nature. The book’s material history—a likely subscription model, a regional printer’s imprint, and a roster of named recipients—has attracted historians of early American print who read it as evidence for women’s negotiated participation in colonial literary markets.

Though overshadowed in later canon formation by Anne Bradstreet and by posthumously edited figures such as Jane Colman Turell, Brewster has drawn renewed attention for the way her volume preserves a female-authored archive of community life and sentiment. Its mixture of intimate address and public exhortation illuminates how provincial poetics, religious feeling, and social obligation intertwined in mid-eighteenth-century New England.

Vrioni began his career with Matelica, a club in Italy’s Marche region, before joining Sampdoria’s youth system in 2015. He gained his first experience in senior football on loan at Pistoiese in Serie C during the 2017–18 season. Further loans took him to Venezia and Cittadella in Serie B. In January 2020, he joined Juventus and was assigned to the club’s under-23 side, which competed in Serie C. He made his Serie A debut on 1 August 2020, coming on as a substitute in a 3–1 defeat by Roma on the final day of the league season.

Juventus loaned Vrioni to Austrian Bundesliga club WSG Tirol for the 2021–22 season. He scored 19 league goals, finishing level with Red Bull Salzburg’s Karim Adeyemi at the top of the division’s scoring chart. In July 2022, Vrioni moved to Major League Soccer, signing for the New England Revolution as a Designated Player. He joined the club midway through the season, following the departure of fellow striker Adam Buksa. In the 2023 Leagues Cup, Vrioni scored a hat-trick in New England’s 5–1 group-stage victory over Mexican club Atlético San Luis. He remained with the Revolution through the 2024 season and was traded to CF Montréal in January 2025.

Born in San Severino Marche, Italy, Vrioni represented Italy at youth level before switching his international allegiance to Albania, for which he was eligible through his family. He played for Albania’s under-21 team before making his senior debut on 14 October 2018, two days after his twentieth birthday. He came on as a substitute in a UEFA Nations League match against Israel in Beersheba, which Albania lost 2–0. His senior international debut thus came while he was on loan at Venezia, nearly two years before his first appearance in Italy’s top flight.

Robert Spottiswood (also Spottiswoode or Spotswood) was a Scottish jurist and royal official whose career traced the fracture lines of the seventeenth-century kingdoms. The younger son of John Spottiswood, archbishop of St Andrews and chancellor of Scotland, he was educated in Scotland and England and pursued legal study on the Continent before being admitted to the Scottish bar. He rose quickly in crown service and was appointed a lord of session, taking the territorial judicial title Lord Newabbey. A trusted adviser to Charles I, he was advanced to the presidency of the Court of Session in the 1630s, where his judgements and administrative reforms reflected both technical command of Scots law and a firm attachment to royal authority.

That attachment set him at odds with the Covenanting movement after 1637. Spottiswood defended episcopacy and the prerogatives of the king, positions that became untenable as the Glasgow Assembly and subsequent revolutionary committees displaced royal officers. Removed from the bench and proscribed, he joined the king at Oxford during the Wars of the Three Kingdoms and served as secretary of state for Scotland in the royalist shadow administration. Acting as a civil official rather than a field commander, he nevertheless became entangled with the fortunes of the royalist army under Montrose. Captured in the aftermath of defeat, and found carrying commissions that attested to his continuing service to Charles, he was tried by the Committee of Estates and executed in early 1646. His scaffold address, circulated soon after, stressed obedience to conscience, the laws of the realm, and the person of the monarch.

Spottiswood’s enduring reputation rests on his learning. His Practicks of the Law of Scotland, compiled from long experience on the bench and in council and published posthumously, became a valued repertory of decisions and maxims. Jurists later praised its clear Latinity, careful citation, and snapshot of legal doctrine before the upheavals of mid-century, seeing in it both a monument to a lost order and a foundation for the restoration of legal continuity.

Healthcare in Chennai is provided by a combination of government hospitals, municipal health centres, private institutions and charitable facilities. As the capital of Tamil Nadu, the city serves as a referral centre for patients from across the state and from neighbouring states. Its large private hospitals also receive patients from overseas, particularly for cardiac surgery, orthopaedic procedures and organ transplantation.

The city’s public hospital system developed around institutions established during the colonial period. The Government General Hospital, now known as the Rajiv Gandhi Government General Hospital, traces its origins to a hospital founded in 1664 to treat soldiers of the British East India Company. It is affiliated with Madras Medical College and provides specialist care as well as clinical training. Stanley Medical College and Kilpauk Medical College also operate major government teaching hospitals. Specialist institutions include the Institute of Child Health and Hospital for Children in Egmore and the Cancer Institute in Adyar, a charitable institution founded in 1954.

Primary care within the city is delivered in part through urban primary health centres administered by the Greater Chennai Corporation. These centres provide outpatient consultations, maternal and child health services, and routine immunisation. The corporation also carries out public health functions such as disease surveillance and mosquito control. More complex cases are referred to larger hospitals, many of which provide services at low or no direct cost to patients.

The expansion of private hospital care accelerated in the late twentieth century. Apollo Hospitals opened its first hospital in Chennai in 1983, and the city subsequently became a centre for private multispecialty care. Private hospitals have contributed to the growth of medical tourism, while public hospitals continue to handle large outpatient and inpatient caseloads. Access to care varies with household income and location, and the concentration of specialist services in large hospitals can require patients from peripheral areas to travel considerable distances.

*Mistborn: The Final Empire* is a fantasy novel by American author Brandon Sanderson, published by Tor Books in 2006. The first volume of the original *Mistborn* trilogy, it was followed by *The Well of Ascension* (2007) and *The Hero of Ages* (2008). The novel combines elements of epic fantasy and the heist story, following a band of thieves who plan to overthrow an apparently immortal ruler.

The story takes place on Scadrial, a world where ash regularly falls from the sky and mysterious mists cover the land at night. For a thousand years, the Lord Ruler has governed the Final Empire, maintaining a social order in which the nobility exploits a vast laboring population known as the skaa. Kelsier, a thief who survived imprisonment in the empire’s most notorious labor camp, assembles a crew to undermine the regime. Among his recruits is Vin, a young street thief who has unknowingly used magic to survive. While Kelsier trains her, Vin assumes the identity of a noblewoman to gather information and encourage rivalries between the great houses. Her friendship with the nobleman Elend Venture complicates her understanding of the society she has been recruited to subvert.

Central to the novel is Allomancy, a system of magic in which practitioners ingest and “burn” metals to produce specific effects. Some metals enhance physical abilities or senses, while others allow users to influence emotions or push and pull on nearby sources of metal. Most Allomancers can burn only one metal and are known as Mistings; those who can use all the Allomantic metals are called Mistborn. Both Vin and Kelsier belong to the latter group. The novel also introduces Feruchemy, a distinct metal-based practice that allows users to store attributes such as strength or memory for later use. The differences between these systems become important to the crew’s investigation of the Lord Ruler’s power.

During his long tenure as a school administrator in Vicksburg, Mississippi, Homer Vernon Cooper became identified with an energetic program of system-wide modernization. He championed stable, centralized budgeting and routine building maintenance at a time when many Southern districts relied on ad hoc appropriations, and he worked with local boards to secure bond issues that financed new classrooms, science facilities, and athletic grounds. Contemporaries credited him with professionalizing record-keeping and pupil accounting, expanding transportation routes that linked outlying neighborhoods to town schools, and encouraging the adoption of standardized courses of study aligned with emerging accreditation norms. He frequently emphasized vocational offerings alongside college-preparatory work, arguing that high schools had to serve the full spectrum of local industry and commerce as well as academic advancement.

Cooper also became a visible figure in regional professional circles, participating in state and Southern conferences where superintendents exchanged models for teacher supervision, salary schedules, and textbook selection. Known for a meticulous command of enrollment and finance data, he preferred incremental reforms that could be sustained through economic cycles, an outlook shaped by the fiscal pressures of the Depression and wartime scarcity. Like other white administrators of his era in Mississippi, he supervised schools within a legally segregated system; his leadership was thus entwined with policies that maintained racially separate facilities and faculty assignments, even as national litigation and federal oversight increasingly pressed districts to dismantle dual structures.

A large white high school erected in the mid-twentieth century carried Cooper’s name, reflecting the esteem in which local civic leaders held his administrative record. In subsequent decades, as federal court orders accelerated desegregation, the campus and its successor institutions were reorganized and retitled, and the honorific designation faded from everyday use. Later assessments of Cooper’s career have tended to underscore this dual legacy: efficient stewardship and expanded educational amenities for many pupils, set against the constraints and inequities of a segregated framework that his administration, like many of its time, helped sustain.

Transportation in Saskatchewan reflects vast distances, a dispersed population, and an export-oriented resource economy. Highways form the backbone of mobility, anchored by the east–west Trans-Canada Highway (1) and the Yellowhead Highway (16), with Highway 11 linking Regina and Saskatoon onward toward Prince Albert and Highway 39 providing a major route to the United States at North Portal. An extensive lattice of paved and gravel secondary and “grid” roads serves farms and small towns, while severe winters, blowing snow, and spring thaw restrictions strongly influence maintenance, routing, and heavy-haul logistics. Trucking dominates domestic freight movement and interfaces with rail at elevator and transload sites.

Railways remain critical for long-haul bulk shipments. Canadian National and Canadian Pacific operate transcontinental mainlines across the province, moving grain, canola products, potash, and manufactured goods to ports at Vancouver and Prince Rupert and to U.S. markets. After widespread branch-line rationalization, a network of short lines—such as Great Western Railway, Great Sandhills Railway, and Last Mountain Railway—preserves service to rural elevators and industrial shippers. Passenger service is limited to VIA Rail’s Canadian, which makes scheduled stops including Saskatoon and Melville.

Air transport connects major centres and remote northern communities. Saskatoon John G. Diefenbaker International and Regina International handle scheduled carriers, cargo, and general aviation, complemented by regional airports and aerodromes across the province. In the boreal north, where lakes and muskeg impede road building, scheduled turboprops, floatplanes in summer, ski-equipped aircraft in winter, and medevac services provide essential links. Seasonal winter roads extend limited ground access to isolated settlements and mining sites.

Urban transit is provided primarily by municipal bus systems in Saskatoon, Regina, and several smaller cities, with paratransit for riders with disabilities. Intercity bus service contracted sharply after the provincially owned Saskatchewan Transportation Company ceased operations in 2017, leaving a patchwork of private and nonprofit providers. Pipelines carry crude oil and natural gas across Saskatchewan to refineries and export hubs, while navigable inland waterways play only a minor role. Logistics is increasingly consolidated at inland intermodal facilities, notably the Global Transportation Hub near Regina.

The by-election in West Tyrone was triggered by the resignation of Sinn Féin MP Barry McElduff in January 2018 after a social media video, posted on the anniversary of the Kingsmill killings, prompted widespread criticism and cross-community condemnation. The poll was held on 3 May 2018, coinciding with local elections in parts of Great Britain but not in Northern Ireland. Campaigning took place against the backdrop of political stalemate at Stormont and ongoing negotiations around Brexit, with the Irish border and future trading arrangements looming large in local debate. Parties also emphasised constituency concerns, including rural services, jobs, and health provision in the Omagh and Strabane area.

Sinn Féin selected Orfhlaith Begley, a young solicitor from the area, to defend the seat. The Democratic Unionist Party, the Social Democratic and Labour Party, and the Ulster Unionist Party all contested, alongside smaller parties and independents, producing a broad field but essentially a familiar nationalist–unionist contest. While the campaign was hard fought, candidates generally acknowledged the sensitivities that had led to the vacancy, and issues of respect for victims and standards in public life featured alongside the core constitutional questions.

Sinn Féin held the constituency with a comfortable margin, as Begley secured a clear plurality of the vote amid the lower turnout typical of by-elections. Her victory consolidated the party’s strong position in a seat it had held since 2001, and she became the first woman to represent West Tyrone at Westminster as well as one of the youngest MPs returned from Northern Ireland in recent decades. In line with Sinn Féin policy, she did not take her seat in the House of Commons, so the result had no effect on parliamentary arithmetic in London. Analysts viewed the outcome as evidence of continuity rather than a realignment in local politics, with unionist and nationalist vote shares broadly tracking recent general election patterns, and with Brexit-related uncertainty reinforcing existing party loyalties rather than reshaping them.

“America First” refers to a recurring strain in United States politics that calls for giving American national interests priority in foreign and economic policy. The phrase has been used by politicians and movements with different objectives, and it does not denote a single doctrine. In some periods it has been associated with opposition to military involvement abroad; in others it has been used to advocate protective tariffs, restrictions on immigration, or a greater willingness to act without the support of international institutions.

Woodrow Wilson used the phrase while defending American neutrality in the early years of World War I. The United States entered the war in 1917, however, and Wilson later championed the creation of the League of Nations. The slogan became closely associated with noninterventionism through the America First Committee, founded in 1940 to oppose U.S. entry into World War II. Its supporters included people from across the political spectrum, but its most prominent spokesman, aviator Charles Lindbergh, drew widespread criticism for a 1941 speech in which he singled out Jews, along with the British and the Roosevelt administration, as groups pressing the country toward war. The committee disbanded after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor.

Donald Trump revived the slogan during his 2016 presidential campaign and made it a theme of his inaugural address in January 2017. His first administration invoked it in withdrawing from the Trans-Pacific Partnership, renegotiating the North American Free Trade Agreement, and pressing NATO allies to spend more on defense. These policies did not amount to a rejection of all international cooperation: the administration remained in NATO and replaced NAFTA with a new agreement involving the same three countries. Supporters described the approach as a correction to arrangements they regarded as unfavorable to the United States, while critics argued that it strained alliances and weakened American influence abroad.

Hoc Mazarin belonged to the family of card games in which players try to empty their hands by laying cards in sequence rather than by winning tricks. It was one of several French games known as hoc, a name also applied to distinct forms played at Lyon and Bordeaux. The Mazarin form was traditionally associated with Cardinal Jules Mazarin, chief minister during the minority of Louis XIV. The name preserves that association, although it does not establish that the cardinal invented the game.

In play, a card laid on the table called for the next higher card of the same suit. The sequence could thus pass from one player to another, depending on who held the required card. A sequence stopped when the next card was unavailable, either because it had already been played or because it was not in any player's hand. The player who had laid the last card could then start a new sequence. This feature placed a premium on remembering which cards had appeared: a card that would ordinarily pass the play to another hand could become a means of retaining the lead.

The special cards known as hocs included the four kings, the queen of spades and the jack of diamonds. They had privileges beyond those of ordinary cards and were associated with payments in counters. These payments gave particular cards a value independent of their usefulness in getting rid of a hand. The game therefore combined the race to go out with a separate interest in when and how the privileged cards could be played.

Hoc Mazarin is usually classified among the stops games, a group that includes the later Newmarket. The defining resemblance lies in the interruption of ascending sequences: control of play depends not simply on holding high cards, but on knowing where a run is likely to end.

The Pisano period of a positive integer \(m\), denoted by \(\pi(m)\), is the length of the repeating cycle of the Fibonacci sequence reduced modulo \(m\). The sequence begins with \(F_0=0\) and \(F_1=1\), and each subsequent term is the sum of the preceding two. For \(m>1\), the period is the least positive index \(n\) for which \(F_n\equiv 0\) and \(F_{n+1}\equiv 1\pmod m\). A return to zero alone does not mark the start of a new cycle: modulo 3, for instance, the first return to zero occurs at \(F_4\), but the pair \(0,1\) does not recur until \(F_8,F_9\). Thus \(\pi(3)=8\).

The repetition begins at the first term rather than after an initial nonrepeating segment. This follows by considering consecutive pairs of residues. The recurrence takes a pair \((a,b)\) to \((b,a+b)\), and the preceding pair can be recovered as \((b-a,a)\). The recurrence therefore permutes the finite set of \(m^2\) possible pairs, so the starting pair must lie on a cycle. In particular, the period is at most \(m^2\).

For relatively prime moduli, the Chinese remainder theorem links their periods: if \(a\) and \(b\) are coprime, then \(\pi(ab)\) is the least common multiple of \(\pi(a)\) and \(\pi(b)\). The starting pair returns modulo \(ab\) exactly when it returns simultaneously modulo both factors. For example, the periods modulo 2 and modulo 5 are 3 and 20, respectively, so the last digits of the Fibonacci numbers repeat every 60 terms. More generally, factoring a modulus reduces the determination of its period to the periods of its prime-power factors. The name refers to Leonardo of Pisa, better known as Fibonacci, who presented the sequence in his *Liber Abaci*.

The European Union Mission in Armenia (EUMA) is an unarmed civilian mission established under the European Union’s Common Security and Defence Policy. At the invitation of the Armenian government, the Council of the European Union established the mission on 23 January 2023, and it began operations on 20 February. Its mandate is to contribute to stability in areas affected by the conflict along the Armenian–Azerbaijani border, improve human security and support efforts to build confidence between the two countries. Its personnel patrol and report on conditions from the Armenian side of the border; the mission has no executive or enforcement powers.

EUMA followed a temporary EU monitoring deployment agreed at a meeting of Armenian and Azerbaijani leaders with European representatives in Prague in October 2022. The European Union Monitoring Capacity in Armenia drew personnel from the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia and operated for two months, ending in December 2022. The subsequent mission was established with an initial two-year mandate and a headquarters in Yeghegnadzor. Its field offices allow observers to patrol different sections of the border and speak with residents about how security conditions affect daily life.

In December 2023, the EU decided to increase the mission’s authorized staffing from 138 to 209, allowing it to expand its patrols. In January 2025, the Council extended the mandate until 19 February 2027 and allocated more than €44 million for the additional two years. Armenia has welcomed the deployment, while Azerbaijan has criticized it. The EU describes the mission as impartial and distinguishes its work from the diplomatic negotiations between the two countries. Although its observations inform EU assessments of the security situation, the mission does not determine the course of the international boundary or take part in the bilateral process of delimiting it.

A Pyle stop is a brief pause made during a diver’s ascent at a depth greater than that of the first decompression stop called for by the original dive schedule. It is named after Richard Pyle, an ichthyologist who collected fish on deep reefs. During ascent, he sometimes paused to vent gas from the fishes’ swim bladders as it expanded with falling pressure. Pyle reported feeling less fatigued after dives on which he made these pauses than after otherwise comparable dives on which he did not. This observation prompted him to describe a systematic way of adding deep stops, although his experience did not establish whether the stops reduced the risk of decompression sickness.

In Pyle’s procedure, the first pause was placed halfway between the maximum depth of the dive and the first scheduled decompression stop. If more than about 9 metres (30 feet) separated the pause from the scheduled stop, another was placed halfway across the remaining interval. The process could be repeated until the gap was small enough. The pauses generally lasted only a few minutes. Pyle also called for recalculating the decompression schedule to account for the extra time spent at depth, rather than simply inserting the pauses and leaving the rest of the ascent unchanged.

Deep stops were proposed as a way to limit the growth of gas bubbles early in the ascent. A competing consideration is that some tissues may still be absorbing inert gas at depths where other tissues have begun to release it. In a controlled U.S. Navy study, a schedule that shifted more of a fixed decompression time to deeper stops produced more cases of decompression sickness than a schedule that concentrated stops at shallower depths. That comparison did not directly test Pyle’s procedure; it showed that the distribution of stop time, as well as its total duration, can affect decompression risk.

Claudio Uberti is an Argentine former government official best known for his tenure as head of the national road concession regulator, the Organismo de Control de Concesiones Viales (OCCOVI), during the administration of Néstor Kirchner. As a close aide to Planning Minister Julio De Vido, he played a visible role in the renegotiation of toll-road and corridor concessions following the 2001–02 economic crisis, when the state sought to recalibrate tariffs, investment schedules, and contract terms with private operators. From 2004 he also served as an informal liaison in the fast-expanding relationship with Venezuela, taking part in mixed commissions and business missions connected to energy and infrastructure deals.

In August 2007 Uberti left office in the wake of the so‑called suitcase scandal, which erupted when Argentine customs seized nearly US$800,000 from a passenger arriving on a chartered flight from Caracas. Media and court records in both countries linked the trip to official delegations; Uberti was reported to have coordinated aspects of the mission, and the executive branch requested his resignation. Subsequent proceedings in the United States resulted in convictions of individuals accused of acting on behalf of Venezuelan officials to conceal the origin and destination of the funds. In Argentina, investigations examined possible administrative irregularities and illicit enrichment; Uberti denied wrongdoing, and litigation moved slowly amid jurisdictional disputes and appeals.

A decade later he reemerged in the sprawling “cuadernos” corruption inquiry. In 2018 he provided testimony as a collaborating defendant under Argentina’s plea-bargain statute, describing alleged delivery of cash from contractors to senior officials in connection with public works and concession oversight. Prosecutors cited his statements alongside those of other witnesses and documentary evidence, while defense attorneys challenged the accounts. As with several high-profile graft cases from the Kirchner era, judicial outcomes remained unsettled into the mid‑2020s.

Basuki Hadimuljono was born in Surakarta, Central Java, on 5 November 1954. He studied geological engineering at Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta and went on to earn a master’s degree and a doctorate in civil engineering from Colorado State University in the United States. He spent more than three decades as a civil servant in Indonesia’s Ministry of Public Works, holding posts in research and development, internal oversight, and spatial planning before entering the cabinet.

President Joko Widodo appointed Basuki minister of public works and housing in October 2014 and retained him for his second term in 2019. Basuki held the post until October 2024. The ministry was responsible for national roads, water resources, and public housing, among other areas, and played a central role in Widodo’s infrastructure program. During Basuki’s tenure, Indonesia expanded its toll-road network, including the Trans-Java corridor, and built dams intended to supply water and support irrigation. The ministry also oversaw the construction of roads, water systems, and government buildings at Nusantara, the planned new capital in East Kalimantan.

In June 2024, while still serving as minister, Basuki was named acting head of the Nusantara Capital Authority following the resignation of its inaugural head, Bambang Susantono. In November, after leaving the cabinet, he was sworn in as head of the authority by President Prabowo Subianto. The appointment shifted his responsibilities from overseeing public works nationwide to administering the development of the new capital, a role that included coordinating infrastructure work and seeking investment for the city.

Outside his administrative duties, Basuki became known for playing the drums at public events. He also attracted attention at the 2022 Group of Twenty summit in Bali, where he was photographed carrying a camera and taking pictures alongside members of the press.

Paola is a town and comune in the province of Cosenza, on the Tyrrhenian coast of Calabria in southern Italy. Its built-up area extends from the seafront to the lower slopes of the Coastal Range, which separates this stretch of shoreline from the valley of the Crati. The older part of the town occupies higher ground, where narrow streets and stairways connect small squares and churches. The railway station and the more recent seaside districts lie on the coastal strip below.

The town is best known as the birthplace of Francis of Paola (1416–1507), founder of the religious order of the Minims. As a young man, Francis withdrew to live as a hermit near Paola, where he attracted followers and established a community.
