It was during the severe epidemic of puerperal fever that swept through Aberdeen between 1789 and 1792 that Gordon made the observations which would secure his lasting place in the history of medicine. Puerperal fever, also known as childbed fever, was a devastating and frequently fatal condition afflicting women in the days following childbirth, and its causes remained deeply obscure to contemporary practitioners. Gordon kept meticulous records of every case he encountered during the epidemic and in 1795 published his findings in a work entitled A Treatise on the Epidemic Puerperal Fever of Aberdeen. In this remarkable text he argued, on the basis of careful epidemiological analysis, that the disease was contagious and that it was transmitted directly from one patient to another by the hands and clothing of the midwives and physicians who attended them. He mapped the cases across the city and demonstrated a clear pattern linking each outbreak to specific attendants, concluding with striking candour that he himself had carried the infection to a number of his own patients.

Gordon's conclusions anticipated by several decades the better-known work of Ignaz Semmelweis and Oliver Wendell Holmes on the same subject. His insistence on the contagious nature of the disease and the responsibility of medical attendants in its spread was both intellectually courageous and professionally damaging, as the implication that practitioners were themselves agents of death provoked considerable hostility among his colleagues.

iAudio is a brand of portable digital audio players manufactured by the South Korean consumer electronics company Cowon Systems, also known as Cowon. The brand gained recognition in the mid-2000s as a competitive alternative to mainstream players such as the Apple iPod, distinguishing itself through superior audio quality, broad file format support, and long battery life. Cowon positioned iAudio devices as premium offerings for audiophiles and music enthusiasts who prioritized sound fidelity over the ecosystem integration that characterized competing products.

The iAudio product line has encompassed a wide range of devices across multiple form factors, from slim flash-based players to larger hard-disk-driven units capable of storing extensive music libraries. Models such as the iAudio X5 and iAudio 7 earned particular praise from reviewers and dedicated user communities for their ability to play lossless audio formats including FLAC and OGG Vorbis at a time when many rival manufacturers restricted playback to MP3 and AAC files. This commitment to open and lossless format compatibility became a defining characteristic of the brand's identity.

Cowon's proprietary BBE sound enhancement technology, along with customizable equalizer settings, allowed iAudio users to tailor their listening experience with a degree of precision uncommon among portable devices of comparable price points. Battery longevity represented another area in which iAudio players frequently outperformed competitors, with certain models achieving playback times that exceeded fifty hours under standard conditions. These attributes cultivated a loyal following, particularly in online audio enthusiast communities where technical specifications were discussed in considerable detail.

As the broader market for dedicated portable audio players contracted following the widespread adoption of smartphones, Cowon continued to release new iAudio models targeting the remaining segment of consumers who preferred standalone devices. The brand maintained its reputation for audio quality and format versatility, sustaining relevance within a niche but persistent market.

Insufflation refers broadly to the act of blowing a gas, powder, or vapour into a body cavity or onto a surface, and the term finds application across medicine, pharmacology, religious ritual, and historical practice. In clinical medicine, the procedure is most commonly associated with the introduction of carbon dioxide gas into the abdominal or pelvic cavity during laparoscopic surgery. This technique, known as pneumoperitoneum, creates a working space that allows surgeons to manipulate instruments and visualise internal structures without making large incisions. Specialised devices called insufflators regulate the flow and pressure of the gas, maintaining optimal conditions throughout the procedure to minimise risk to the patient.

Beyond surgical contexts, insufflation has long been employed as a method of drug delivery. Substances in powdered form can be introduced directly into the nasal passages, where the richly vascularised mucous membranes allow for rapid absorption into the bloodstream. This route of administration bypasses first-pass metabolism in the liver, producing comparatively swift pharmacological effects. The nasal insufflation of medicinal snuffs was common in early modern European and indigenous American medical traditions, and the practice informed later pharmaceutical developments in the delivery of antihistamines, corticosteroids, and other compounds through nasal sprays and inhalers.

Historical and theological literature records the symbolic use of insufflation as well. In certain Christian baptismal rites, the officiating clergy would breathe or blow upon the candidate as a gesture of spiritual animation, drawing on the biblical association between breath and the bestowal of life or the Holy Spirit. Similar acts of ritual breathing appear in other religious traditions and magical practices, reinforcing the cross-cultural significance attributed to breath as a vehicle of vital force or divine power. The word itself derives from the Latin insufflare, meaning to blow into, compounded from the prefix in and the verb sufflare, to puff or blow.

The Phelps and Gorham Purchase was a large land transaction completed in 1788 by which Oliver Phelps and Nathaniel Gorham acquired approximately six million acres of territory in western New York from the state of Massachusetts. The arrangement arose from a complicated series of overlapping colonial claims that had long created jurisdictional uncertainty over lands west of the Genesee River. Massachusetts held a preemptive right to purchase the soil from the Indigenous inhabitants under a compromise reached at the Hartford Convention of 1786, by which New York retained political sovereignty over the region while Massachusetts retained the underlying title that could be extinguished only through direct negotiation with the Native peoples who occupied the land.

Phelps and Gorham entered into an agreement with Massachusetts in April 1788, contracting to pay one million dollars in depreciated Massachusetts securities for the entire tract. The two men then moved quickly to negotiate with the Seneca Nation, whose members constituted the principal Indigenous occupants of the territory and whose consent was legally necessary to validate any transfer. A treaty concluded at Buffalo Creek in July 1788 resulted in the Seneca ceding the eastern portion of the purchase, roughly two and a half million acres lying east of the Genesee River together with a narrow strip to the west. However, the Seneca declined to part with the remaining western lands at that time, and Phelps and Gorham found themselves unable to meet their financial obligations for the full acreage. They consequently returned the unextinguished western portion to Massachusetts in 1790, retaining only the land they had successfully cleared of Native title.

The portion the partners retained was subsequently surveyed and opened to settlement, with the town of Canandaigua emerging as an early center of administration and commerce. Phelps in particular devoted considerable energy to promoting emigration from New England into the newly available lands, contributing to the rapid transformation of the region's demographic and economic character during the final decade of the eighteenth century.

The novel follows the intertwined fates of three families living on opposite sides of a mountain range that serves as both a geographical and ideological boundary in a fictitious Central European country during the turbulent decades between the two world wars. The author, drawing heavily on her own family's displacement during the 1930s, constructs a narrative in which the physical landscape becomes inseparable from the psychological states of her characters. The mountain pass that connects the two valleys is open only during certain seasons, and this enforced periodicity of contact shapes the rhythms of love, betrayal, and reconciliation that drive the plot forward.

Critics have noted that the novel's structure mirrors its thematic concerns with unusual precision. Each of the three sections is narrated from a different altitude, beginning in the lowland towns where commerce and politics hold sway, ascending through the forested middle slopes where the novel's most ambiguous moral encounters take place, and culminating in the high meadows where language itself seems to thin out and the characters are left with gesture and silence. This vertical architecture has been read as an allegory of social class, of spiritual aspiration, and of the difficulty of achieving any stable perspective on historical events while one is still living through them.

The title refers not only to the literal darkness that descends over the mountain communities during the long winter months but also to the broader sense of a civilization dividing against itself, unable to maintain the connections that once seemed permanent and self-evident. The recurring image of lanterns carried across the pass in darkness, which opens and closes the novel, has become one of the more discussed symbols in the literature of the period, suggesting simultaneously the fragility and the stubborn persistence of human effort to reach across dividing distances.

The by-election was held on 1 March 2018 to fill the vacancy in the Westminster constituency of West Tyrone created by the resignation of Barry McElduff, who had stepped down from his seat following a controversy in which he had posted a video on social media on the anniversary of the Kingsmill massacre. McElduff, a Sinn Féin member of Parliament, had been holding a loaf of Kingsmill bread on his head in the footage, an act widely condemned as deeply offensive to the families of the victims of the 1976 atrocity. He initially apologised and took a brief leave of absence from his party duties before ultimately tendering his resignation from Parliament in February 2018.

Sinn Féin selected Órfhlaith Begley as its candidate for the by-election. Begley, a councillor on Derry City and Strabane District Council, was considered a strong choice for the party given the constituency's strongly nationalist character. As had long been the established practice of Sinn Féin members elected to Westminster, she made clear that she would not take her seat in the House of Commons if elected, in keeping with the party's abstentionist policy. The Ulster Unionist Party, the Social Democratic and Labour Party, and several smaller parties and independent candidates also contested the election.

The result was a comfortable victory for Begley, who secured the seat with a substantial majority over her nearest rival. The turnout was considerably lower than at the preceding general election, a pattern commonly observed in parliamentary by-elections. Begley's election was seen as a consolidation of Sinn Féin's hold over the constituency, which the party had represented since 2001. Commentators noted that the by-election had taken place against the backdrop of the continuing collapse of the devolved institutions at Stormont, with the Northern Ireland Assembly having been without a functioning executive since January 2017.

Federal Route 1 is the longest federal road in Malaysia, stretching approximately 500 kilometres from the Thai border in the north to the causeway linking Johor Bahru with Singapore in the south. Running along the western side of Peninsular Malaysia, the route passes through or near many of the country's most significant urban centres, including Alor Setar, Ipoh, Kuala Lumpur, and Seremban, before continuing southward through Melaka and into Johor. The road has historically served as the primary overland artery connecting the peninsula from one end to the other, and its development closely mirrors the broader story of infrastructure growth and economic modernisation in Malaysia during the twentieth century.

The origins of the route can be traced to the colonial era, when British administrators recognised the need for a reliable road network to facilitate the movement of troops, administrators, and commercial goods between the federated and unfederated Malay states. Early stretches were often unpaved and prone to seasonal disruption, but incremental improvements through the mid-century transformed the corridor into a metalled all-weather highway. The construction of the North–South Expressway from the 1980s onwards provided motorists with a faster alternative for long-distance travel, yet Federal Route 1 retained its importance as a local connector serving towns and settlements that lie away from the expressway interchanges.

The road passes through a diverse landscape, beginning in the flat rice paddies of Kedah before descending into the tin-mining valleys of Perak and entering the densely populated Klang Valley. South of Kuala Lumpur the highway traverses rolling plantation terrain where oil palm and rubber estates dominate the countryside. Sections of the route within major urban areas, particularly in Kuala Lumpur, have been upgraded and widened over the decades and are now integrated into the city's complex arterial road network, often carrying names such as Jalan Ipoh or Jalan Cheras depending on the direction of travel.

The Gold Coast's relationship with Australian rules football stretches back to the late nineteenth century, when the game began spreading northward from its Victorian heartland into Queensland. Early matches were played on rough, often sun-baked ovals by communities of Victorian and South Australian migrants who had carried their sporting loyalties with them as they moved north in search of work and opportunity. By the early twentieth century, district competitions had taken root in the region, though these were modest affairs operating under constant pressure from the dominant rugby codes that commanded far greater public support across Queensland more broadly.

The postwar decades brought significant demographic change to the Gold Coast as the region transformed from a quiet seaside destination into one of Australia's fastest growing urban centres. Migrants from Victoria and South Australia arrived in considerable numbers throughout the 1950s and 1960s, bringing renewed enthusiasm for the game and swelling the ranks of local clubs. Junior competitions expanded noticeably during this period, and the Gold Coast Amateur Football League worked to establish a firmer administrative foundation for the sport across its various districts. Grounds were gradually improved, volunteer networks strengthened, and rivalries between clubs such as Southport and Labrador gave the competition an identity and intensity that began drawing spectators in respectable numbers.

The national competition's arrival on the Gold Coast represented the most transformative moment in the region's football history. After years of lobbying and planning, the Gold Coast Football Club entered the Australian Football League in 2011 under the Suns banner, bringing top-level football to the region for the first time. The franchise was constructed largely through the national draft's father-son and academy systems, designed to build a genuinely local playing group over time. Early seasons proved difficult as the expansion side navigated the considerable challenges typical of newly established clubs, yet attendances at Metricon Stadium demonstrated genuine grassroots appetite for the game among the Gold Coast population.

A thyristor-switched capacitor is a type of reactive power compensation device used in electrical power systems to regulate voltage and improve power factor. It operates by connecting one or more capacitor banks to a transmission or distribution network through pairs of anti-parallel thyristors, which act as electronically controlled switches. Because thyristors can be triggered into conduction at precisely chosen moments within each cycle of the alternating current waveform, the device offers a level of controllability that conventional mechanically switched capacitors cannot match.

The fundamental operating principle relies on the thyristors being fired at the instant when the voltage across the capacitor equals the system voltage, thereby minimizing the transient current that would otherwise accompany an abrupt switching event. When both thyristors in an anti-parallel pair are conducting, the capacitor bank is effectively connected to the network and supplies reactive power. Conversely, when the gate signals are removed, the thyristors cease to conduct at the next natural current zero crossing, disconnecting the capacitor from the system. This natural commutation characteristic means that thyristor-switched capacitors produce relatively low levels of harmonic distortion compared with devices that interrupt current at arbitrary points in the cycle.

In practical installations, several capacitor banks of equal or unequal rating are arranged in parallel branches, each controlled by its own thyristor pair. By selectively switching individual branches into or out of service, the total reactive power output can be varied in discrete steps. The switching speed is typically limited to one half-cycle of the fundamental frequency, which corresponds to approximately ten milliseconds in a fifty-hertz system. This response time is considerably faster than mechanical contactors or circuit breakers, making the thyristor-switched capacitor well suited to applications where load fluctuations are rapid, such as arc furnace compensation or the stabilization of voltage in systems subject to frequent and irregular changes in demand.

Jay Zeamer Jr. was an American military aviator who became one of the most decorated officers of the Second World War, earning the Medal of Honor for an extraordinary mission over the Pacific theater in 1943. Born on July 25, 1918, in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, Zeamer developed an early fascination with aviation and pursued his passion through his studies at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he graduated in 1942 before entering the United States Army Air Forces.

Assigned to the Southwest Pacific theater, Zeamer initially struggled to secure a regular flying assignment, as commanding officers were reluctant to trust him with aircraft due to his unconventional and intensely independent nature. Undeterred, he gradually assembled a volunteer crew of similarly overlooked airmen, and together they adopted and rehabilitated a battered, war-weary Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress that other units had essentially abandoned. Through meticulous personal effort, Zeamer and his crew restored the aircraft to flying condition, outfitting it with an unusually heavy armament configuration that gave it exceptional defensive firepower. The crew flew dozens of dangerous volunteer missions over enemy-held territory, earning a reputation for audacity and skill.

The mission that brought Zeamer his greatest recognition took place on June 16, 1943, when he piloted a photographic reconnaissance flight over Bougainville Island. Shortly after completing the mapping run, the aircraft was intercepted by a large formation of Japanese Zero fighters. In the ferocious engagement that followed, Zeamer was severely wounded, sustaining multiple injuries that left him nearly incapacitated. Despite his condition, he continued to pilot the aircraft, allowing his crew to defend against repeated attacks until the enemy withdrew. His bombardier, Joseph Sarnoski, also received the Medal of Honor posthumously for his actions during the same engagement, making the mission one of only a handful in American history to produce two Medal of Honor recipients simultaneously.

Ansei Uchima was a Japanese American printmaker, painter, and educator whose work played a significant role in introducing and popularizing the traditional Japanese art of mokuhanga, or woodblock printing, to Western audiences during the mid-twentieth century. Born in 1921 in Florin, California, to Japanese immigrant parents, Uchima spent much of his formative years navigating between two distinct cultural worlds, an experience that would profoundly shape both his artistic sensibility and his thematic concerns. Following the attack on Pearl Harbor, he and his family were among the thousands of Japanese Americans forcibly relocated to internment camps under Executive Order 9066, a traumatic chapter that nonetheless deepened his introspective engagement with questions of identity, displacement, and belonging.

After the war, Uchima studied in the United States before traveling to Japan, where he immersed himself in the classical techniques of woodblock printing under masters who had inherited centuries-old traditions of the craft. He became particularly drawn to the subtle gradations of color achievable through mokuhanga, a method that employed water-based inks on carefully prepared woodblocks to produce effects of remarkable delicacy and atmospheric depth. His mature prints are distinguished by their luminous, often ethereal quality, evoking misty landscapes, translucent waters, and abstract forms that resist easy categorization as either purely Eastern or purely Western in spirit.

Uchima went on to teach at the New School for Social Research and later at Sarah Lawrence College, where he became a respected and influential figure among students seeking to learn the technical and philosophical dimensions of Japanese printmaking. His work was exhibited widely throughout the United States, Japan, and Europe, earning him international recognition and numerous awards. He remained dedicated throughout his career to bridging cultural traditions, believing that art could serve as a medium for genuine cross-cultural understanding and dialogue.

Asterias amurensis, commonly known as the northern Pacific seastar or Japanese seastar, is a species of starfish belonging to the family Asteriidae. Native to the coastal waters of northern Japan, China, Korea, and Russia's Far East, the species has attracted considerable scientific and conservation attention owing to its remarkable capacity for invasion and its ecological impacts in regions far beyond its natural range. The animal typically displays five arms radiating from a central disc, though individuals with four or six arms are occasionally encountered. Its coloration varies considerably, ranging from pale yellow and orange to purple or brown, often with mottled or banded patterns along the aboral surface. Adults commonly measure between ten and thirty centimetres in diameter, though larger specimens have been recorded.

The species is a voracious generalist predator, feeding on a broad array of bivalves, gastropods, polychaete worms, barnacles, and other echinoderms. This dietary flexibility is considered a key factor in its success as an invasive organism. Asterias amurensis reproduces through broadcast spawning, releasing eggs and sperm directly into the water column, where fertilization occurs externally. A single female may release in excess of twenty million eggs during a single spawning event, contributing to population explosions under favorable conditions. The planktonic larvae, known as bipinnaria and brachiolaria stages, are capable of surviving for several weeks before settling and undergoing metamorphosis into juvenile seastars.

The species was first introduced to Australian waters, particularly Port Phillip Bay in Victoria, during the late twentieth century, almost certainly via ballast water discharged from vessels originating in Japanese ports. Populations established themselves rapidly in southern Australia, where the absence of natural predators and the abundance of commercial shellfish provided ideal conditions for proliferation. The resulting ecological and economic consequences prompted extensive research into management strategies, including physical removal programs, chemical deterrents, and biological control investigations.

Homer Vernon Cooper was an American civil engineer and bridge designer whose contributions to infrastructure development in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries left a lasting mark on structural engineering practice in the United States. Born in 1839 in Rockport, New York, Cooper received his early education in engineering through a combination of formal study and practical apprenticeship, a common path for technically minded young men of his era. He went on to serve as an officer in the Union Army during the Civil War, gaining experience in military engineering that would inform his later civilian career.

Following the war, Cooper turned his attention to railroad bridge construction, an industry undergoing rapid transformation as American railways expanded westward and demanded ever more robust and standardized structures. He became closely associated with the firm of Carnegie, Phipps and Company and later worked extensively with Andrew Carnegie's steel operations, helping to bring new materials and methods to bridge fabrication. His most enduring intellectual contribution, however, was the development of a standardized system for classifying the loads that railroad bridges must be designed to withstand. Published in 1894, Cooper's load classification system introduced a series of hypothetical locomotive configurations, designated by letter and number combinations, that allowed engineers across the country to design and evaluate bridges against a common benchmark. The system, known informally as Cooper's E loadings, became widely adopted throughout the American railroad industry and remained influential for decades, providing a consistent framework that facilitated both the design of new structures and the assessment of existing ones.

Cooper is perhaps most prominently associated, in a somber sense, with the Quebec Bridge disaster of 1907, in which a partially constructed cantilever span over the Saint Lawrence River collapsed catastrophically, killing seventy-five workers. As consulting engineer on the project, Cooper bore a measure of professional responsibility for the tragedy.

Migliorismo, from the Italian word meaning "meliorism" or more precisely "the tendency toward improvement," refers to a political and ideological current that emerged within the Italian Communist Party during the 1970s and 1980s, associated principally with the reformist wing led by figures such as Giorgio Napolitano. The term described a disposition toward gradualist, pragmatic reform rather than revolutionary transformation, and its adherents were sometimes called miglioristi, a label applied both by supporters as a badge of moderate pride and by critics as a marker of ideological compromise.

The miglioristi distinguished themselves from more orthodox communist factions by their acceptance of parliamentary democracy as a legitimate and permanent framework for political action, rather than as a provisional stage to be superseded. They drew intellectual sustenance from the broader European social democratic tradition, from Antonio Gramsci's conception of cultural and political hegemony, and from a reading of Italian history that emphasized the value of institutional stability. This placed them in frequent tension with the party's left wing, which viewed their accommodating posture toward the established order as a form of capitulation to bourgeois norms and to the influence of Christian Democracy, which had governed Italy almost without interruption since the postwar period.

The concept gained renewed salience during the debates surrounding the dissolution of the Italian Communist Party in 1991 and the subsequent formation of the Democratic Party of the Left. Critics argued that migliorismo represented not merely a tactical adjustment but a fundamental abandonment of socialist purpose, substituting the management of existing conditions for any transformative political vision. Defenders countered that realism about the limits of historical possibility was not defeatism but wisdom, and that incremental improvement in the conditions of working people constituted a genuine and durable form of political achievement. The debate touched on broader questions about the relationship between idealism and pragmatism in left-wing political thought.

Claudio Uberti is an Italian businessman and sports executive who became widely known for his central role in the operations of Internazionale Milano, one of Italy's most prominent football clubs, during the mid-2000s. Working closely alongside Massimo Moratti, the club's owner and president, Uberti served as a key intermediary and commercial director whose responsibilities extended well beyond the conventional boundaries of club administration. His influence touched areas including transfer negotiations, sponsorship arrangements, and the cultivation of international partnerships, making him one of the more powerful behind-the-scenes figures in Italian football during that period.

Uberti came to particular public attention in 2006 when he was implicated in the broader investigation surrounding Italian football governance known as the Calciopoli scandal. Investigators examining alleged irregularities in the designation of match officials uncovered telephone intercepts that placed Uberti in contact with figures connected to the refereeing apparatus. His conversations, along with those involving officials from several other clubs, formed part of the evidence that Italian football authorities and prosecutors used in assessing whether systematic efforts had been made to influence the assignment of referees to competitive fixtures. The scandal resulted in severe sporting sanctions for Juventus and lesser penalties for other clubs, while the precise culpability of individuals and institutions continued to be debated by journalists, legal experts, and supporters for years afterward.

Beyond the controversies of that period, Uberti maintained a professional profile connected to commercial and financial dimensions of sport. His career illustrated the increasingly complex and professionalized nature of football club management in the early twenty-first century, where individuals occupying informal or semi-formal executive positions could exercise considerable influence over both sporting and financial outcomes. His name has remained associated in Italian football discourse primarily with the Calciopoli affair and the turbulent era it represented for the sport's institutional credibility.

Reagan v. Farmers' Loan and Trust Company was a landmark decision handed down by the United States Supreme Court in 1894, arising from a challenge to the rate-setting authority of the Texas Railroad Commission. The case grew out of the commission's establishment of maximum freight and passenger rates on railroads operating within the state of Texas, which the Farmers' Loan and Trust Company, acting as a receiver for several railroad lines, contended were so unreasonably low as to be confiscatory and therefore unconstitutional.

The central legal question before the Court concerned whether a federal court possessed jurisdiction to enjoin the enforcement of state-imposed railroad rates and, more fundamentally, whether the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protected railroad companies from regulations that effectively deprived them of their property by denying them any reasonable return on their investment. John H. Reagan, the first chairman of the Texas Railroad Commission and the case's nominal defendant, argued in defense of the state's broad authority to regulate commerce within its borders, maintaining that the rates were a legitimate exercise of the police power.

Writing for a unanimous Court, Justice David Brewer affirmed that federal courts did indeed have equitable jurisdiction to hear such disputes and to restrain the enforcement of confiscatory rates. The opinion established the significant constitutional principle that while states possess undoubted authority to regulate the rates charged by common carriers, that authority is not unlimited. If the rates fixed by a regulatory body are so low that they deny the company a fair and reasonable compensation for its services, they constitute an unconstitutional taking of private property without due process of law. The ruling thus marked an important boundary between permissible state regulation and regulatory action that crossed into constitutional violation, shaping the subsequent development of utility and railroad rate jurisprudence for decades to come.

George Le Grand Jacob was born in 1805 and pursued a career in the service of the East India Company, rising through the ranks of the Bombay Army to become one of the more influential political officers operating on the northwestern frontiers of British India during the mid-nineteenth century. His long tenure in the region brought him into sustained contact with the complex tribal confederacies and princely states of Kathiawar and Baluchistan, territories where the exercise of British influence depended as much on personal diplomacy and local knowledge as on military force.

Jacob served as Political Superintendent of Southern Maratha Country and later held prominent positions that placed him at the center of negotiations with chiefs whose cooperation was essential to maintaining order along contested frontier zones. He developed a reputation as a thoughtful and sometimes unconventional administrator, one who advocated strongly for policies that he believed would foster genuine stability rather than merely enforce a superficial compliance. His views occasionally brought him into conflict with superiors who favored more coercive approaches, and he was not reluctant to commit his arguments to paper, producing official reports and correspondence that reveal a mind keenly alert to the economic and social grievances that drove instability in the regions under his charge.

Beyond his administrative labors, Jacob was a prolific writer whose published works addressed questions of history, geography, and political philosophy as they pertained to British India. His book on the views and opinions of Major General John Jacob, the distinguished commander of the Scinde Irregular Horse and his own close relation, helped shape how subsequent generations understood that officer's contributions to frontier warfare and civil administration. George Le Grand Jacob retired from active service and died in 1881, leaving behind a body of writing that continued to inform debates about British policy on the subcontinent long after his death.

Ziapelta is an extinct genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 74 to 75 million years ago, in what is now the southwestern United States. The genus is known from a single species, Ziapelta sanjuanensis, whose name references both the Zia sun symbol of New Mexico and the San Juan Basin, the geological formation from which the fossil material was recovered. The holotype specimen was discovered in the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico, a geological unit that has yielded a diverse assemblage of Late Cretaceous fauna.

Ziapelta belongs to the family Ankylosauridae and is characterized by the presence of a prominent tail club, a feature shared with other members of this clade. The skull of Ziapelta displays a number of distinctive osteoderms, the bony skin projections that armored ankylosaurs are well known for, arranged in complex patterns across the cranial surface. Among the most notable anatomical features is the pronounced squamosal horn, a large curved projection located at the rear corners of the skull. These horns are more dramatically curved than those observed in many related genera, contributing to the animal's recognizable appearance and aiding researchers in distinguishing Ziapelta from contemporaneous ankylosaurs found in the same region.

Phylogenetic analyses place Ziapelta within the Ankylosaurinae subfamily, grouping it with derived ankylosaurids from North America and Asia. Its discovery contributed meaningfully to understanding the biogeographic distribution of ankylosaurid dinosaurs during the Campanian stage of the Cretaceous, a time when North America was divided by the Western Interior Seaway into two landmasses. The presence of Ziapelta in the southwestern portion of the continent, known as Appalachia and Laramidia, provided researchers with additional data regarding the evolutionary radiation of armored dinosaurs across these distinct faunal provinces.

Martha Wadsworth Brewster (1710–1757) was an American colonial poet whose work represents one of the earliest known collections of verse published by a woman in British North America. Born in Lebanon, Connecticut, she spent much of her life in that region and drew deeply upon her Puritan faith, her domestic experiences, and the turbulent events of her time to produce poetry that combined religious devotion with a surprisingly personal and sometimes fierce voice.

Her principal publication, Poems on Divers Subjects, appeared in 1757, making her one of a small handful of women in the colonial period to see an original collection of her work through the press. The volume included elegies, meditations, and verse epistles addressed to friends, family members, and figures of public significance. Brewster wrote with evident familiarity with the English literary tradition, drawing on the cadences of earlier poets while shaping her lines to reflect the particularities of New England religious culture. Her elegies in particular demonstrate a formal confidence, moving between grief and consolation with the assurance of a writer who had long regarded verse composition as a serious vocation rather than a casual pastime.

Brewster lived through the period of the French and Indian War, and some of her poems engage with the anxieties that conflict produced among frontier communities in Connecticut. She understood hardship at a personal level as well, having endured illness and the loss of people close to her, and these experiences lend her meditative poems an emotional directness that distinguishes them from more conventional religious verse of the era. Scholars of early American literature have increasingly recognized her contributions as evidence that women's literary production in the colonial period was richer and more varied than older accounts had suggested, placing Brewster within a network of female writers who asserted their voices despite considerable cultural constraints.

Saskatchewan's vast geography and sparse population have shaped a transportation network dominated by road and rail infrastructure, both of which developed primarily to serve the province's agricultural economy. The road system is among the most extensive in Canada relative to population, with tens of thousands of kilometres of paved and gravel roads connecting rural municipalities, small towns, and the two major urban centres of Saskatoon and Regina. Provincial highways radiate outward from these cities in a grid pattern that reflects the original Dominion Land Survey system, allowing efficient movement of grain and other commodities from farm to market. Highway 1, the Trans-Canada Highway, traverses the southern portion of the province and remains the most heavily traveled corridor, linking Saskatchewan to Manitoba in the east and Alberta in the west.

Rail transportation played a foundational role in the settlement and economic development of the province during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The Canadian Pacific Railway established the first major lines through the southern prairies, and subsequent construction by the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk Pacific railways extended service to communities throughout the province. At its peak, Saskatchewan possessed one of the densest rural rail networks on the continent, with branch lines reaching virtually every significant grain-producing area. However, decades of rationalization beginning in the latter half of the twentieth century led to extensive abandonment of branch lines, fundamentally altering rural transportation patterns and placing greater pressure on provincial highways.

Air travel serves both intercity passengers and remote or time-sensitive needs across the province. Regina and Saskatoon operate the principal commercial airports, offering scheduled service to major Canadian cities and select international destinations. A number of smaller regional airports accommodate charter flights, medical evacuations, and general aviation activity in communities where road distances to major centres make air access particularly valuable to residents.

Robert Spottiswood was born in 1596, the eldest son of John Spottiswood, Archbishop of St Andrews and one of the most powerful ecclesiastical figures in early seventeenth-century Scotland. Educated in part through his father's considerable influence, Robert pursued a legal career and rose to prominence during the reign of Charles I, eventually becoming Lord President of the Court of Session in 1633, a position that placed him among the foremost legal officers of the Scottish crown. His appointment reflected both his genuine legal abilities and the broader political ambitions of his father, who was at that time navigating the delicate task of extending royal authority over Scottish religious and civil affairs.

Spottiswood's tenure as Lord President was marked by his close identification with royal policy at a moment of mounting tension between the crown and significant sections of Scottish society. He was a committed supporter of Charles I's programme of ecclesiastical reform, which culminated in the disastrous attempt to impose a new prayer book upon the Church of Scotland in 1637. The resulting popular outrage and the formation of the National Covenant in 1638 fundamentally undermined the position of those, like Spottiswood, who had cast their fortunes with the king. When the Covenanting movement gained ascendancy, he was removed from his judicial office and found himself increasingly marginalized within Scottish public life.

He subsequently followed the royalist cause into exile, accompanying the king's supporters as the conflicts of the Three Kingdoms drew Scotland into prolonged military and political upheaval. Spottiswood spent much of his later years on the Continent, deprived of his estates and offices by the Covenanting regime. He died in 1646, before any prospect of a royalist restoration could be realized, leaving behind him a career that illustrated with particular clarity the precarious fate of those who had bound themselves too tightly to the policies of an embattled monarch.

Livestock production is one of the largest human uses of land on Earth. Pasture and cropland devoted to animal feed together account for roughly three-quarters of all agricultural land, yet animal products supply a considerably smaller share of the world's calories and protein. A widely cited 2018 meta-analysis by Joseph Poore and Thomas Nemecek estimated that meat, aquaculture, eggs, and dairy occupy about 83 percent of global farmland while providing only 37 percent of protein and 18 percent of calories. This disproportion arises largely from the inefficiency of converting plant matter into animal tissue. Ruminants such as cattle and sheep are especially land-intensive, although they can also graze on terrain unsuitable for crop cultivation.

The expansion of grazing land and feed crops is a leading driver of deforestation, particularly in tropical regions. In the Amazon basin, clearing for cattle pasture has been identified as the single largest cause of forest loss, and soybean cultivation, much of it destined for animal feed, has contributed further pressure in Brazil's Cerrado savanna. The resulting habitat conversion is a major factor in global biodiversity decline, as it fragments ecosystems and displaces native species.

Animal agriculture is also a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations estimated in 2013 that the livestock sector was responsible for about 14.5 percent of anthropogenic emissions. Methane produced by enteric fermentation in the digestive systems of ruminants constitutes the largest single component, followed by emissions from feed production, land-use change, and manure management, which releases both methane and nitrous oxide.

Water quality is affected as well. Runoff from manure and fertilized feed crops carries excess nitrogen and phosphorus into rivers, lakes, and coastal waters, where it can trigger eutrophication and algal blooms. In severe cases, these processes create hypoxic "dead zones," such as the one that forms seasonally in the Gulf of Mexico.

Chennai has long been regarded as one of India's foremost centres of medical care, a reputation that has earned it the informal title of the country's "health capital." The city's institutional medicine dates to the colonial period. The Government General Hospital, now the Rajiv Gandhi Government General Hospital, traces its origins to a small hospital established by the East India Company in 1664 to treat soldiers stationed at Fort St. George. Madras Medical College, founded in 1835, is among the oldest institutions of Western medical education in Asia. Later public institutions such as Stanley Medical College and Kilpauk Medical College expanded the city's capacity to train physicians and serve a growing urban population.

Alongside this public sector, Chennai developed a strong network of private and charitable hospitals in the second half of the twentieth century. The Cancer Institute in Adyar, established in 1954 through the efforts of the physician and social reformer Muthulakshmi Reddy, became a leading centre for oncology care and research, notable for providing treatment to patients regardless of their ability to pay. Sankara Nethralaya, founded in 1978, grew into one of the country's most prominent ophthalmic hospitals. The opening of Apollo Hospitals on Greams Road in 1983 is widely cited as a turning point in Indian healthcare, marking the emergence of large corporate hospital chains offering specialised tertiary care.

The concentration of specialist facilities, combined with comparatively low treatment costs and the availability of English-speaking medical staff, has made Chennai a major destination for medical tourism. Patients travel to the city from other Indian states as well as from Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, the Middle East and parts of Africa, seeking procedures in cardiology, orthopaedics, organ transplantation and oncology. Critics have noted, however, that this growth has coincided with persistent pressure on government hospitals, which continue to serve the majority of the city's lower-income residents and often operate beyond their intended capacity.

The phrase gained wide currency during the presidential campaign of 1916, when supporters of Woodrow Wilson used it alongside the slogan "He kept us out of war" to emphasize American neutrality in the conflict then raging in Europe. Warren G. Harding employed similar language in 1920, presenting a return to "normalcy" and a rejection of the League of Nations as a restoration of national priorities after the upheaval of the First World War. In these early uses, the expression generally signaled a preference for nonintervention in European affairs rather than a fully articulated doctrine.

The term acquired its most enduring associations with the founding of the America First Committee in September 1940. Organized initially by students at Yale University, among them R. Douglas Stuart Jr., the committee grew to claim hundreds of thousands of members and became the most prominent organization opposing American entry into the Second World War. Its best-known spokesman, the aviator Charles Lindbergh, drew large crowds but also intense criticism, particularly after a speech in Des Moines in September 1941 in which he named Jewish Americans among the groups he accused of pushing the nation toward war. The remarks were widely condemned as antisemitic and damaged the committee's standing. Following the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the organization voted to dissolve, and the phrase remained politically tainted for decades afterward.

The slogan reappeared in the 1990s, when the conservative commentator Pat Buchanan invoked it in his presidential campaigns to argue for restrictions on immigration, skepticism toward free-trade agreements, and reduced military commitments abroad. Donald Trump adopted it as a central theme of his 2016 campaign and declared in his inaugural address that "from this day forward, it's going to be only America first." Supporters described the approach as a pragmatic defense of domestic workers and national sovereignty, while critics argued that it weakened alliances and evoked the phrase's earlier history.

Born in Gardone Val Trompia, in the province of Brescia, to a family of Albanian origin, Vrioni grew up in northern Italy and began playing organised football in the local youth system before being noticed by scouts from larger clubs. He joined the academy of Sampdoria as a teenager, where his height, physical presence and finishing in the penalty area marked him as a traditional centre-forward. He progressed through the Genoese club's youth ranks and featured in the Primavera championship, earning his first involvement with the senior squad while still in his late teens.

Opportunities in Serie A proved limited, however, and Vrioni spent much of his early professional career on loan in the lower divisions of Italian football, a common path for young forwards seeking regular playing time. These spells gave him experience of senior competition, though his goal output during this period was modest. In 2019 he moved to Juventus, where he was assigned to the club's newly established under-23 side competing in Serie C. Playing against seasoned professionals in the third tier, he continued his development, and he was occasionally called upon to train with the first team.

The most significant turning point in his career came with a loan move to Austria, where he joined WSG Tirol in the Austrian Bundesliga. There, Vrioni established himself as a prolific scorer, finishing among the league's leading goalscorers and attracting attention from clubs abroad. His performances in Austria led to a permanent transfer to Major League Soccer, where he joined the New England Revolution and adapted to the demands of North American football.

At international level, Vrioni chose to represent Albania, the country of his parents, rather than Italy. After appearing for Albania's youth teams, he made his debut for the senior national side and became part of the squad's rotation of attacking options.

*Mistborn: The Final Empire* is set in a world where ash falls continually from the sky and mysterious mists cover the land each night. For a thousand years the Final Empire has been ruled by the Lord Ruler, an immortal emperor revered as a god, who is said to have defeated a cataclysmic force known as the Deepness. Under his rule society is rigidly divided between the nobility, who enjoy wealth and privilege, and the skaa, a vast underclass of laborers kept in conditions resembling slavery. The Steel Ministry, an ecclesiastical bureaucracy, enforces the emperor's will, and its most feared members are the Steel Inquisitors, whose eyes are pierced by metal spikes.

The novel follows Vin, a young half-skaa thief who survives on the streets of the imperial capital, Luthadel. She is unaware that she possesses rare innate abilities until she is discovered by Kelsier, a charismatic crew leader known as the Survivor of Hathsin, the only person known to have escaped the brutal Pits of Hathsin. Kelsier recognizes Vin as a Mistborn, someone capable of using every form of Allomancy, and takes her under his tutelage. He has assembled a crew of skilled specialists for an audacious scheme: to overthrow the Lord Ruler, incite a skaa rebellion, and seize the empire's treasury of the precious metal atium.

The book's magic is built around Allomancy, in which certain individuals ingest specific metals and "burn" them to gain particular powers, such as pushing or pulling on nearby metal, heightening their senses, or influencing others' emotions. Sanderson also introduces Feruchemy, practiced by the Terris steward Sazed, which allows its users to store physical or mental attributes in metal for later use. A third discipline, Hemalurgy, is only partially revealed. Critics frequently singled out the rule-based consistency of these systems as a distinctive feature of the novel, which later became the first volume of a trilogy.

The European Union Mission in Armenia (EUMA) is a civilian mission conducted under the EU's Common Security and Defence Policy. The Council of the European Union established it on 20 January 2023, and it formally began operations the following month. It succeeded the EU Monitoring Capacity, a short-term deployment of roughly forty observers that was agreed upon at a meeting in Prague in October 2022 between Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, French President Emmanuel Macron, and European Council President Charles Michel. That initial deployment followed the deadly clashes along the Armenia–Azerbaijan border in September 2022, which prompted calls for an international presence to reduce tensions in the area.

The mission's mandate is to contribute to stability in Armenia's border regions, to build confidence between the parties, and to support the environment for normalisation efforts between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Its monitors are unarmed and conduct patrols exclusively on the Armenian side of the border. They observe and report on the security situation, and their findings are used to inform EU institutions and member states. The mission's headquarters is located in Yeghegnadzor in Vayots Dzor Province, and it maintains forward operating bases in several border regions. Its initial complement of around one hundred personnel was later expanded, and in early 2025 the Council extended the mandate for a further two years.

Reactions to the mission have been divided. The Armenian government welcomed the deployment as a deterrent and a source of impartial information. Azerbaijan, which did not consent to monitoring on its territory, has repeatedly criticised the mission, characterising it as a source of bias and as an instrument of Western influence in the region. Russia, traditionally Armenia's principal security partner through the Collective Security Treaty Organization, also objected, describing the presence of the mission as geopolitically motivated. Several analysts have noted that the mission signalled a broader shift in Armenia's foreign policy orientation towards closer engagement with Europe.

Hoc Mazarin was one of several varieties of hoc, a family of French card games that enjoyed considerable popularity in the middle decades of the seventeenth century. The name links the game to Cardinal Jules Mazarin, chief minister of France during the minority of Louis XIV, whose fondness for gambling was well known at court. Whether the cardinal actually devised the variant, or whether his name was simply attached to it as a mark of fashion, is uncertain. Contemporary writers used it in a way that suggests the association was widely accepted, and the game seems to have spread among courtiers and the wealthier classes of Paris during the 1650s.

The word "hoc" referred to certain privileged cards that could be played at any moment and that carried the right to begin a new run of play. According to the descriptions preserved in later compendia of games, notably the various editions of the *Académie universelle des jeux*, hoc games combined several distinct phases within a single deal. Players typically competed first for combinations held in the hand, in a manner reminiscent of older vying games such as primero. The deal then proceeded to a play-out in which cards were laid down in ascending sequence until a player could not continue. Holding hocs gave a decisive advantage in this stage, since they allowed a player to break a sequence and take control of the play. The aim was to be first to dispose of one's cards, and players were paid according to the cards their opponents still held.

Hoc Mazarin is generally distinguished from Hoc de Lyon, a related form that differed in its scoring and in the number of players it accommodated. Both declined in favour toward the end of the century, overtaken by newer games. Historians of card play have nonetheless noted the structural resemblance between hoc and later games such as comète and poque, and some regard it as an ancestor of those games.

The Pyle stop is named after Richard Pyle, an ichthyologist at the Bishop Museum in Honolulu who, during the early 1990s, conducted numerous deep dives on coral reefs to collect fish specimens. Pyle observed that on dives where he paused partway through his ascent to vent the swim bladders of captured fish with a hypodermic needle, he tended to surface feeling noticeably less fatigued than on dives where he ascended directly to his first scheduled decompression stop. Reasoning that the brief pause might be limiting the formation or growth of bubbles in his tissues, he began incorporating such stops deliberately and later described the practice in articles and presentations aimed at technical divers.

As commonly formulated, a Pyle stop is a short pause, typically of about two minutes, made at the depth halfway between the bottom depth and the first decompression stop calculated by a conventional dissolved-gas algorithm. After this stop, the diver recalculates the midpoint between the new depth and the first required stop, and makes another brief pause there if the remaining distance is sufficiently large, often taken to be more than about three metres. The process is repeated until the gap becomes negligible, after which the diver continues with the standard schedule. Pyle stops are generally treated as additions to the schedule, and the time spent at them is not credited against the required shallower stops.

The technique became influential within the technical diving community and contributed to wider interest in so-called deep stops, which also emerged from bubble-based decompression models such as the Varying Permeability Model and the Reduced Gradient Bubble Model. Subsequent research has complicated this picture. Trials conducted by the United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit, published in 2011, found a higher incidence of decompression sickness with a deep-stop schedule than with a comparable shallow-stop schedule, prompting many practitioners to reconsider or moderate the use of extended deep stops.

The Pisano period π(n) is the length of the cycle with which the Fibonacci sequence repeats when its terms are reduced modulo a positive integer n. Because each Fibonacci number depends only on the two preceding terms, and there are only finitely many pairs of residues modulo n, the reduced sequence must eventually return to the starting pair (0, 1). Since the recurrence can also be run backward, the sequence is purely periodic rather than merely eventually periodic. For example, modulo 2 the sequence runs 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, …, giving π(2) = 3, while modulo 3 it repeats every eight terms, so π(3) = 8. The name honours Leonardo Pisano, better known as Fibonacci, although the systematic study of these periods is much more recent. Donald Dines Wall's 1960 paper "Fibonacci Series Modulo m" established many of the basic results.

Several general properties make the function tractable. If m and n are coprime, then π(mn) is the least common multiple of π(m) and π(n). Computing π(n) for any n therefore reduces to the case of prime powers. For a prime p other than 2 and 5, the behaviour depends on whether 5 is a quadratic residue modulo p. When p is congruent to ±1 modulo 10, π(p) divides p − 1. When p is congruent to ±3 modulo 10, π(p) divides 2(p + 1) but not p + 1. The prime 5 is exceptional, with π(5) = 20. Apart from π(2) = 3, every Pisano period is even. The bound π(n) ≤ 6n holds for all n, with equality exactly when n = 2·5^k.

For prime powers, it is known that π(p^k) = p^(k−1)·π(p) whenever π(p²) ≠ π(p). Whether that inequality ever fails is an open problem known as Wall's question. A prime for which it fails would be a Wall–Sun–Sun prime, and extensive computer searches have found none. In decimal terms, these results explain why the final digit of Fibonacci numbers repeats every 60 terms, the final two digits every 300 terms, and the final three digits every 1,500 terms.

Li Baoyu spent the greater part of his early career in Yangzhou, where the prosperity of the salt merchants had drawn a large community of painters, calligraphers, and poets seeking patronage. Contemporary accounts describe him as a reserved figure who preferred the company of a small circle of friends to the elaborate garden gatherings hosted by wealthy collectors. He nevertheless secured the support of several merchant families, whose commissions allowed him to devote himself to painting without pursuing an official post, a path he appears to have abandoned after failing the provincial examinations twice.

His surviving works are dominated by studies of plum blossoms, bamboo, and rocks, subjects long associated with the scholar-amateur tradition. Critics have noted, however, that Li departed from established conventions in his handling of ink, favoring broad, wet strokes that blurred the boundaries between forms. In his plum paintings especially, branches often dissolve into areas of pale wash, an effect that some later commentators praised as evoking mist or early spring light, while others dismissed it as careless. Li's inscriptions, written in a compact running script, frequently contain short verses that comment wryly on his poverty or on the vanity of fame, adding a personal dimension to otherwise traditional compositions.

In his later years Li withdrew to a modest residence outside the city, where he is said to have taught painting to a handful of students and to have reduced his output considerably. Much of his work from this period was dispersed after his death, and many attributions remain uncertain because of the circulation of copies produced by followers. Interest in his paintings revived in the twentieth century, when scholars studying the eccentric painters of the Yangzhou region began to reassess lesser-known artists from that milieu. Today his works are held in several museum collections, and he is regarded as a minor but distinctive voice within the regional painting traditions of his era.

The town's identity is inseparable from its most famous native, Francis of Paola, who was born there in 1416 and went on to found the Order of Minims, a mendicant community devoted to penance and perpetual Lenten observance. As a young man he withdrew to a cave near the town to live as a hermit. Followers soon gathered around him, and the first nucleus of his religious community took shape on the slopes just above the settlement. The complex that grew from these beginnings, the Sanctuary of Saint Francis of Paola, became one of the principal pilgrimage destinations of southern Italy. It includes the original cloister and church, along with a large modern basilica added in the early twenty-first century. Francis died in France in 1507 and was canonized in 1519. He was later proclaimed patron saint of Calabria, and in 1943 Pope Pius XII named him patron of Italian seafarers. That designation echoes the popular legend that he crossed the Strait of Messina using his cloak as a boat.

Religious devotion continues to shape the town's calendar. The principal celebrations take place in early May and draw large numbers of pilgrims and visitors. They feature processions through the historic centre and down toward the shore, where the saint's maritime patronage is commemorated.

Beyond its religious significance, Paola occupies a strategic position on the Tyrrhenian coast of the province of Cosenza. It lies on a narrow strip of land between the sea and the steep ridges of the Coastal Range. This setting has long made the town a natural point of passage between the coast and the interior valley of the Crati. In the modern era Paola became an important railway junction. It stands on the main line linking Salerno with Reggio Calabria and serves as the coastal terminus of the line that crosses the mountains to Cosenza. A tunnel opened in the late twentieth century substantially improved that mountain connection. As a result, the town's station handles considerable traffic for travellers bound for the provincial capital and the University of Calabria.

Born in Lisbon in 1904, Valadares studied physical and chemical sciences at the University of Lisbon, where he developed an early interest in the emerging field of radioactivity. Like several promising Portuguese scientists of his generation, he went abroad to complete his training. In Paris he joined the Radium Institute, then directed by Marie Curie, and became part of the international circle of researchers who worked in her laboratory during the early 1930s. His doctoral research there concerned the spectroscopy of radiation emitted by radioactive substances, and he collaborated with Salomon Rosenblum, whose work on the fine structure of alpha-particle spectra was then attracting considerable attention. Valadares received his doctorate in Paris in the mid-1930s and gained a reputation for careful experimental technique, particularly in the study of gamma rays and X-rays associated with radioactive decay.

On returning to Portugal, Valadares took up a teaching position at the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Lisbon, where he sought to establish a modern programme of experimental research in nuclear and atomic physics. Together with a small group of colleagues, he helped to found a centre for physical research and to train students in laboratory methods that were largely new to the country. This period is often regarded as a formative moment for Portuguese physics, since it introduced research practices modelled on the leading European institutions of the time.

His career in Portugal was cut short in 1947, when the authoritarian Estado Novo government of António de Oliveira Salazar dismissed a number of university professors suspected of opposition to the regime. Valadares was among those removed from their posts. He subsequently emigrated to France, where he resumed his research within the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique. There he continued to work in nuclear spectroscopy, eventually holding senior research positions and contributing to laboratories devoted to nuclear and mass spectrometry. He remained in France for the rest of his life and died in Paris in 1982.

Basuki Hadimuljono was born on 5 November 1954 in Surakarta, Central Java. He studied civil engineering at Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta, graduating in 1979, and then joined the Department of Public Works as a civil servant. His early assignments centred on water resources, a field he pursued further abroad at Colorado State University in the United States, where he earned a master's degree and later a doctorate in civil engineering. On returning to Indonesia he rose steadily through the ministry's technical and administrative ranks, holding a series of senior posts that included directing spatial planning policy and serving as the ministry's inspector general. This long career inside the bureaucracy gave him a reputation as a technocrat rather than a party politician.

In October 2014 President Joko Widodo appointed Basuki as Minister of Public Works and Public Housing in the newly formed Working Cabinet. The portfolio became central to the administration's development agenda, which prioritised large-scale infrastructure as a means of reducing logistics costs and narrowing regional inequality. Under his leadership the ministry oversaw an expansion of the national toll road network, including the completion of the Trans-Java corridor and progress on the Trans-Sumatra toll road, alongside the construction of numerous dams, irrigation systems, border posts and public housing programmes. He was reappointed for a second term in 2019 and was also given temporary responsibilities in other portfolios when vacancies arose.

Basuki became closely associated with the planned national capital, Nusantara, in East Kalimantan, where his ministry handled much of the early construction. In 2024 he was entrusted with leading the Nusantara Capital City Authority, first in an acting capacity and subsequently on a permanent basis under President Prabowo Subianto. Outside government, he is known for his enthusiasm for music, particularly drumming, and has occasionally performed with bands at public events. Observers have frequently cited his hands-on style of inspecting project sites in person.

The sinking of the *Robin Moor* took place on 21 May 1941, while the United States was still formally neutral in the Second World War. The freighter, owned by the Seas Shipping Company and operated as part of its Robin Line service, had departed New York bound for ports in southern and eastern Africa with a general cargo and a small number of passengers in addition to her crew. Roughly 750 miles west of Freetown, in the tropical South Atlantic, she was stopped by the German submarine *U-69*, commanded by Kapitänleutnant Jost Metzler. After examining the ship's papers, the German commander concluded that some of her cargo constituted contraband destined for the British Empire and ordered the ship abandoned.

The crew and passengers were given a short interval to take to the lifeboats, after which the vessel was sent to the bottom by torpedo and gunfire. Although the submarine provided the survivors with a modest quantity of provisions before departing, it made no radio report of their position, leaving the occupants of the boats adrift far from regular shipping lanes. For nearly two weeks nothing was known of their fate. One boat was eventually picked up by a Brazilian merchant vessel and its occupants landed at Recife, while the remaining boats were found by a British ship and their survivors brought to Cape Town. Remarkably, everyone aboard survived the ordeal.

News of the sinking provoked considerable indignation in the United States. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, addressing Congress in June 1941, denounced the attack as the act of an international outlaw and cited it as evidence of Germany's disregard for the freedom of the seas. The incident coincided with a broader hardening of American policy, including the freezing of German assets and the closure of German consulates, and it became one of several episodes cited in the gradual movement of the United States toward open conflict with Germany.

Forrest's professional breakthrough came in 2002, when he faced Shane Mosley for the World Boxing Council welterweight championship at Madison Square Garden. Mosley entered the bout undefeated and was widely regarded as one of the best fighters in the sport regardless of weight class, while Forrest was viewed by many observers as a considerable underdog despite having defeated Mosley years earlier at the 1992 United States Olympic trials. Forrest used his height and reach advantage to control the fight from the outset, knocking Mosley down twice in the second round and going on to win a clear unanimous decision. He repeated the result in a rematch later that year, cementing his reputation as one of the leading welterweights of his era.

His run at the top of the division ended abruptly in January 2003, when he lost his title to the Nicaraguan brawler Ricardo Mayorga by third-round stoppage. Forrest lost the rematch by decision several months later, and persistent injuries to his left shoulder and elbow subsequently kept him out of the ring for an extended period. After undergoing surgery, he mounted a gradual comeback and, in 2007, won the vacant WBC light middleweight championship by defeating Carlos Baldomir. He lost the belt to Sergio Mora in 2008 but reclaimed it in an immediate rematch, outboxing Mora over twelve rounds.

Outside the ring, Forrest was known for his charitable work, particularly Destiny's Child, Inc., an organization he founded to provide group homes and support for adults with intellectual disabilities. His involvement in the project was frequently cited by colleagues as a reflection of his character.

In July 2009, Forrest was shot and killed in Atlanta after pursuing a man who had robbed him at a gas station. His death prompted widespread tributes from the boxing community, and three men were later convicted in connection with the killing.

*The Swallows of Kabul* (French: *Les Hirondelles de Kaboul*) is a novel by the Algerian author Yasmina Khadra, the pen name of former army officer Mohammed Moulessehoul. First published in French in 2002, it appeared in English in 2004 in a translation by John Cullen. The book is often grouped with Khadra's *The Attack* and *The Sirens of Baghdad* as an informal trilogy examining the tensions between the Muslim world and the West, as well as the human consequences of fundamentalism and war.

The novel is set in Kabul during the rule of the Taliban in the late 1990s, a city portrayed as ruined, dust-choked, and governed by fear and public violence. The narrative follows two couples whose lives become fatally intertwined. Atiq Shaukat is a jailer who guards women condemned to death, a veteran of the war against the Soviets who has grown weary and embittered. His wife, Mussarat, who once nursed him back to health, is now gravely ill. Mohsen Ramat, the son of a once-prosperous family, lives with his wife Zunaira, an educated woman who held a professional career before the Taliban barred women from public life. After Mohsen impulsively joins a crowd in stoning an adulterous woman, he is consumed by shame, and his marriage begins to unravel. A quarrel between the couple ends in Mohsen's accidental death, and Zunaira is sentenced to execution, placing her in Atiq's custody.

Critics have praised the novel for its compressed, lyrical prose and its depiction of ordinary people struggling to preserve dignity and affection under an oppressive regime. Its themes include the degradation of love, the moral corruption produced by collective violence, and the possibility of self-sacrifice. In 2019 the book was adapted into an animated feature film directed by Zabou Breitman and Éléa Gobbé-Mévellec, which premiered in the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival.

The term "chiefdom" was introduced into anthropological usage by Kalervo Oberg in 1955, in a study of lowland South American societies, and was later given wider theoretical prominence by Elman Service, whose 1962 evolutionary typology placed chiefdoms between egalitarian tribes and bureaucratic states. In this scheme a chiefdom is a regional polity in which several communities are organized under the permanent authority of a paramount figure, whose position is typically hereditary and justified by genealogical proximity to founding ancestors or deities. Robert Carneiro offered a more concise definition, describing the chiefdom as "an autonomous political unit comprising a number of villages or communities under the permanent control of a paramount chief."

A central feature distinguishing chiefdoms from less hierarchical societies is institutionalized inequality of rank. Individuals and lineages are graded by descent, and access to prestige goods, ritual office, and productive land is often unevenly distributed. Unlike states, however, chiefdoms generally lack a specialized administrative apparatus, a standing legal code, or a monopoly on legitimate force. Authority rests heavily on kinship, personal loyalty, and religious sanction, which tends to make such polities unstable; many cycle between periods of consolidation and fragmentation as rival heirs contest succession.

Early theorists, Service among them, emphasized the chief's role as a redistributor who collected surplus from specialized local producers and allocated it across the polity. Subsequent fieldwork, notably Timothy Earle's research in Hawaii, challenged this functionalist account, showing that chiefly control often depended instead on command over irrigation works, craft production, warfare, and the staging of feasts and ceremonies. Archaeologists commonly distinguish simple chiefdoms, with a single tier of authority above the village, from complex chiefdoms featuring multiple levels of subordinate chiefs. Frequently cited examples include the island societies of Polynesia, the Mississippian mound centers of eastern North America such as Cahokia, and various polities of Iron Age Europe and precolonial Africa. The concept remains debated, with critics arguing that it compresses highly diverse social arrangements into a single evolutionary stage.

*Dolphin Tale 2* picks up several years after the events of the first film, with the Clearwater Marine Aquarium continuing its work under the direction of Dr. Clay Haskett, played by Harry Connick Jr. The central conflict arises when Panama, the elderly dolphin who had served as Winter's companion, dies. Winter, the bottlenose dolphin who lost her tail and was fitted with a prosthetic, becomes withdrawn and increasingly erratic in her behavior. Federal regulations governing marine mammals in captivity require that a solitary dolphin be housed with another of its kind, and the aquarium staff face the prospect of Winter being transferred to another facility unless a suitable companion can be found.

The film interweaves this crisis with the personal concerns of its younger characters. Sawyer Nelson, played by Nathan Gamble, has been offered a place in a prestigious semester-at-sea program and struggles with the decision to leave Winter behind. Hazel Haskett, played by Cozi Zuehlsdorff, wrestles with her own ambitions and her place in her father's work. Ashley Judd, Kris Kristofferson, and Morgan Freeman reprise their roles from the original film, and the surfer Bethany Hamilton appears as herself.

As in its predecessor, the narrative draws on real events at the Clearwater aquarium. A young dolphin named Hope, rescued in December 2010 after being found beside her dead mother, plays herself in the film, and her arrival forms the basis for the story's resolution. Winter likewise portrays herself, continuing the production's emphasis on authenticity. Charles Martin Smith returned as both writer and director, and principal photography took place largely on location in Clearwater, Florida.
