Released by Warner Bros. in September 2014, the film received a generally favorable response from critics, who noted its sincerity and suitability for family audiences, though some found it less engaging than the first installment. It earned less at the box office than *Dolphin Tale*.

The concept for the film originated with Dave Grohl, who conceived of a horror comedy built around the Foo Fighters while the band was recording what would become their tenth studio album, *Medicine at Midnight*. The sessions took place in a rented house in Encino, Los Angeles, which members of the band reportedly felt had an unsettling atmosphere. Grohl developed a story treatment, and the screenplay was written by Jeff Buhler and Rebecca Hughes. BJ McDonnell, a camera operator on several horror productions who had previously directed *Hatchet III* and music videos for heavy metal acts, was hired to direct. Principal photography took place largely at the same Encino residence, giving the production a self-referential quality, since the plot concerns the band attempting to record an album in a mansion with a violent history.

All six members of the band at the time appear as fictionalized versions of themselves: Grohl, Nate Mendel, Pat Smear, Taylor Hawkins, Chris Shiflett, and Rami Jaffee. The supporting cast includes Whitney Cummings, Leslie Grossman, and Will Forte, with appearances by Jenna Ortega and Jeff Garlin. Lionel Richie makes a cameo as himself, and the filmmaker John Carpenter appears briefly. Carpenter also contributed to the film's music, writing its theme alongside his frequent collaborators Cody Carpenter and Daniel Davies. The production emphasized practical gore effects, in keeping with the low-budget horror films of the 1980s that Grohl cited as inspiration.

Open Road Films released *Studio 666* theatrically in the United States in February 2022. Critical reception was mixed: reviewers generally praised the band's evident enthusiasm and the film's gory set pieces while criticizing its length, uneven pacing, and the limited acting range of its musician leads. Commercial performance was modest. In connection with the release, the band issued an extended play under the name Dream Widow, the fictional heavy metal group whose fate drives the film's plot. The film gained additional poignancy after Hawkins died the following month while the band was on tour in South America.

Zervas emerged from the interwar period with a reputation as a politically ambitious officer whose fortunes were closely bound to the factional struggles of the Greek army. A committed Venizelist in his early career, he took part in several of the coups and counter-coups that marked the 1920s, and in 1926 his command of the Republican Guard made him a significant figure in the overthrow of the dictator Theodoros Pangalos. His involvement in subsequent conspiracies led to his removal from active service, and for much of the following decade he lived on the margins of public life, reportedly sustaining himself through gambling and various business dealings.

The Axis occupation of Greece in 1941 transformed his position. In September of that year Zervas helped found the National Republican Greek League (EDES), a republican and anti-monarchist organisation that nominally recognised the exiled general Nikolaos Plastiras as its leader. In July 1942 Zervas took to the mountains of Epirus, his native region, and began organising armed bands under the name of the National Groups of Greek Guerrillas (EOEA). Later that year his forces joined the communist-led ELAS and a team of British saboteurs in destroying the Gorgopotamos viaduct, one of the most celebrated resistance operations in occupied Europe.

Cooperation with ELAS proved short-lived. Distrust between the two movements escalated into open fighting in October 1943, and although the British brokered a temporary settlement at Plaka in early 1944, relations remained hostile. Under British influence, and partly to secure continued material support, Zervas gradually abandoned his republican stance and declared his acceptance of the monarchy, a shift that alienated some of his original supporters. Following the outbreak of the Dekemvriana in Athens in December 1944, ELAS launched a decisive offensive against EDES, forcing Zervas and his remaining men to evacuate to Corfu. His forces were also responsible for the violent expulsion of the Cham Albanian population from Thesprotia during 1944 and 1945, an episode that remains controversial.

Sandaime J Soul Brothers was formed in 2010 under the entertainment agency LDH as the third incarnation of the J Soul Brothers name, a lineage that began in 1999 when Hiro, a former member of the dance group Zoo, founded the original J Soul Brothers. That first group later evolved into Exile, which became one of the most commercially successful acts in Japan. The revival of the name was intended to carry forward the original concept of a collective that combined vocal performance with dance. The new lineup was assembled from existing performers within the wider Exile Tribe and from newcomers chosen through a nationally publicized audition.

The group consists of seven members: two vocalists and five performers. The vocalists, Ryuji Imaichi and Hiroomi Tosaka, were selected through the Exile Vocal Battle Audition 2, held in 2010. The performers are Naoki Kobayashi, who serves as leader, along with Naoto, Kenjiro Yamashita, Takanori Iwata, and Elly. Naoki and Naoto also became members of Exile, reflecting the close organizational ties between the groups under the Exile Tribe banner.

The group made its debut in November 2010 with the single "Best Friend's Girl," released through the Avex label Rhythm Zone. Over the following years it built a substantial following through television appearances, arena concerts, and a steady stream of singles. Its commercial breakthrough came in 2014 with "R.Y.U.S.E.I.," whose distinctive "running man" dance step became a widespread fad and helped the song win the Grand Prix at the Japan Record Awards that year. The group won the same award again the following year with "Unfair World," making it one of the few acts to receive the honor in consecutive years.

Alongside group activities, individual members have pursued careers in acting, solo music, and fashion, and the group has become a prominent fixture of Japanese popular culture.

Volumes emerged from the Los Angeles heavy music scene in the late 2000s, quickly becoming associated with the progressive metalcore movement often labeled "djent." The band's sound centered on heavily syncopated, low-tuned guitar riffs played on extended-range instruments, layered with atmospheric textures and electronic flourishes. A defining feature from the outset was its use of two vocalists, one specializing in harsh screams and the other in a more rhythmic, hip-hop-influenced delivery. This interplay set the group apart from many contemporaries and drew comparisons to both nu metal and the technical metal acts then gaining attention online.

The band's early releases, beginning with an independent EP, circulated widely through social media and music blogs, helping it build a following before signing with an independent label. Its debut full-length album, *Via*, was released in 2011 and established the group's reputation for dense, groove-driven compositions. Extensive touring followed, including appearances alongside established metalcore and progressive metal bands, which expanded its audience in North America and abroad. The follow-up, *No Sleep*, refined the band's approach with greater emphasis on melody and song structure while retaining the polyrhythmic intensity of its earlier work.

Over the following years Volumes underwent several lineup changes, particularly among its vocalists, a pattern that shaped the stylistic direction of later recordings. After signing with Fearless Records, the band released *Different Animals* in 2017, an album that incorporated more clean singing and accessible hooks, a shift that drew mixed reactions from longtime listeners but broadened its reach. Guitarist Diego Farias, widely credited as a principal songwriter and architect of the band's signature sound, departed the group and died in 2021, prompting tributes from across the progressive metal community. The remaining members continued to record and perform, positioning the band as a lasting presence within the genre it helped popularize.

When a slave clock loses contact with its reference, it enters a mode known as holdover. Instead of reverting to the free-running behavior of its local oscillator, the clock continues to generate timing signals using information learned while it was still locked. In a typical implementation, the disciplining circuitry records a running estimate of the frequency correction applied to the oscillator, often averaged over minutes or hours so that short-term noise from the reference does not contaminate it. When the reference disappears, the control loop is frozen or replaced by this stored value. More sophisticated designs also model the oscillator's aging rate and its sensitivity to temperature, and they extrapolate these trends to compensate for drift that would otherwise accumulate.

The quality of holdover depends mainly on the stability of the local oscillator. An ordinary crystal oscillator may keep acceptable frequency for only minutes. An oven-controlled crystal oscillator can often hold a phase error within a few microseconds for several hours. Rubidium and other atomic standards extend this to days. For this reason, holdover performance is a common way to distinguish grades of equipment. Telecommunications standards such as Telcordia GR-1244 and the ITU-T G.81x series specify the maximum frequency drift allowed during the first day of holdover for each clock stratum or category.

Holdover has become especially important in systems that rely on satellite navigation signals for timing. Cellular base stations using time-division duplexing must keep phase alignment within roughly a microsecond of neighboring cells. Jamming, antenna faults or obstructed sky views can interrupt GNSS reception, and a well-designed holdover capability lets a site keep operating until the signal returns or a technician arrives. Network operators often specify a required holdover period together with a maximum permitted time error. They may also combine local oscillators with packet-based timing protocols, so that a backup reference can limit drift during prolonged outages.

The film follows Jeff Lang, a Seattle obstetrician whose comfortable suburban life begins to unravel after a family of raccoons repeatedly tears up the expensive new sod in his backyard. Determined to protect his lawn, Jeff resorts to increasingly drastic measures, eventually setting out poison. The decision proves to be the first in a chain of small compromises that escalate into far more serious moral failings. Jeff's marriage to his wife, Nealy, has grown distant, and he drifts into an affair with Rebecca, a friend from his medical school days, which entangles him with her volatile husband, Peter.

Meanwhile, Jeff's eccentric neighbor Lila, a lonely woman devoted to her cats, discovers that one of her pets has died after consuming the poison. Rather than going to the authorities, she uses the knowledge as leverage, drawing Jeff into an uncomfortable sexual relationship and extracting promises from him. At the same time, Jeff's friend and pickup basketball partner, Lincoln, reveals that he is suffering from kidney failure, and Jeff, wrestling with mounting guilt, volunteers to become a donor. The narrative intercuts these threads as Jeff attempts to manage the consequences of each lie, only to find that every effort to restore order generates new complications.

Writer and director Jacob Aaron Estes, whose previous feature was the 2004 drama *Mean Creek*, conceived the film as a dark comedy about the way ordinary people rationalize selfish behavior. Tobey Maguire starred as Jeff, with Elizabeth Banks as Nealy, Laura Linney as Lila, Kerry Washington as Rebecca, Ray Liotta as Peter, and Dennis Haysbert as Lincoln. Principal photography took place in the Seattle area.

The film premiered at the 2011 Sundance Film Festival and was later acquired for distribution in the United States, receiving a video-on-demand release followed by a limited theatrical run in late 2012. Critical response was mixed; reviewers frequently praised the ensemble, particularly Linney's performance, while some found the film's shifts in tone uneven.

Gordon's most enduring contribution arose from his work during the epidemic of puerperal fever that afflicted Aberdeen between 1789 and 1792. As physician to the Aberdeen Dispensary, a post he had taken up in 1785 after service as a naval surgeon and further medical study in Edinburgh, Leiden and London, he attended many of the women who fell ill. He kept careful records of each case, noting the date of delivery, the attendant who had conducted it and the subsequent course of the illness. From these observations he concluded that the disease did not arise from atmospheric conditions or from some inherent weakness in the patient, as prevailing medical opinion held, but was carried from one lying-in woman to another by the midwives and physicians who attended them.

Gordon set out his findings in *A Treatise on the Epidemic Puerperal Fever of Aberdeen*, published in London in 1795. In it he argued that the fever was a specific contagion, closely related to erysipelas, and that its spread could be predicted by tracing the movements of particular practitioners. With notable candour he acknowledged that he himself had been responsible for transmitting the infection to a number of his patients. He recommended that the clothing of attendants be fumigated, that the bedding and garments of affected women be burned, and that those who had treated the disease wash themselves thoroughly before attending further births. He also advocated aggressive bloodletting, which was consistent with the medical practice of the time.

The treatise provoked considerable resentment in Aberdeen, partly because Gordon had identified by name the midwives associated with infected cases. His practice declined, and he returned to the Royal Navy shortly afterwards. He died in 1799 at the age of forty-seven. His conclusions anticipated by several decades the better-known arguments of Oliver Wendell Holmes and Ignaz Semmelweis, and his work came to be recognised as a significant early contribution to the understanding of contagious disease.

The episode opens with the host introducing the show's central premise: guests appear before a studio audience to describe a single trait, habit, or circumstance that ended a romantic relationship, and the panel and audience then debate whether the issue was a legitimate "dealbreaker" or a problem that could have been resolved. In this inaugural installment, the format is presented in a deliberately rough form. Segments run longer than in later episodes, and the voting mechanism, which became a signature element of the program, is introduced partway through rather than at the beginning. Commentators have often cited this unevenness as evidence that the producers were still refining the concept during taping.

The first guest describes a partner's refusal to share passwords to personal devices, framing it as a matter of trust, while the panel argues that the request itself signaled deeper insecurity. This exchange set the tone for much of the series, in which the stated dealbreaker frequently gave way to a broader discussion of communication and expectation. A second segment treats a dispute over household finances and introduces the recurring "counter-testimony" device, in which a former partner is heard by recorded message to offer a contrasting account. Critics later regarded this device as both the program's most compelling feature and its most ethically contested one.

Reception of the episode was mixed. Some reviewers praised its candor and its willingness to let ordinary participants speak at length without heavy editing, noting that the conversational pacing distinguished it from more sensational relationship programs. Others found the debates repetitive and questioned whether the audience vote trivialized the personal experiences being discussed. Nonetheless, the episode is generally credited with establishing the visual style, panel dynamics, and moral framing that defined subsequent installments, and it is frequently referenced in retrospective discussions of how the format evolved over its run.

The series follows Charlie Morningstar, the princess of Hell and daughter of Lucifer, who opens a hotel intended to rehabilitate sinners so that they might be redeemed and admitted to Heaven. Her project is motivated by the annual "extermination," a purge in which an army of angels descends upon Hell to cull its growing population of damned souls. Charlie is assisted by her partner Vaggie, while the hotel's first residents and staff include the adult film star Angel Dust, the bartender Husk, the housekeeper Niffty, and the ambitious inventor Sir Pentious. The hotel's most enigmatic benefactor is Alastor, a powerful Overlord known as the Radio Demon, whose motives for supporting Charlie's venture remain deliberately ambiguous throughout the narrative.

Created by Vivienne Medrano, who works under the name VivziePop, the project originated as an independently produced pilot released on YouTube in October 2019. Animated largely through crowdfunding and Medrano's studio SpindleHorse Toons, the pilot attracted tens of millions of views and cultivated a substantial online fanbase before the property was acquired by A24 for development as a full series. Bento Box Entertainment joined as an animation partner, and the first season premiered on Amazon Prime Video in January 2024.

The transition to television brought significant changes, most notably a recasting of much of the voice ensemble. The series features a cast drawn heavily from Broadway, including Erika Henningsen as Charlie, Jeremy Jordan as Lucifer, Blake Roman as Angel Dust, and Amir Talai as Alastor, alongside Stephanie Beatriz as Vaggie and Keith David as Husk. Reflecting this theatrical background, each episode is structured as a musical, with original songs written by Sam Haft and Andrew Underberg.

Critical reception was mixed to positive, with reviewers praising the music, vocal performances, and visual style while some found the pacing uneven. The show's popularity led Amazon to renew it for multiple additional seasons.

Manchester United began the season under Ole Gunnar Solskjær with most matches played behind closed doors because of the COVID-19 pandemic. The club's summer business was relatively modest. Donny van de Beek arrived from Ajax, and Alex Telles joined from Porto. On transfer deadline day, the club signed the experienced Uruguayan striker Edinson Cavani on a free transfer, along with the teenager Facundo Pellistri. Amad Diallo, whose move from Atalanta had been agreed earlier, joined in January.

The opening weeks were turbulent. United lost 3–1 at home to Crystal Palace in their first league fixture, and on 4 October suffered a 6–1 defeat to Tottenham Hotspur at Old Trafford. The team recovered with a strong run of results, many of them achieved after conceding first. After a 1–0 win at Burnley in January 2021, United briefly went top of the Premier League. On 2 February they beat Southampton 9–0, equalling the record for the largest victory in Premier League history.

In Europe, United were drawn in Group H of the UEFA Champions League alongside Paris Saint-Germain, RB Leipzig and İstanbul Başakşehir. Despite winning their opening two fixtures, they finished third and transferred to the UEFA Europa League. There they progressed to the final in Gdańsk, where they drew 1–1 with Villarreal before losing 11–10 in a penalty shoot-out, with David de Gea's kick saved by Gerónimo Rulli. In the domestic cups, United were eliminated by Manchester City in the semi-finals of the EFL Cup and by Leicester City in the quarter-finals of the FA Cup.

Off the pitch, the club's involvement in the proposed European Super League in April 2021 provoked widespread anger. United withdrew within days, and executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward announced his resignation. Supporters' protests against the Glazer family's ownership led to the postponement of the home match against Liverpool on 2 May. United finished second in the league with 74 points, while Bruno Fernandes ended the season as the club's top scorer with 28 goals in all competitions.

In medicine, insufflation most commonly refers to the deliberate introduction of a gas into a body cavity in order to expand it and improve access or visibility. The practice is central to laparoscopic surgery, in which carbon dioxide is pumped into the abdomen to create a pneumoperitoneum, lifting the abdominal wall away from the underlying organs and giving the surgeon a working space in which to manipulate instruments. Carbon dioxide is favored because it is non-combustible, inexpensive, and readily absorbed by the tissues and eliminated through the lungs, which reduces the risk of persistent gas pockets after the procedure. Pressures are typically maintained at around 12 to 15 millimetres of mercury, a range intended to balance adequate exposure against the physiological effects of raised intra-abdominal pressure. Recognized complications include hypercapnia, reduced venous return to the heart, gas embolism, and the referred shoulder pain that many patients experience afterward as residual gas irritates the diaphragm. Similar techniques are used in colonoscopy, where air or carbon dioxide distends the bowel, and in certain gynecological and thoracic procedures.

The term also has a long history outside modern surgery. In the eighteenth century, the insufflation of tobacco smoke into the rectum was promoted as a means of reviving apparently drowned persons, and organizations such as the Royal Humane Society, founded in London in 1774, distributed resuscitation equipment along the River Thames. The practice declined in the early nineteenth century as physicians grew skeptical of its efficacy and concerned about the toxicity of nicotine.

In religious usage, insufflation denotes a ritual act of breathing upon a person or object to signify the conferral of the Holy Spirit or the expulsion of evil. It has featured in early Christian baptismal rites and survives in some liturgical traditions, notably in the blessing of baptismal water. It is sometimes distinguished from exsufflation, a breathing-out associated specifically with exorcism.

iAUDIO players earned a reputation among audio enthusiasts for sound quality and broad format support that often exceeded what larger competitors offered. Cowon Systems, the South Korean company behind the brand, had begun as a software developer, and its experience with the JetAudio media player informed the audio processing built into its hardware. Many iAUDIO devices included the company's JetEffect equalizer and sound enhancement suite, along with licensed technologies such as BBE processing. Reviewers frequently praised these features for letting listeners tailor playback in ways that the simpler controls of rival players did not allow.

Format compatibility was another distinguishing trait. Several models in the line played Ogg Vorbis and FLAC files at a time when most mainstream portable players were limited to MP3 and WMA. This made the brand popular with users who had built their music libraries around open or lossless formats. The hard-disk-based iAUDIO X5, released in the mid-2000s, was especially notable in this respect. It also offered USB host functionality, which allowed photographs to be transferred directly from a digital camera without an intermediary computer, along with video playback on its small color screen.

Battery life became a recurring selling point as the range matured. Compact flash-memory models such as the iAUDIO 7 were marketed with playback times measured in days rather than hours, a figure that set them apart in a market where shorter endurance was common. Other models in the series, including the U-series and later numbered devices such as the iAUDIO 9 and 10, combined slim designs with FM radio, voice recording, and text viewing.

Over time, Cowon shifted much of its marketing toward products sold under the company's own name, such as the D2 and S9, and the iAUDIO label came to be applied to a narrower portion of the catalog.

The narrative centres on Brenda, identified only by the initial of her surname to protect her identity, whose account forms the emotional and structural core of the work. Rather than presenting her experiences as a single linear chronicle, the piece moves between her recollections and the institutional settings in which she sought help, including police stations, courtrooms and social service offices. This structure emphasises the gap between the private reality of abuse and the public mechanisms meant to address it. Brenda's voice is frequently foregrounded against long pauses and sparse ambient sound, a stylistic choice that critics have linked directly to the title's paradox of a scream that goes unheard.

A recurring theme is the difficulty of being believed. Brenda describes repeated attempts to report her situation, each met with procedural obstacles, scepticism or advice to reconcile with her abuser. Commentators have noted that the work avoids casting individual officials as villains, instead presenting their responses as products of a system that, at the time, treated violence within the home as a largely domestic matter outside the proper scope of law. In this sense the story functions as both personal testimony and broader social critique.

Reception at the time of release was marked by strong reactions. Advocacy groups working with survivors of domestic violence praised its unsentimental depiction and used it in training and awareness sessions, while some reviewers found its restrained pacing demanding. Later assessments have tended to situate it within a wider movement of socially engaged documentary and docudrama that sought to bring hidden forms of harm into public discussion. Scholars of media and gender have cited it as an example of how anonymity can be used not merely as protection but as a deliberate statement, suggesting that Brenda's experience was representative of many women whose names would never appear in official records.

The arrangement that made the purchase possible had its origins in the Treaty of Hartford of 1786, which settled the rival claims of New York and Massachusetts to the lands west of the Hudson Valley. Under its terms New York retained sovereignty over the territory, while Massachusetts received the preemption right, the exclusive privilege of acquiring title from the Haudenosaunee nations who occupied it. In 1788 Oliver Phelps and Nathaniel Gorham, acting for a syndicate of investors, contracted with Massachusetts to buy this right for roughly six million acres at a price of one million dollars, payable in three annual installments of the state's depreciated consolidated securities.

Ownership of the preemption right alone conferred no usable land, so Phelps traveled west that summer to negotiate with the Seneca and their allies at Buffalo Creek. The resulting agreement extinguished Native title to about 2.6 million acres lying east of the Genesee River, together with a tract on the river's western bank intended to serve a gristmill and sawmill, in exchange for a modest cash payment and a small perpetual annuity. Phelps established a land office at Canandaigua in 1789, and surveyors divided the territory into ranges and townships, laying the groundwork for rapid settlement by migrants from New England.

The venture soon met financial difficulty. The proposal that the federal government assume state debts drove up the market value of the Massachusetts securities that Phelps and Gorham had expected to acquire cheaply, leaving them unable to meet their obligations. They surrendered the unpurchased western lands to Massachusetts and in 1790 sold much of their remaining eastern holdings to the financier Robert Morris, who resold them to a group of British investors known as the Pulteney Associates. Massachusetts subsequently conveyed the preemption right for the western lands to Morris as well, setting the stage for the Treaty of Big Tree and the Holland Land Purchase later in the decade.

Elegar's development as a player was gradual rather than sudden, and contemporaries often remarked that his value to a team was easier to see over the course of a full season than in any single game. Tall and long-armed, he was used mainly near the basket, where his responsibilities centered on rebounding, interior defense, and finishing close-range shots created by teammates. Coaches who worked with him tended to praise his willingness to accept a supporting role, a trait that made him a dependable presence in rotations built around higher-scoring guards and wings.

His collegiate years established the pattern that would define much of his career. As an underclassman he saw limited minutes behind more experienced frontcourt players, using the time to improve his footwork and conditioning. By his final seasons he had become a regular starter, and his statistical output rose accordingly, though observers noted that his contributions on the defensive end, such as altering shots, holding position against stronger opponents, and limiting second-chance opportunities, were not fully captured by box scores. Local newspaper coverage from the period frequently described him as the steadying influence in a young lineup.

After completing his college eligibility, Elegar pursued a professional career, a path common among big men of his era who were not immediately established at the highest level of the sport. His time as a professional involved movement between teams and leagues, and his role varied with each roster, but he generally remained the kind of player valued for size, positional discipline, and reliability rather than for individual scoring.

In later accounts, former teammates have emphasized his temperament as much as his play, recalling him as even-keeled and supportive in the locker room. Those recollections have shaped how he is remembered: less as a star than as an example of the role player whose work underpinned the success of the teams around him.

The by-election was triggered by the resignation of Barry McElduff, the Sinn Féin Member of Parliament who had won the seat at the 2017 general election. In early January 2018, on the anniversary of the Kingsmill massacre, McElduff posted a video to social media in which he appeared with a Kingsmill-branded loaf of bread balanced on his head. The 1976 massacre, in which ten Protestant workmen were shot dead in south County Armagh, remains one of the most notorious atrocities of the Troubles. McElduff said the timing was unintentional and that no offence had been meant. Relatives of the victims, unionist politicians and the sole survivor of the attack nonetheless condemned the post as deeply hurtful. Sinn Féin initially suspended McElduff for three months, but as criticism intensified he announced his resignation from Parliament in mid-January, saying he did not wish his continued presence to cause further distress.

Sinn Féin selected Órfhlaith Begley, a solicitor from Carrickmore, as its candidate. The Democratic Unionist Party nominated Tom Buchanan, a long-serving member of the Northern Ireland Assembly. The Social Democratic and Labour Party chose Daniel McCrossan, an Assembly member for the constituency. The Ulster Unionist Party and the Alliance Party also stood candidates. The campaign took place against the backdrop of the continuing suspension of the Northern Ireland Executive and the ongoing negotiations over Brexit, with the question of the Irish border featuring prominently in debate.

Polling took place on 3 May 2018. Begley won comfortably, taking nearly half of the votes cast and a majority of almost 8,000 over Buchanan, who finished second. Her victory made her the first woman to represent West Tyrone at Westminster. At 26, she was also among the youngest members of the House of Commons. In keeping with Sinn Féin's longstanding policy of abstentionism, she declined to take her seat, and so did not swear the oath of allegiance or vote in parliamentary divisions.

A thyristor-switched capacitor (TSC) consists of three principal components connected in series: a capacitor bank, a bidirectional thyristor valve, and a small current-limiting reactor. The thyristor valve is formed from pairs of thyristors connected in inverse parallel, so that current can be conducted in either direction once the devices are fired. In high-voltage installations, many thyristors are connected in series within each valve so that together they can withstand the full blocking voltage. The reactor limits the rate of rise of current through the thyristors and damps oscillations. Together with the capacitor, it also forms a series resonant circuit whose natural frequency is deliberately placed away from the dominant harmonics of the power system, typically between the third and fifth harmonics, to avoid amplifying harmonic currents already present on the network.

Unlike the thyristor-controlled reactor, with which it is often combined in a static VAR compensator, the TSC is not operated with phase-angle control. A capacitor cannot be connected to an alternating voltage at an arbitrary instant without producing a severe inrush current. The thyristors are therefore fired only at the moment when the voltage across the valve is zero or near zero, which normally occurs when the supply voltage equals the residual voltage on the capacitor. Under ideal conditions this allows the capacitor to be brought into circuit with no transient. Once conducting, the thyristors remain on for complete cycles, so the TSC either supplies its full rated reactive power or none at all. Finer control is obtained by dividing the total capacitance into several independently switched branches.

When the TSC is switched off, the thyristors stop conducting at a natural current zero, which coincides with a peak of the capacitor voltage. The capacitor is consequently left charged to the peak of the supply voltage. The blocked valve must then withstand up to twice the peak supply voltage, a requirement that strongly influences the valve's design and cost.

Federal Route 1 is the oldest and longest north–south trunk road in Peninsular Malaysia, running from Bukit Kayu Hitam on the Thai border in Kedah to Johor Bahru at the southern tip of the peninsula. Its alignment follows the western coastal plain, linking many of the country's principal towns and state capitals, including Alor Setar, Ipoh, Kuala Lumpur and Seremban, before continuing through the interior of northern Johor toward the Strait of Johor. Because it traces settlement patterns established during the colonial period, the route passes directly through the centres of numerous smaller towns, which gives it a markedly different character from the limited-access expressways built later.

Much of the road originated as a series of separate colonial-era roads constructed by the British administration in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. These were intended to connect tin-mining districts, rubber estates and administrative centres with ports and railway stations. Over time the segments were joined into a continuous highway, and after independence the federal government assumed responsibility for its maintenance and gradual upgrading under the national route numbering system.

For several decades Federal Route 1 served as the main artery for road traffic along the west coast, carrying freight, long-distance buses and private vehicles. Its importance as a through route declined after the completion of the North–South Expressway in the 1990s, which runs broadly parallel to it and offers faster travel on a tolled, grade-separated alignment. Nevertheless, the older road remains heavily used for local and regional journeys, and it serves as a toll-free alternative for motorists wishing to avoid expressway charges.

The standard of the road varies considerably along its length. Sections near major urban areas have been widened into dual carriageways with interchanges and traffic lights, while rural stretches often remain single carriageways with one lane in each direction. Bypasses have been constructed around several congested towns to divert through traffic from their centres.

The arrival of the Brisbane Bears in the Victorian Football League in 1987 brought elite-level Australian rules football to the Gold Coast for the first time. Although the club carried the name of the state capital, it was based at Carrara Stadium, roughly 80 kilometres south of Brisbane. The arrangement proved difficult from the outset. Crowds were modest, the club struggled on the field, and the venue's distance from Brisbane's population centre limited its appeal to supporters in the city it purported to represent. Financial difficulties compounded these problems, and in 1993 the Bears relocated to the Gabba in Brisbane. The move ended the Gold Coast's brief tenure as a home for national league football and left the region without a top-flight team for nearly two decades.

During this period the code was sustained largely at the community and state-league level. The Southport Sharks, founded in 1961, emerged as the most prominent local club, winning numerous premierships in Queensland's senior competitions and building a substantial licensed-club base that gave it unusual financial strength. Junior participation also expanded as the region's population grew rapidly through migration from southern states, where the game was traditionally dominant.

By the mid-2000s the Australian Football League had identified the Gold Coast as a priority for expansion, viewing the fast-growing corridor as strategically important in a market long dominated by the rugby codes. After Southport promoted an early bid, the AFL took direct control of the venture and granted a licence for a new club. The Gold Coast Suns fielded a team in the TAC Cup in 2009 and the Victorian Football League in 2010 before entering the AFL in 2011 under coach Guy McKenna, with Gary Ablett Jr. recruited as inaugural captain. Carrara Stadium was substantially redeveloped to host the new club, restoring the venue to a central place in the region's sporting life.

Asterias amurensis, commonly known as the northern Pacific seastar, is native to the coastal waters of the northwestern Pacific Ocean, where it occurs along the shores of Japan, Korea, northern China and the Russian Far East. It typically inhabits shallow, sheltered waters such as estuaries, bays and the protected margins of the continental shelf, and it is most often found on soft sediments of mud or sand, although it also occupies rocky reefs and artificial structures such as wharf pilings. The species tolerates a broad range of temperatures and salinities, a trait that has contributed significantly to its success outside its native range.

Adults generally reach a diameter of up to about 50 centimetres and possess five arms that taper to distinctive pointed, often upturned tips. The upper surface is usually yellow to orange, frequently mottled with red or purple, while the underside is a uniform yellow. Small, irregularly arranged spines cover the body, and those along the edges of the arms form a jagged margin.

The seastar is a voracious and generalist predator, feeding primarily on bivalve molluscs such as mussels, scallops, oysters and clams, but it will also consume gastropods, crustaceans, other echinoderms and carrion. Like many asteroids, it can evert its stomach to digest prey externally. In Japan, dense aggregations have long been regarded as a pest of commercial shellfish farms.

Reproduction is highly prolific. A single large female may release up to 20 million eggs in a spawning season, and fertilisation occurs externally in the water column. The resulting planktonic larvae can drift for several weeks to a few months before settling, allowing wide dispersal. This extended larval stage is thought to have enabled the species' introduction into southern Australia, most likely through ballast water discharged by ships. It was first recorded in Tasmania in the 1980s and later became established in Port Phillip Bay, Victoria, where it now threatens native marine communities.

*Divided by Night* is the fourth studio album by the American electronic duo The Crystal Method, consisting of Scott Kirkland and Ken Jordan. It was released in 2009 and was the first full-length record issued on the pair's own label, Tiny e Records. The album followed a period in which the duo had worked largely on soundtrack material and the mix album *Community Service II*. That gap of several years between original studio releases shaped both the expectations surrounding the record and the direction Kirkland and Jordan chose to pursue.

Recording took place largely at the duo's studio in the Los Angeles area. There they continued the hybrid approach that had defined their work since *Vegas*, combining breakbeat rhythms, analog synthesizers and rock-influenced dynamics. Compared with earlier releases, however, *Divided by Night* placed greater emphasis on collaboration with vocalists and instrumentalists from outside electronic music. The reggae singer Matisyahu appears on "Drown in the Now," and Emily Haines of Metric contributes vocals to "Come Back Clean." The electro-pop group LMFAO is featured on "Sine Language," while the former Joy Division and New Order bassist Peter Hook appears on "Kling to Me." Kirkland later described the guest-driven structure as an attempt to keep the material from settling into a single mood across the length of the album.

Critical response was mixed. Several reviewers praised the production quality and the energy of the instrumental tracks, noting that the duo's command of large-scale, festival-oriented arrangements remained intact. Others felt that the variety of guest performers gave the record an uneven character and that the strongest moments recalled the band's late-1990s work rather than extending it. Commercially, the album performed respectably on dance and electronic charts in the United States. It also supported an extended touring cycle, during which many of its tracks were reworked for live performance.

On the morning of June 16, 1943, Zeamer took off from Port Moresby in a battered B-17E Flying Fortress, serial number 41-2666, which his crew had salvaged and heavily modified with additional machine guns. The aircraft, often called "Old 666," had acquired a reputation as a jinxed plane before Zeamer's crew adopted it. Their assignment was a solitary photographic reconnaissance and mapping flight over the western coast of Bougainville in the Solomon Islands, intended to gather information ahead of planned Allied landings. Zeamer volunteered the crew to extend the mission to cover the Japanese airfield on Buka, an addition that significantly increased the danger.

As the bomber completed its mapping run, it was intercepted by a large formation of Japanese fighters, generally reported as about twenty aircraft. In the engagement that followed, which lasted roughly forty minutes, the B-17 sustained severe damage and several crew members were wounded. Zeamer was struck early in the fight, suffering serious injuries to his legs and arms, yet he continued maneuvering the aircraft so that his gunners could bring their weapons to bear. The bombardier, Second Lieutenant Joseph Sarnoski, kept firing from the nose despite mortal wounds and died before the aircraft returned. The crew was credited with destroying several enemy fighters.

With the oxygen system and other equipment damaged, Zeamer brought the bomber down to a lower altitude and, drifting in and out of consciousness from blood loss, helped direct the flight back to New Guinea, where the plane landed at Dobodura. Zeamer's survival was considered doubtful, and he spent more than a year recovering in military hospitals. Both he and Sarnoski received the Medal of Honor, with Sarnoski's awarded posthumously, while every other member of the crew was awarded the Distinguished Service Cross, making it among the most highly decorated crews in American military history.

Uchima's artistic formation was shaped decisively by the years he spent in Japan. Born in Stockton, California, to Japanese immigrant parents, he traveled to Tokyo as a young man to pursue his studies, initially in architecture, and the outbreak of the Pacific War left him unable to return to the United States. He remained in Japan through the war and the difficult years of the occupation, gradually turning from architecture toward painting and then printmaking. During this period he came into contact with the sōsaku hanga, or "creative print," movement, whose adherents rejected the traditional division of labor among designer, carver, and printer in favor of an artist who carried out every stage of the work. The example of Kōshirō Onchi, a leading figure of the movement and an early champion of abstraction in Japanese printmaking, proved especially important to him.

By the 1950s Uchima had developed a distinctive approach to the color woodblock print. Working with water-based pigments and hand-burnished impressions, he built up compositions through numerous blocks and successive printings, often layering translucent tones to produce effects of depth, atmosphere, and shimmering light. His imagery moved steadily away from recognizable subjects toward lyrical abstraction, in which floating bands, soft-edged forms, and fields of graduated color evoked natural phenomena such as wind, water, and seasonal change without depicting them directly.

Uchima returned to the United States in 1959 and settled in the New York area, where his work attracted attention among critics and collectors interested in the convergence of Asian technique and Western abstraction. He received Guggenheim Fellowships and joined the faculty of Sarah Lawrence College, where he taught printmaking for many years and influenced a generation of students. His prints entered the collections of major museums in both the United States and Japan, and he is regarded as an important bridge between postwar Japanese creative printmaking and American abstract art.

Cooper's early career was shaped by the agricultural depression that gripped the rural Midwest in the years following the First World War. After completing his studies at a regional normal school, he returned to his home county and taught for several terms in a one-room schoolhouse, an experience he later credited with forming his lifelong interest in public education. Contemporaries described him as a reserved but persistent organizer, more comfortable in committee rooms and county fairgrounds than on the speaker's platform. During this period he also helped found a local cooperative grain elevator, which brought him into contact with farm advocacy groups and gave him his first taste of public administration.

His entry into elected office came in the early 1930s, when he won a seat in the state legislature on a platform emphasizing farm credit relief and the consolidation of struggling rural school districts. Although he was initially regarded as a minor figure, Cooper gained a reputation for careful attention to budgetary detail, and he was soon appointed to the appropriations committee. There he became associated with efforts to redistribute state education funding toward poorer districts, a cause that drew both praise from reform advocates and resistance from legislators representing wealthier urban constituencies.

Cooper's tenure was not without controversy. Critics argued that his consolidation proposals threatened the independence of small communities, and several of his bills were defeated or substantially amended. Nevertheless, his persistence contributed to the eventual adoption of a revised funding formula that remained in use for decades. In his later years he withdrew from active politics and devoted himself to local historical work, compiling records of early settlement in his region and corresponding with archivists and genealogists. His papers, including correspondence, legislative notes, and personal diaries, were donated by his family to a state historical society, where they remain a resource for scholars of rural education policy.

The term itself originated as a somewhat ironic label, derived from the Italian verb *migliorare* ("to improve"), and was applied to those within the Italian Communist Party (PCI) who argued that the party's task in a developed capitalist democracy was to reform and gradually improve existing society rather than to prepare for its revolutionary overthrow. Although critics initially used the word to suggest a lack of ambition or ideological timidity, the current's adherents eventually accepted it, presenting their position as a realistic adaptation of communist politics to the conditions of postwar Western Europe.

The intellectual roots of migliorismo are usually traced to Giorgio Amendola, who from the 1960s urged the PCI to overcome its separation from the socialist tradition and to work toward a unified party of the Italian left. After Amendola's death in 1980, leadership of the tendency passed largely to Giorgio Napolitano, alongside figures such as Gerardo Chiaromonte and Emanuele Macaluso. The current was particularly strong in the Milan federation of the party, where it cultivated ties with business circles, trade unions and local administrators.

Throughout the 1980s the miglioristi frequently found themselves at odds with the party majority under Enrico Berlinguer, whose emphasis on the "moral question" and whose hostility toward Bettino Craxi's Italian Socialist Party they regarded as politically counterproductive. They favoured dialogue with the socialists, closer alignment with European social democracy and a more positive assessment of the market economy and of Italy's Western alliances.

Following the dissolution of the PCI in 1991, most miglioristi joined the Democratic Party of the Left and welcomed its admission to the Socialist International, seeing in it a vindication of their long-standing positions. Several of the current's members later held high office, most notably Napolitano, who served as President of the Republic from 2006 to 2015, and historians have since debated whether migliorismo anticipated the subsequent evolution of the Italian left or merely accommodated itself to it.

The dispute arose shortly after the Texas Legislature created the Railroad Commission of Texas in 1891 and empowered it to fix maximum charges for the carriage of freight and passengers within the state. John H. Reagan, the former Confederate Postmaster General who had left the United States Senate to chair the new body, led the commission as it issued a schedule of rates that railroad interests regarded as ruinously low. The Farmers' Loan and Trust Company, a New York corporation acting as trustee for bondholders of the International and Great Northern Railroad, brought suit in federal circuit court against the commissioners and the state attorney general. It argued that the prescribed rates would prevent the railroad from earning enough to pay operating expenses and interest on its bonds, and that enforcing them would deprive the bondholders of their property without due process of law.

The commissioners contended that the action was in substance a suit against Texas and therefore barred by the Eleventh Amendment. Writing for a unanimous Court, Justice David J. Brewer rejected that view, reasoning that a suit to restrain state officers from enforcing an unconstitutional measure did not become a suit against the state merely because those officers acted under color of state law. The Court also noted that the Texas statute itself authorized interested parties to challenge the commission's rates in court.

On the merits, Brewer acknowledged that the power to regulate rates belonged to the legislature and that courts could not substitute their own judgment about what charges were wise. Nevertheless, he held that the judiciary retained authority to determine whether a rate schedule was so unreasonable as to amount to confiscation. Finding that the Texas rates left the railroad without just compensation, the Court upheld the injunction against their enforcement, though it narrowed the decree so that the commission was not barred from exercising its other lawful functions. The decision built upon earlier rate cases and anticipated the fuller valuation doctrine announced in Smyth v. Ames four years later.

Uberti's public profile rose during the presidency of Néstor Kirchner, when he was appointed head of the Órgano de Control de Concesiones Viales (OCCOVI), the federal agency charged with supervising highway concessions and toll operators. The body fell within the orbit of the Ministry of Federal Planning, Public Investment and Services, then led by Julio De Vido, and Uberti was widely regarded as one of De Vido's trusted collaborators. Beyond his formal responsibilities over road infrastructure, he became an informal intermediary in the expanding commercial and political relationship between Argentina and Hugo Chávez's Venezuela, a role that later led critics to describe a "parallel embassy" operating outside conventional diplomatic channels.

His career in government ended abruptly in August 2007. A private aircraft chartered by the Argentine state energy company ENARSA arrived in Buenos Aires from Caracas carrying Argentine and Venezuelan officials and businessmen. Customs agents at Aeroparque Jorge Newbery discovered that Guido Antonini Wilson, a Venezuelan-American entrepreneur, was carrying close to 800,000 US dollars in undeclared cash in a suitcase. Uberti had been aboard the flight, and the ensuing controversy, quickly dubbed the "valijagate" or suitcase scandal, forced his resignation within days. The affair became an international matter when proceedings in the United States suggested that the money had been intended for the presidential campaign of Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, an allegation her government rejected.

Uberti remained largely out of public view for more than a decade until the so-called Notebooks case (causa de los Cuadernos) emerged in 2018. Investigators examining records of alleged bribe payments from contractors to officials sought testimony from former members of the planning ministry, and Uberti agreed to cooperate with prosecutors under Argentina's plea-bargaining statute for "repentant" defendants. In his statements he described the collection and transfer of cash from businesses holding road concessions, testimony that drew considerable attention and was contested by defence lawyers for other accused figures.

Jacob's career in western India was shaped as much by his facility with languages as by his military training. After entering the Bombay Army as a young cadet, he devoted himself to the study of Hindustani, Marathi and Persian, and his proficiency soon drew him away from regimental duty and into the political service of the East India Company. These appointments placed him at the junction between the Company's administration and the princely states of the region, where diplomacy, the settlement of disputes, and the supervision of local rulers were often of greater consequence than force of arms. His service in Kathiawar brought him into contact with the peninsula's numerous chieftains and their complicated rivalries, and he acquired a reputation as an officer who understood the customs and sensibilities of the people he dealt with.

Alongside his official duties, Jacob pursued a lively interest in the antiquities of the country. While stationed in Kathiawar he took part in efforts to record the ancient rock inscriptions at Girnar, near Junagadh, which preserve a version of the edicts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka. Accurate copies of such texts were of great value to scholars in Europe and India who were then piecing together the decipherment of early Indian scripts, and his contribution earned him a modest place in the history of Indian epigraphy.

The rebellion of 1857 tested Jacob in a different way. Placed in charge at Kolhapur when disaffection spread to the troops there, he acted with decision to contain the outbreak and prevent it from spreading through the southern Maratha country. His conduct was widely praised by contemporaries and brought him official recognition. In later life he set down his recollections in *Western India Before and During the Mutinies*, a work that combined personal reminiscence with reflections on British policy toward Indian states, and which remains a useful source for historians of the period.

Spottiswood's legal career advanced rapidly under the patronage of the crown and the influence of his father, Archbishop John Spottiswoode. After studying at the University of Glasgow and at Exeter College, Oxford, he spent several years travelling on the Continent, where he gained a reputation for learning in civil law, theology and the classical languages. On his return to Scotland he was admitted to the bench of the Court of Session in 1622, taking the judicial title of Lord New Abbey. In 1633 Charles I appointed him Lord President of the court, a promotion that placed him at the head of the Scottish judiciary while still in his thirties.

His close association with the episcopal establishment made him a target once opposition to the king's religious policies erupted in the late 1630s. The Covenanting movement regarded him as an instrument of royal and prelatical authority, and during the political settlement of 1641 he was effectively removed from his office. He withdrew to the king's side, and in 1643 or 1644 Charles named him Secretary of State for Scotland in place of the Earl of Lanark, an appointment the Covenanting authorities refused to recognise.

Spottiswood later joined the royalist forces of the Marquess of Montrose, carrying the king's commission to him. He was captured after Montrose's defeat at Philiphaugh in September 1645 and was tried by the Scottish Parliament, then sitting at St Andrews, which condemned him for treason. He was beheaded at St Andrews in January 1646. Contemporary accounts state that he was prevented from addressing the crowd from the scaffold and that he met his death with notable composure.

Beyond his political career, Spottiswood is remembered as a legal writer. His collection of decisions and observations on Scots law, known as his Practicks, was published posthumously in 1706 and remained a valued source for historians of early modern Scottish jurisprudence.

Saskatchewan's transportation network has been shaped by its vast area, its dispersed rural population, and an economy long dependent on moving agricultural and resource commodities to distant markets. The province maintains one of the most extensive road systems in Canada relative to its population, comprising provincial highways along with a dense web of municipal grid roads laid out according to the Dominion Land Survey. Two national routes cross the province from east to west. The Trans-Canada Highway (Highway 1) serves the southern cities of Regina, Moose Jaw, and Swift Current, while the Yellowhead Highway (Highway 16) links Yorkton, Saskatoon, North Battleford, and Lloydminster. North of the agricultural belt, the road network thins considerably, and many remote communities rely on gravel roads, seasonal winter roads built over frozen lakes and muskeg, or air service.

Rail transport played a decisive role in the settlement of the province in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when the Canadian Pacific Railway and the predecessors of Canadian National built lines that determined the location of hundreds of towns and grain elevators. Although many branch lines were abandoned in the latter half of the twentieth century, both major railways continue to operate main lines through Saskatchewan, and a number of shortline railways, some community-owned, carry grain and other freight to connecting points. Passenger rail is limited to VIA Rail's Toronto–Vancouver service, *The Canadian*, which stops at Saskatoon and several smaller communities. Regina lost its passenger service in 1990.

Intercity bus travel declined sharply after the provincial government dissolved the Saskatchewan Transportation Company in 2017 and Greyhound Canada withdrew from western Canada the following year, leaving private operators to fill some of the gaps. Air travel is centred on Saskatoon John G. Diefenbaker International Airport and Regina International Airport, supplemented by regional carriers serving the north. The province also operates a small number of river ferries where highways cross major waterways.

Martha Wadsworth was born in 1710 in Lebanon, Connecticut, a farming community in the eastern part of the colony. Little is recorded of her early education, but her later writing shows a close familiarity with the Bible, with Puritan devotional literature, and with the hymns of Isaac Watts, whose meters and phrasing she frequently echoed. In 1732 she married Oliver Brewster, a descendant of the Plymouth elder William Brewster, and the couple settled in Lebanon, where they raised several children. Her household and religious life supplied much of the material for her verse, which ranges from domestic reflection to spiritual meditation.

Brewster's reputation rests on a single volume, *Poems on Divers Subjects*, printed in New London in 1757 and reissued in Boston the following year. The collection is widely regarded as one of the earliest books of poetry published by a woman under her own name in the American colonies. Its contents include devotional lyrics, verse paraphrases of scripture, poems addressed to family members, and pieces responding to public events, among them the anxieties of the French and Indian War. Several poems reflect the evangelical fervor of the Great Awakening, which had swept through Connecticut in the previous decade and deeply shaped the spiritual culture of towns such as Lebanon.

A frequently repeated anecdote holds that some of Brewster's contemporaries doubted a woman could have written such verses, and that she was challenged to compose a poetic paraphrase of a scriptural passage on the spot in order to prove her authorship. Whether or not the story is accurate in its details, it has often been cited to illustrate the obstacles faced by colonial women who sought a public voice in print.

The date of Brewster's death is uncertain. Her work received comparatively little attention for nearly two centuries, but later scholars of early American literature have recovered her as a significant figure in the history of women's writing in New England.

Greenhouse gas emissions are among the most widely studied effects of livestock production. A 2013 assessment by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations estimated that livestock supply chains account for about 14.5 percent of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions, with cattle raised for beef and milk responsible for roughly two thirds of that total. Much of this takes the form of methane, which is produced by enteric fermentation in the digestive systems of ruminants and by the decomposition of stored manure. Nitrous oxide released from manure and from fertilizers applied to feed crops is another major contributor. Because methane has a relatively short atmospheric lifetime but a high warming potential, reductions in ruminant emissions are often cited as a means of slowing near-term warming.

Land use is a second major area of concern. Pasture and cropland devoted to feed together occupy the majority of the world's agricultural land. A 2018 analysis published in *Science* by Joseph Poore and Thomas Nemecek estimated that meat, dairy, eggs and aquaculture use about 83 percent of farmland while supplying 18 percent of calories and 37 percent of protein. Expansion of grazing land and of feed crops such as soybeans has been a leading driver of deforestation in the tropics, particularly in the Amazon basin, where cattle ranching is associated with most of the cleared area. The resulting loss of habitat is regarded as a significant pressure on biodiversity.

Animal agriculture also affects water resources and air quality. Irrigating feed crops consumes considerable fresh water, and nitrogen and phosphorus carried in runoff from manure and fertilized fields can cause eutrophication in rivers, lakes and coastal waters, contributing to hypoxic zones such as the one in the northern Gulf of Mexico. Ammonia volatilized from animal waste contributes to the formation of fine particulate matter. The severity of these effects varies considerably with species, production system and region.

*Ziapelta* is known from a single specimen, catalogued as NMMNH P-64484 and housed at the New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science in Albuquerque. The fossil was recovered from the Kirtland Formation of the San Juan Basin in northwestern New Mexico. These rocks date to the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, roughly 74 to 73 million years ago, and belong to the Kirtlandian land vertebrate age. The material consists of a nearly complete skull, a portion of the first cervical half-ring (a bony collar of fused osteoderms that protected the neck), and several isolated osteoderms from elsewhere on the body. The specimen was described and named in 2014 by Victoria Arbour and colleagues. The generic name combines the Zia sun symbol, which appears on the state flag of New Mexico, with the Latin *pelta*, meaning "small shield." The specific name, *sanjuanensis*, refers to the San Juan Basin.

The skull of *Ziapelta* combines features that distinguish it from other North American ankylosaurids. Its snout bears a conspicuous, roughly triangular armor plate on the midline between the nostrils. The horns projecting from the squamosal bones at the back corners of the skull are long and curve noticeably downward. The cranial armor is ornamented with a distinctive pattern of polygonal scales, or caputegulae, and the osteoderms of the cervical half-ring are tall and sharply keeled. Together these traits allowed the describers to separate *Ziapelta* from contemporaneous forms such as *Nodocephalosaurus*, which is also known from the Kirtland Formation, and from the ankylosaurids of Alberta and Montana.

Phylogenetic analyses place *Ziapelta* within Ankylosaurinae, among the derived North American taxa related to *Anodontosaurus*, *Euoplocephalus*, and *Scolosaurus*, although its exact position remains uncertain. The genus is significant as evidence that ankylosaurids were more diverse in southern Laramidia than earlier records suggested. It also contributes to ongoing debate about whether northern and southern dinosaur faunas of western North America were distinct.

The novel is set in the Final Empire, a bleak dominion on the world of Scadrial where ash falls constantly from a red sky and unnatural mists cover the land each night. For a thousand years the empire has been ruled by the Lord Ruler, an apparently immortal figure worshipped as a god. He rose to power after supposedly defeating a mysterious threat known as the Deepness. Beneath him, society is rigidly divided between the nobility, descended from his early supporters, and the skaa, an oppressed underclass who labor on plantations and in the forges and mills of the capital city, Luthadel.

The story follows Vin, a distrustful sixteen-year-old street thief who discovers that she is a Mistborn, a person able to use all the powers of Allomancy. This system of magic lets its practitioners ingest and "burn" specific metals to gain abilities such as enhanced strength, heightened senses, the manipulation of emotions, and the pushing or pulling of nearby metal objects. Most Allomancers, called Mistings, can burn only a single metal, which makes Mistborn exceptionally rare and dangerous. Vin is recruited by Kelsier, a charismatic thief known as the Survivor of Hathsin, who escaped the Lord Ruler's brutal mines. He has assembled a crew of specialists to attempt what he presents as the ultimate heist: toppling the empire itself.

Under the guidance of Kelsier and the Terrisman steward Sazed, Vin trains in Allomancy and infiltrates the aristocracy in the guise of a provincial noblewoman, Valette Renoux. At the balls of the Great Houses she meets Elend Venture, an idealistic heir whose company complicates her view of the nobility. Sanderson structures the narrative around the conventions of a caper story while questioning familiar fantasy tropes, in particular by imagining a world in which the prophesied hero has failed. Each chapter opens with an excerpt from a logbook whose significance becomes clear only as the plot nears its conclusion.

Chennai is frequently described as the health capital of India, a reputation built on its concentration of multi-specialty and super-specialty hospitals and on the comparatively low cost of treatment. The city draws a large share of the country's medical tourists, with patients arriving from other Indian states as well as from Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, the Middle East and several African nations. Commonly sought procedures include cardiac surgery, organ transplantation, joint replacement, ophthalmic care and cancer treatment.

The public sector has deep historical roots in the city. The Rajiv Gandhi Government General Hospital, which traces its origins to a small facility established by the East India Company in 1664, is regarded as one of the oldest hospitals in the country and is attached to Madras Medical College, founded in 1835. Other major government institutions include the Government Stanley Hospital, the Government Kilpauk Medical College Hospital, the Government Royapettah Hospital, the Institute of Child Health and Hospital for Children in Egmore, and the Institute of Mental Health in Kilpauk. These hospitals provide free or heavily subsidised treatment and serve large numbers of patients from across Tamil Nadu and neighbouring states. Primary care is delivered through a network of urban health centres and dispensaries administered by the Greater Chennai Corporation.

Private and non-profit providers expanded rapidly from the late twentieth century onward. Apollo Hospitals, opened in 1983 by Prathap C. Reddy, is widely credited as the first corporate hospital in India and remains headquartered in the city. Sankara Nethralaya, established in 1978, is a prominent charitable eye hospital, while the Cancer Institute in Adyar, founded in 1954 under the leadership of Muthulakshmi Reddy, is among the country's leading oncology centres. Other notable institutions include the Madras Medical Mission, MIOT International and the Sri Ramachandra Medical Centre. Chennai has also played a leading role in deceased-donor organ transplantation, supported by a state-run registry that coordinates the allocation of organs among public and private hospitals.

Vrioni was born on 15 October 1998 in San Severino Marche, in the Italian region of Marche, to Albanian parents, and began playing football with local side Matelica before entering the youth system of Sampdoria in 2014. A tall, left-footed centre-forward, he was sent on loan to gain senior experience, first with Pistoiese in Serie C during the 2017–18 season and then with Venezia in Serie B the following year. A further loan to Cittadella followed in the first half of the 2019–20 campaign.

In January 2020 Vrioni was acquired by Juventus, who initially assigned him to their reserve side, Juventus U23, competing in Serie C. He was part of the squad that won the Coppa Italia Serie C that season, and he made his Serie A debut for the first team in the closing weeks of the 2019–20 campaign under Maurizio Sarri, as the club secured the league title. Opportunities with the senior side remained limited, however, and in 2021 he was loaned to WSG Tirol of the Austrian Bundesliga. The move proved the turning point of his early career: he scored 17 league goals and finished among the division's leading scorers, drawing attention from clubs abroad.

In July 2022 Vrioni signed for the New England Revolution of Major League Soccer as a Designated Player, joining for a reported fee of close to four million dollars. His first months in the United States were disrupted by injury, but he went on to become a regular member of the club's attack in subsequent seasons.

At international level Vrioni was eligible to represent both Italy and Albania. He appeared for Albanian youth teams before briefly switching to play for Italy at under-19 and under-20 level, and ultimately committed his senior international future to Albania, for whom he made his full debut in 2018.

The European Union Mission in Armenia (EUMA) is a civilian mission deployed under the Common Security and Defence Policy. It was established by a decision of the Council of the European Union on 23 January 2023 and formally launched on 20 February 2023. It succeeded the European Union Monitoring Capacity, a temporary deployment of some forty observers drawn from the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia, which had operated along the Armenian side of the border with Azerbaijan from October to December 2022 following the clashes of September that year.

The mission's stated objectives are to contribute to stability in the border areas of Armenia, to build confidence and improve human security in conflict-affected communities, and to support the normalisation of relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Its personnel are unarmed and carry no executive powers. They conduct regular patrols and report their observations to Brussels. EUMA operates exclusively on Armenian territory, as Azerbaijan has not consented to any presence on its side of the border.

The headquarters is located in Yeghegnadzor, in Vayots Dzor Province, with forward operating bases in Kapan, Goris, Jermuk, Martuni and Ijevan. The initial mandate ran for two years with a staff of roughly one hundred, about half of them observers. In December 2023 the Council agreed to expand the mission to 209 personnel, and in January 2025 the mandate was extended until February 2027. Markus Ritter, a German Federal Police officer, was appointed as the first Head of Mission, while operational command rests with the Managing Director of the Civilian Planning and Conduct Capability in Brussels. Canada became the first non-EU state to contribute personnel.

The deployment was welcomed by the Armenian government, which had requested it, but it drew criticism from both Azerbaijan and Russia. Baku has accused the observers of engaging in "binocular diplomacy", while Moscow has characterised the mission as an attempt to undermine Russian influence and mediation efforts in the South Caucasus.

Play in Hoc Mazarin falls into two distinct parts, and it is this composite structure that gives the game its historical interest. In the first part, the players compete for three separate stakes, placed in advance, which are awarded for the best point, the best sequence and the best tricon. The point goes to the player holding the highest total of card values in a single suit, the sequence to the longest or highest run of consecutive cards in one suit, and the tricon to the best set of three or four cards of the same rank. These combinations may be contested by raising, much as in the vying games of the period, so that a player with a weak hand might yield a stake rather than pay to see an opponent's cards. A stake that goes unclaimed is usually carried forward to the following deal.

The second part is a game of the stops type. The eldest hand leads a card, conventionally the lowest held, and continues to play upward in numerical order without regard to suit for as long as he can. When he is unable to supply the next rank, the turn passes to an opponent who can. Six cards have special status and are themselves known as hocs: the four kings, the queen of spades and the jack of diamonds. A hoc can stand in for any card needed to keep a run going, and it stops the sequence, so that whoever plays it earns a payment from each opponent and may begin afresh with a card of his choice. The first player to get rid of all his cards wins the deal and is paid by the others according to the number of cards left in their hands.

The game was normally played by two or three persons with a full pack of fifty-two cards, fifteen being dealt to each of two players and twelve to each of three.

The phrase gained national prominence during the presidency of Woodrow Wilson, who used it in 1915 and 1916 to describe American neutrality in the First World War. Republican candidate Warren G. Harding adopted the slogan in his successful 1920 campaign, pairing it with opposition to the League of Nations and support for protective tariffs and immigration restriction. During the same decade the expression was also taken up by nativist organizations, including the Ku Klux Klan, which gave it lasting associations with xenophobia in the eyes of later critics.

The term is most closely identified with the America First Committee, a non-interventionist pressure group founded in September 1940 to oppose United States entry into the Second World War. At its height the committee claimed some 800,000 members, and its most prominent spokesman was the aviator Charles Lindbergh. His September 1941 speech in Des Moines, Iowa, which accused British, Jewish, and Roosevelt administration interests of pushing the country toward war, drew widespread condemnation as antisemitic. The committee dissolved within days of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, and the slogan largely disappeared from mainstream political discourse for decades afterward.

The phrase was revived in the 1990s by the commentator Pat Buchanan, who used it in his presidential campaigns to advocate economic nationalism, reduced immigration, and withdrawal from overseas commitments. It returned to the center of American politics in 2016, when Donald Trump embraced it as the organizing theme of his foreign policy. In his inaugural address of January 2017, Trump declared that "from this day forward, it's going to be only America first." His administration subsequently withdrew from the Trans-Pacific Partnership and the Paris Agreement, imposed tariffs on steel, aluminum, and a wide range of Chinese goods, and renegotiated the North American Free Trade Agreement. Supporters characterized these measures as a restoration of national sovereignty, while critics argued that they weakened alliances and diminished American influence abroad.

The practice takes its name from Richard Pyle, an ichthyologist based in Hawaii, who in the 1980s was making deep dives to collect fish from the so-called twilight zone of coral reefs, at depths between about 180 and 220 feet. Pyle noticed that he felt markedly less fatigued and unwell after some dives than after others, and on reviewing his logs he found that the more comfortable dives were those on which he had caught specimens.
