Fish brought up from depth must have their swim bladders vented with a hypodermic needle to prevent the expanding gas from killing them, and Pyle habitually paused for two or three minutes well below his first scheduled decompression stop to do this. He concluded that the pause itself, rather than any other feature of the dive, accounted for the difference.

From this observation he devised a simple procedure that could be applied to any decompression schedule. The diver calculates the midpoint between the maximum depth and the first required decompression stop and halts there for roughly two minutes. If the distance between this new stop and the first required stop exceeds about 30 feet (9 metres), a further stop is inserted at the midpoint of the remaining interval, and the process is repeated until the gap is smaller than that threshold. The decompression schedule is then recalculated to take account of the additional time spent at depth.

Pyle described the method in articles published in the mid-1990s, and it was adopted widely among technical divers, since it appeared consistent with bubble-based decompression models that favour limiting bubble formation early in the ascent. Subsequent experimental work, notably a study by the United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit published in 2011, cast doubt on the benefit of deep stops, suggesting that the extra time at depth allows slower tissues to continue absorbing inert gas and may increase rather than reduce the risk of decompression sickness.

The periodicity of the Fibonacci numbers under modular reduction follows from a simple counting argument. Each term of the sequence modulo n is determined by the two preceding terms, and there are only n² possible pairs of residues, so some pair must eventually recur. Because the recurrence can also be run backwards, the sequence is purely periodic, returning to the initial pair 0, 1 rather than entering a cycle after some preliminary stretch. The length of this cycle is the Pisano period, commonly denoted π(n). For example, the Fibonacci numbers modulo 3 run 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 2, 2, 1 before repeating, so π(3) = 8. The first few values, beginning with n = 1, are 1, 3, 8, 6, 20, 24, 16, 12, 24 and 60. The last of these reflects the fact that the final decimal digits of the Fibonacci numbers repeat every sixty terms, an observation recorded by Joseph-Louis Lagrange in 1774.

Several general properties are known. With the exception of π(2) = 3, every Pisano period for n greater than 2 is even. If m and n are coprime, then π(mn) is the least common multiple of π(m) and π(n), a consequence of the Chinese remainder theorem. This reduces the study of the function to prime powers. For a prime p, π(p^k) divides p^(k−1)·π(p), and equality is conjectured to hold in every case. A counterexample would require the existence of a Wall–Sun–Sun prime, none of which has been found. For primes congruent to 1 or 4 modulo 5, the period divides p − 1, whereas for primes congruent to 2 or 3 modulo 5 it divides 2(p + 1). The special cases are π(2^k) = 3·2^(k−1) and π(5^k) = 4·5^k.

The period never exceeds 6n, and this bound is attained exactly when n has the form 2·5^r with r at least 1, as in π(10) = 60 and π(50) = 300. A systematic account of these results was given by D. D. Wall in 1960.

Basuki was appointed Minister of Public Works and Housing by President Joko Widodo in October 2014, heading a ministry newly formed through the merger of the Ministry of Public Works and the Ministry of Public Housing. A career civil servant rather than a party politician, he had spent more than three decades in the public works bureaucracy, serving as Director General of Water Resources, Inspector General, head of the ministry's research and development agency, and Director General of Spatial Planning. He had also led the national team that responded to the Sidoarjo mudflow disaster in East Java in 2006.

As minister, Basuki became one of the central figures in the administration's infrastructure drive. His ministry oversaw the construction of dozens of dams, thousands of kilometres of national roads and toll roads, including substantial sections of the Trans-Java and Trans-Sumatra networks, as well as irrigation systems, border crossing posts, and subsidised housing under the One Million Houses programme. He was also responsible for the venues and supporting facilities built or renovated for the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta and Palembang, among them the refurbished Gelora Bung Karno sports complex. Widodo retained him in the same post after re-election in 2019, making him one of the few ministers to serve through both terms.

Basuki drew public attention for his informal manner and his habit of making frequent field inspections, and Widodo once jokingly referred to him as "Daendels", after the Dutch colonial governor-general who built the Great Post Road. He was also known as the drummer of Elek Yo Band, an amateur group composed of cabinet ministers that performed at several public events.

In June 2024, following the resignation of Bambang Susantono, Basuki was named acting head of the Nusantara Capital City Authority, the body charged with developing Indonesia's planned new capital in East Kalimantan. After his ministerial term ended in October 2024, President Prabowo Subianto appointed him as the authority's permanent head.

Li Baoyu's family had long been settled in the Hexi region, where they were known as breeders of horses and traced their descent from An Xinggui, who had helped the early Tang court subdue the rebel ruler Li Gui. He was originally named An Chongzhang, and he made his reputation as an officer on the northwestern frontier before the outbreak of the An Lushan Rebellion drew him into the campaigns in central China. Ashamed to share a surname with the rebel leader, he petitioned Emperor Suzong for a new one. The emperor granted him the imperial surname Li, and his household registration was transferred to the capital, Chang'an.

His most celebrated military service came under the general Li Guangbi during the defence of Heyang against Shi Siming in 759. Entrusted with the southern fortress and asked to hold it for two days, Li Baoyu is said to have deceived the besieging commander by feigning a willingness to surrender. He used the delay to strengthen his defences, then renewed the fight and drove off the attackers. The episode was recorded by traditional historians as an example of his resourcefulness, and it contributed to the wider Tang success in holding the Heyang position.

In the years that followed he was rewarded with a series of senior commands, including the military governorship of Zelu, and he was created Duke of Liang. After Tibetan forces briefly occupied Chang'an in 763, Emperor Daizong posted him to Fengxiang, west of the capital, where he was responsible for guarding the approaches against further incursions and for suppressing banditry in the mountains to the south. He held honorary chancellor rank, though he is recorded as having declined some of the highest titles offered to him. This modesty was praised by contemporaries. His younger cousin Li Baozhen served as his deputy at Zelu and later became a prominent general in his own right. Li Baoyu died in 777 and received posthumous honours from the court.

After completing his degree in physical and chemical sciences at the University of Lisbon in 1926, Valadares obtained a grant that allowed him to pursue research abroad, first in Geneva and then in Paris. At the Institut du Radium he worked under Marie Curie, preparing a doctoral thesis on the spectroscopy of radioactive elements, which he defended at the University of Paris in 1933. During this period he also became interested in applying X-rays to the scientific examination of paintings, a technique he later introduced in Portugal in collaboration with the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga.

Returning to Lisbon, he joined the Faculty of Sciences and became one of the driving forces behind the modernisation of its physics laboratory, then directed by Cyrillo Soares. Together with colleagues such as Aurélio Marques da Silva, he sought to establish a research culture in an institution that had until then been devoted almost exclusively to teaching. In 1943 he helped found the journal Portugaliae Physica, intended to give Portuguese physicists a means of publishing original work and making it known internationally.

His academic career in Portugal ended abruptly in 1947, when the Salazar government dismissed a number of university teachers regarded as politically unreliable. Valadares, whose democratic sympathies were well known, was among those removed from their posts. At the invitation of Irène Joliot-Curie he settled in France, where he joined the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique and resumed his investigations in nuclear and atomic spectroscopy, working for a time with Salomon Rosenblum at the Bellevue laboratory. He eventually rose to the rank of research director and headed the Centre de Spectrométrie Nucléaire et de Spectrométrie de Masse at Orsay.

Throughout his exile he maintained close contact with younger Portuguese scientists, many of whom trained in his laboratory. He was able to revisit Portugal after the revolution of 1974, and received official recognition there before his death in Paris in 1982.

Paola lies on the Tyrrhenian coast of the province of Cosenza, where the slopes of the Coastal Chain descend steeply toward the sea. The historic centre occupies a hillside terrace some distance above the shoreline, while the modern quarter and the marina have grown up along the narrow coastal plain around the railway station. The origin of the town's name is uncertain. One tradition connects it with a Roman landowner of the Aemilius Paullus family, and another derives it from the Latin *pabula*, meaning pastures.

During the Middle Ages the settlement passed through the hands of several feudal lords, including the Ruffo family, before coming under the Spinelli, marquises of Fuscaldo, at the end of the fifteenth century. Like many communities on the Calabrian coast, Paola was exposed to raids from the sea, and in 1555 it was sacked by the Ottoman corsair Turgut Reis, known in Italy as Dragut. The town and its religious buildings were badly damaged in the attack.

Paola is best known as the birthplace of Saint Francis of Paola, born there in 1416, who founded the Order of Minims and died in France in 1507. The sanctuary dedicated to him stands in the gorge of the Isca torrent above the town, on the site where he lived as a young hermit and gathered his first followers. The complex includes a basilica, a cloister and a number of places associated with miracles attributed to the saint. It remains one of the principal pilgrimage destinations in southern Italy. Francis was canonised in 1519 and was later proclaimed patron saint of Calabria and of Italian seafarers. The town holds its main celebrations in his honour in early May.

Paola is also an important railway junction, where the line to Cosenza branches inland from the main Tyrrhenian route linking Naples and Reggio Calabria. The Cosenza line passes beneath the Coastal Chain through the Santomarco tunnel.

The film was conceived after the Foo Fighters rented a mansion in Encino, California, to record their tenth studio album, *Medicine at Midnight*. Dave Grohl developed a story inspired by the house's atmosphere, and the screenplay was written by Jeff Buhler and Rebecca Hughes. BJ McDonnell, who had previously directed *Hatchet III* and worked with the band Slayer on music videos, was hired to direct. Principal photography took place largely in the same house where the album had been recorded, and the project was kept secret until its announcement in late 2021. All six members of the band (Grohl, Taylor Hawkins, Nate Mendel, Pat Smear, Chris Shiflett and Rami Jaffee) appear as fictionalized versions of themselves, alongside a supporting cast that includes Whitney Cummings, Leslie Grossman, Will Forte, Jeff Garlin and Jenna Ortega.

The plot follows the band as they move into a decaying mansion with a grim musical past in order to record a long-overdue album. Grohl, struggling with creative block, discovers a recording left in the basement by a band called Dream Widow, whose sessions decades earlier had ended in bloodshed. He becomes possessed by a demonic force that drives him to complete an ever-expanding epic song, and his bandmates are killed off in increasingly gruesome fashion. The film leans heavily on practical gore effects and pays affectionate tribute to horror cinema of the 1970s and 1980s. Filmmaker John Carpenter makes a brief cameo as a studio engineer and also contributed to the film's theme music.

Open Road Films released *Studio 666* theatrically in the United States on February 25, 2022. It received mixed reviews from critics, who generally praised the band's enthusiasm and the splatter effects while faulting the running time and uneven humor, and it performed modestly at the box office. The film was released only a month before Hawkins's death in March 2022.

The novel is set in Kabul in the late 1990s, when the city lay under Taliban rule, and follows two married couples whose lives converge. Atiq Shaukat, a former mujahid, works as a jailer guarding condemned prisoners, while his wife Musarrat, who once nursed him back to health during the war against the Soviets, is dying of an incurable illness. Mohsen Ramat, a young man from a once-prosperous family, and his wife Zunaira, a former lawyer barred from her profession, cling to memories of a more liberal city. Early in the narrative Mohsen finds himself drawn into a crowd stoning a woman accused of adultery and, to his own horror, throws a stone. His confession of this act to Zunaira opens a rift between them that widens after the couple are humiliated by Taliban enforcers during a walk through the streets.

During a subsequent quarrel Zunaira pushes Mohsen, who falls and is killed. She is condemned to death and placed in Atiq's custody, where the jailer, seeing her unveiled, becomes consumed by her beauty. Musarrat, recognising in her husband an emotion she believed lost to him, offers to take the prisoner's place beneath the burqa at the public execution. The substitution succeeds, but Zunaira vanishes, and Atiq's frantic search for her ends in madness and violence at the hands of a mob.

Written in French by the Algerian author Mohammed Moulessehoul under the pen name Yasmina Khadra, the book was published in 2002 as *Les Hirondelles de Kaboul*, with an English translation by John Cullen appearing in 2004. Critics praised its spare prose and its portrait of how totalitarian rule corrodes private affection and individual conscience, though some questioned its distance from Afghan experience. It was shortlisted for the International Dublin Literary Award and adapted as an animated film in 2019, directed by Zabou Breitman and Éléa Gobbé-Mévellec.

Forrest's rise to wider prominence came in the early 2000s, after a long apprenticeship in the welterweight division. His first attempt at the vacant IBF welterweight title, against Raul Frank in August 2000, ended in a no contest when an accidental clash of heads left Frank unable to continue. The two met again in May 2001 at Madison Square Garden, where Forrest won a clear unanimous decision to claim his first world championship. He soon relinquished that belt to pursue a more lucrative bout with Shane Mosley, the unbeaten WBC champion, who was then widely regarded as one of the best fighters in the world pound for pound.

The two men had history: Forrest had defeated Mosley as an amateur at the 1992 United States Olympic trials. When they met as professionals in January 2002, Forrest was a considerable underdog, yet he knocked Mosley down twice in the second round and controlled the remainder of the fight to win a unanimous decision. He repeated the victory in a rematch held in Indianapolis that July, and was named Fighter of the Year by The Ring magazine for 2002.

His reign ended abruptly in January 2003, when the hard-punching Nicaraguan Ricardo Mayorga stopped him in the third round of a unification bout. Forrest lost the rematch by majority decision six months later. Serious shoulder and elbow injuries then required surgery and kept him out of the ring for roughly two years.

Returning in 2005, Forrest campaigned at light middleweight, earning a disputed decision over Ike Quartey in 2006 before outpointing Carlos Baldomir in July 2007 to win the vacant WBC title. He lost the belt to Sergio Mora in June 2008 but regained it in an immediate rematch three months later, in what proved to be his final fight. He was shot and killed during a robbery in Atlanta in July 2009.

On 21 May 1941, while sailing unescorted from New York to Mozambique by way of South Africa, *Robin Moor* was stopped in the tropical Atlantic by the German submarine *U-69*, commanded by Kapitänleutnant Jost Metzler. The encounter took place roughly 750 nautical miles west of Freetown, Sierra Leone, well outside the zones in which Germany had declared unrestricted submarine warfare. The vessel was flying the flag of the United States, then still a neutral power, and carried a mixed commercial cargo that included automobiles, tinplate and other general goods. After examining the ship's papers, Metzler declared that the freighter was carrying contraband destined for Germany's enemies and informed her master, Captain W. E. Myers, that she would be sunk.

The nine officers, twenty-nine crewmen and eight passengers, among them a small child, were given a short time to abandon ship in four lifeboats. *U-69* then sank the freighter with a torpedo and gunfire. Before departing, the submarine's crew passed some provisions to the survivors, reportedly tins of bread and butter, and Metzler is said to have promised to report their position by radio. No rescue followed from this assurance, and the boats were left to make their own way across hundreds of miles of open ocean.

The lifeboats eventually became separated. Three were found on 2 June by the British merchant ship *City of Wellington*, which carried their occupants to Cape Town. The fourth, with eleven people aboard, drifted for eighteen days before being sighted by the Brazilian steamer *Osório* and landed at Pernambuco. All forty-six people survived. News of the sinking reached the American public only after the first survivors came ashore. It provoked considerable indignation, and President Franklin D. Roosevelt, in a message to Congress on 20 June 1941, denounced the attack as the act of an outlaw nation.

In the summer of 1942, under pressure from British agents who had grown impatient with his delays, Zervas left Athens for the mountains of his native Epirus and began organising the armed bands of the National Republican Greek League (EDES). The organisation had been founded the previous September on a republican and vaguely socialist platform, with the exiled General Nikolaos Plastiras as its nominal political head, though effective control in the field rested with Zervas himself and his deputy, Komninos Pyromaglou. His forces remained concentrated in Epirus and parts of Aetolia-Acarnania, where local and family ties gave him a dependable base of support.

The most celebrated operation of this period was the destruction of the Gorgopotamos railway viaduct on the night of 25 November 1942. Zervas's men fought alongside guerrillas of the communist-led ELAS under Aris Velouchiotis, and a team of British saboteurs commanded by Brigadier Eddie Myers. The attack severed the rail link between Thessaloniki and Athens for several weeks and became one of the best-known acts of sabotage in occupied Europe. It was also the last occasion on which the two principal Greek resistance organisations cooperated on such a scale.

Relations with ELAS deteriorated steadily thereafter. Zervas, formerly a committed Venizelist and anti-monarchist, sent a message of loyalty to King George II in March 1943, a gesture that strengthened his standing with the British but alienated many of his republican followers. Open fighting between the two movements broke out in October 1943 and continued until the Plaka agreement of February 1944 fixed their respective zones. His opponents accused him of reaching tacit understandings with the German command during these months, a charge that remains disputed among historians. In December 1944, ELAS launched a general offensive against EDES, and within days Zervas's forces were driven to the coast and evacuated by the Royal Navy to Corfu.

In anthropological theory, the chiefdom occupies an intermediate position between egalitarian tribal societies and the bureaucratic state. Elman Service, whose 1962 typology of band, tribe, chiefdom and state shaped much later scholarship, characterized it as a society organized around a permanent central office that coordinated economic, religious and social life. Unlike the leaders of tribal societies, who typically earned influence through personal achievement, a chief generally inherited his position. Rank was commonly determined by genealogical proximity to a founding ancestor, so that entire lineages could be ordered by seniority. Robert Carneiro later defined the chiefdom in political terms, as an autonomous unit comprising a number of villages or communities under the permanent control of a paramount chief.

Scholars frequently distinguish between simple and complex chiefdoms. A simple chiefdom consists of a single tier of authority above the local community, often embracing a few thousand people, whereas a complex chiefdom contains two or more levels of hierarchy, with subordinate chiefs owing tribute and allegiance to a paramount. Such polities are thought to be inherently unstable, prone to cycles of consolidation and collapse as rival elites compete for followers and as subordinate centres break away. The archaeologist Timothy Earle has emphasized that chiefs maintained power by controlling staple production, long-distance exchange in prestige goods, military force and ideology, rather than through a formal apparatus of administrators.

Early accounts stressed redistribution, in which the chief collected surplus produce and reallocated it among his people. Later research on Polynesian societies, particularly Hawaii, suggested that such mobilized goods chiefly supported the elite and their retainers, financing feasts, monumental construction and warfare. Archaeologists commonly identify chiefdoms through settlement hierarchies, differentiated burials and public monuments, as at the Mississippian centres of the southeastern United States. The concept has nonetheless drawn criticism, with some researchers, notably Timothy Pauketat, arguing that it imposes a rigid evolutionary scheme on historically diverse societies.

Sandaime J Soul Brothers from Exile Tribe was formed in 2010 as the third generation of the J Soul Brothers name, a lineage that traces back to the group founded by Hiro in 1999 and renamed Exile in 2001. The lineup was assembled under the management company LDH and consists of seven members. Naoto and Naoki Kobayashi, both of whom had performed with the second-generation group before joining Exile, were appointed leaders. They were joined by performers Elly, Kenjiro Yamashita and Takanori Iwata. The two vocalists, Ryuji Imaichi and Hiroomi Tosaka, were selected through the Exile Presents Vocal Battle Audition 2, a nationwide contest that drew tens of thousands of applicants.

The group made its debut on the Avex label Rhythm Zone in November 2010 with the single "Best Friend's Girl", followed by a self-titled first album in 2011. Their early releases leaned toward ballads and mid-tempo R&B. Over the next few years they moved toward a harder, dance-oriented sound influenced by electronic dance music and hip-hop, and this shift helped set them apart from Exile itself.

Their commercial breakthrough came in 2014 with "R.Y.U.S.E.I.", an EDM-driven single whose "running man" choreography became a widely imitated phenomenon in Japan. The song won the Grand Prix at the 56th Japan Record Awards. The group repeated the achievement the following year with the ballad "Unfair World", becoming one of the few acts to win the prize in consecutive years. The 2015 album Planet Seven ranked among the best-selling releases of the year in Japan, and the accompanying Blue Planet dome tour drew more than a million spectators.

Since then the members have increasingly pursued individual activities alongside group work. Imaichi and Tosaka have released solo recordings, Iwata has built a career as a film and television actor, and Elly has performed as a rapper under the name Crazyboy.

Set several years after the events of the first film, the story returns to the Clearwater Marine Aquarium in Florida, where Winter, the bottlenose dolphin fitted with a prosthetic tail, has become a popular attraction and a source of inspiration for visitors with disabilities. When Panama, the elderly dolphin who had served as Winter's surrogate mother and poolmate, dies of old age, Winter becomes withdrawn and uncooperative, at one point injuring Sawyer Nelson during a routine session. An inspector from the United States Department of Agriculture reminds the aquarium's director, Dr. Clay Haskett, that regulations forbid keeping a dolphin in isolation, since the animals are highly social. The staff are given thirty days to find a suitable female companion or see Winter transferred to a marine park in Texas.

Hopes initially rest on Mandy, a stranded dolphin recovering from sunburn and a lung infection, but Clay insists that the aquarium's mission of rescue, rehabilitation and release must take precedence, and Mandy is returned to the ocean once she is healthy. The decision strains his relationship with his daughter Hazel, who is eager to be treated as an adult member of the team. Sawyer, meanwhile, hesitates over an offer to join a prestigious semester-at-sea program, reluctant to leave while Winter's future is uncertain. The arrival of Hope, an orphaned calf too young to have learned how to survive in the wild, provides a final chance, although the first attempt to introduce the two dolphins fails when Hope is unsettled by Winter's unusual movement in the water.

Charles Martin Smith wrote and directed the film, with Harry Connick Jr., Ashley Judd, Nathan Gamble, Cozi Zuehlsdorff, Kris Kristofferson and Morgan Freeman reprising their roles. Winter and Hope appear as themselves, and surfer Bethany Hamilton makes a brief cameo. Warner Bros. Pictures released the film in the United States on September 12, 2014.

Volumes formed in Los Angeles, California, in 2009, emerging from the same online-driven progressive metal movement that produced many of the bands associated with the term "djent." The group distinguished itself early by employing two lead vocalists, Michael Barr and Gus Farias, whose alternating screams were set against the low-tuned, syncopated guitar work of Diego Farias and Daniel Braunstein. The original lineup was completed by bassist Raad Soudani and drummer Nick Ursich. Their self-released EP, *The Concept of Dreaming*, appeared in 2010 and circulated widely through social media and file-sharing communities, earning the band a contract with Mediaskare Records.

The band's debut full-length album, *Via*, was released in 2011 and was praised for balancing rhythmic heaviness with ambient and melodic passages. Its follow-up, *No Sleep* (2014), expanded on this approach by incorporating more clean singing and electronic textures, and it entered the Billboard 200, the group's first appearance on that chart. Extensive touring followed, but the period was also marked by internal strain, and Barr announced his departure in 2015.

Myke Terry, formerly of Bury Your Dead, was subsequently recruited as his replacement, and the band signed with Fearless Records. *Different Animals*, issued in 2017, leaned further into hip hop and R&B influences, a shift that divided listeners but broadened the group's audience. Further upheaval came at the end of the decade, when Gus Farias left the band and Barr returned to share vocal duties with Terry. In February 2020, Diego Farias, who had recently stepped away from the group to focus on production work, died at the age of twenty-seven.

The remaining members dedicated their subsequent work to his memory. *Happier?*, released in 2021, was received as a return to the band's earlier sound while retaining the melodic sensibility of its later material, and Volumes has since continued to record and tour.

The film centers on Jeff Lang, a Seattle obstetrician played by Tobey Maguire, whose comfortable but stagnant marriage to Nealy (Elizabeth Banks) begins to unravel after a seemingly trivial domestic problem. When raccoons repeatedly tear up the expensive new sod in the couple's backyard, Jeff becomes fixated on getting rid of them, eventually resorting to poison. This decision sets off a chain of escalating consequences, among them the accidental death of a cat belonging to his eccentric neighbor Lila, portrayed by Laura Linney. At the same time, Jeff drifts into a brief affair with Rebecca (Kerry Washington), the wife of his friend Peter (Ray Liotta), and soon finds himself entangled in blackmail, deception, and an unwanted pregnancy. His attempts to redeem himself lead him to donate a kidney to Lincoln (Dennis Haysbert), an ailing acquaintance from his pickup basketball games, whose gratitude takes a violent and unexpected form.

Writer and director Jacob Aaron Estes, who had previously made the drama *Mean Creek* (2004), conceived the story as a dark comedy of manners in which small moral lapses compound into catastrophe. Principal photography took place in and around Seattle, and the completed film premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in January 2011. Its distribution rights were acquired there by the Weinstein Company in one of the festival's larger deals that year. The release was delayed considerably, however, and the film did not reach American audiences until late 2012, when it was made available through video on demand ahead of a limited theatrical run.

Critical response was mixed. Reviewers frequently praised the performances, singling out Linney's turn as the unpredictable neighbor and Haysbert's quietly sympathetic work, while faulting the film for an uneven tone that wavered between farce and moral fable. Some critics admired its willingness to follow its protagonist's self-justifications to bleak conclusions, but others found the satire heavy-handed and the narration intrusive. The film earned little at the box office during its brief theatrical engagement.

When a clock loses its external reference, most commonly a signal from a Global Navigation Satellite System such as GPS, it is said to enter holdover. In this state the local oscillator, which had previously been disciplined by the reference, must continue to provide time and frequency on its own. The quality of the holdover is determined by how slowly the output drifts away from the value it would have had if the reference were still available. Because no free-running oscillator is perfectly stable, the accumulated time error grows continuously, and the duration for which a system can remain within its required tolerance is known as the holdover period.

Several factors contribute to the drift observed during holdover. Ageing of the quartz crystal or atomic resonator produces a gradual and largely predictable change in frequency, while variations in ambient temperature cause shorter-term fluctuations that are harder to anticipate. Any residual frequency offset present at the moment the reference was lost produces a time error that increases linearly, whereas ageing produces an error that grows quadratically with elapsed time. Random noise processes within the oscillator add a further component that cannot be corrected by prediction.

To extend holdover performance, modern disciplined oscillators often employ adaptive algorithms that learn the behaviour of the oscillator while the reference is present. By recording how the control signal has responded to temperature and ageing over hours or days, the system can continue to apply estimated corrections after the reference disappears. Kalman filtering is commonly used for this purpose.

Requirements vary considerably between applications. Cellular base stations using time-division duplexing typically need phase alignment within a few microseconds, which a high-quality oven-controlled crystal oscillator may sustain for several hours and a rubidium standard for a day or longer. Power grid measurement units and financial timestamping systems impose their own limits, and the choice of oscillator reflects a compromise between cost, power consumption and the expected length of reference outages.

The series follows Charlie Morningstar, the optimistic princess of Hell and daughter of Lucifer, who opens a hotel intended to rehabilitate sinners so that their souls may be redeemed and admitted to Heaven. Her project is motivated by the annual Extermination, a purge in which angelic forces led by Adam descend to cull Hell's population. She is assisted by her girlfriend and manager Vaggie; the hotel's first resident, the adult film performer Angel Dust; and Alastor, a powerful and enigmatic figure known as the Radio Demon, whose reasons for supporting the venture remain unclear. Other staff include the bartender Husk, the housekeeper Niffty, and the inventor Sir Pentious, who arrives as a spy before becoming a sincere guest.

Vivienne Medrano, known online as VivziePop, developed the concept over several years and produced a pilot episode through her studio SpindleHorse Toons, financed largely by supporters on Patreon. Released on YouTube in October 2019, the pilot drew tens of millions of views and built a substantial fan following. In 2020, A24 announced that it had picked up the project for a full series, with Bento Box Entertainment later joining as an animation partner. Most roles were recast with performers from Broadway theatre, including Erika Henningsen as Charlie, Stephanie Beatriz as Vaggie, Blake Roman as Angel Dust, Amir Talai as Alastor, Keith David as Husk, and Jeremy Jordan as Lucifer. The songs, a central feature of every episode, were written by Sam Haft and Andrew Underberg.

The first season of eight episodes premiered on Amazon Prime Video in January 2024, and the series was subsequently renewed for further seasons. Critics generally praised its animation, musical numbers, and vocal performances, while some found its pacing rushed and its humor uneven. Its soundtrack reached the Billboard charts. A companion series set in the same universe, Helluva Boss, has been released on YouTube since 2020.

Gordon's reputation rests chiefly on his study of the epidemic of puerperal fever that afflicted Aberdeen between December 1789 and March 1792. As physician to the Aberdeen Dispensary he attended many of the town's poorer women in childbirth, and he kept careful records of each case, noting the date of delivery, the patient's residence, the outcome, and the name of the midwife or practitioner who had been present. From these tables he observed that the disease did not strike at random, as would be expected if it arose from some noxious quality of the atmosphere. Instead it followed particular attendants from one lying-in woman to the next. He concluded that the fever was carried by those who had recently visited or delivered infected patients, and he acknowledged candidly that he himself had been the means of conveying it to a considerable number of women.

He published these findings in 1795 as *A Treatise on the Epidemic Puerperal Fever of Aberdeen*. In it he also drew attention to the close relationship between puerperal fever and erysipelas, which had been prevalent in the town at the same time. He recommended that the bedclothes and garments of the sick be burned or thoroughly fumigated, and that nurses and physicians wash themselves and have their clothing purified before attending another patient. His preferred treatment was copious early bleeding and purging, which followed the therapeutic conventions of his day and did little to commend the work to later readers.

The treatise was poorly received in Aberdeen. By identifying the midwives associated with fatal cases, Gordon provoked resentment among practitioners and the public alike, and his practice suffered. Recalled to naval service soon afterwards, he contracted tuberculosis and died in 1799 at his brother's farm in Aberdeenshire. His conclusions anticipated by roughly half a century those of Oliver Wendell Holmes and Ignaz Semmelweis, and Holmes acknowledged his work.

The 2020–21 season was Manchester United's 29th in the Premier League and their 46th consecutive season in the top flight of English football. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the campaign began later than usual, and almost all matches were played behind closed doors. Under manager Ole Gunnar Solskjær, the club strengthened its squad with the signings of Donny van de Beek from Ajax, Alex Telles from Porto and the free agent Edinson Cavani, while the young wingers Facundo Pellistri and Amad Diallo were also recruited.

United made a poor start to the league season, losing 3–1 at home to Crystal Palace on the opening weekend and 6–1 to Tottenham Hotspur at Old Trafford in October. Results improved markedly thereafter, and a 1–0 victory away to Burnley in January briefly took the club to the top of the table. In February, United beat Southampton 9–0, equalling the record margin of victory in the Premier League. They finished the season as runners-up to Manchester City with 74 points and went unbeaten away from home in the league throughout the campaign.

In the UEFA Champions League, United were drawn alongside Paris Saint-Germain, RB Leipzig and İstanbul Başakşehir. Despite winning their first two matches, they finished third in the group after a 3–2 defeat in Leipzig and dropped into the UEFA Europa League. There they eliminated Real Sociedad, Milan, Granada and Roma to reach the final in Gdańsk, where they drew 1–1 with Villarreal before losing 11–10 in a penalty shoot-out, with goalkeeper David de Gea missing the decisive kick.

Domestically, United reached the semi-finals of the EFL Cup, losing 2–0 to Manchester City, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Leicester City in the quarter-finals. Bruno Fernandes finished as the club's leading scorer with 28 goals in all competitions. The closing weeks of the season were also marked by supporter protests against the club's owners, the Glazer family, following the failed European Super League proposal.

The episode opens with Glenn Quagmire failing to turn up for a planned fishing trip with Peter Griffin and Joe Swanson, who go to his house and find him unconscious after an episode of autoerotic asphyxiation. He is rushed to hospital, where his sister Brenda arrives to sit by his bedside, accompanied by her boyfriend Jeff. It quickly becomes apparent that Jeff is domineering and violent, belittling Brenda in front of others and beating her in private. After Quagmire recovers, he invites the couple to stay with him, and he and the Griffins grow increasingly alarmed by the bruises Brenda tries to conceal and by the excuses she makes for her partner. An intervention organised by Lois fails when Brenda defends Jeff and announces that she is pregnant and that the two plan to marry.

Convinced that his sister will eventually be killed, Quagmire persuades Peter and Joe that the only solution is to murder Jeff. The three take him on a supposed hunting trip, but Jeff realises their intentions and turns on them, leading Quagmire into the woods for a brutal fight. Jeff appears to strangle Quagmire to death, only for Quagmire, whose earlier habits have left him accustomed to being choked, to revive and crush Jeff against a tree with a car. The men bury the body and forge a note telling Brenda that Jeff has left her.

The episode was written by Alec Sulkin and directed by Dominic Bianchi, with Kaitlin Olson voicing Brenda and Ralph Garman voicing Jeff. It was first broadcast on Fox in the United States on October 30, 2011, as part of the show's tenth season. Critical response was largely negative. Reviewers objected to the uneasy mixture of graphic domestic abuse and the series' customary cutaway humour, and several argued that the programme was ill-suited to handling the subject. The Parents Television Council also condemned the episode for its depiction of violence against women.

In surgical practice, insufflation most commonly refers to the introduction of gas into a body cavity in order to create working space for the operator. During laparoscopy, carbon dioxide is delivered into the peritoneal cavity through a Veress needle or a trocar placed under direct vision, producing a pneumoperitoneum that lifts the abdominal wall away from the viscera. Carbon dioxide is preferred because it is inexpensive, non-flammable, and highly soluble in blood, which allows absorbed gas to be buffered and eliminated through the lungs and reduces the danger posed by accidental gas embolism. Intra-abdominal pressure is usually maintained between 12 and 15 mmHg in adults, with lower values used in children. Higher pressures can impede venous return, raise the diaphragm, and compromise ventilation. Absorption of the gas may also cause hypercapnia and acidosis, so anaesthetists routinely monitor end-tidal carbon dioxide and adjust ventilation accordingly.

Gas insufflation is likewise used in endoscopy of the gastrointestinal tract. Room air was the traditional distending agent in colonoscopy, but carbon dioxide has increasingly replaced it because its rapid absorption lessens post-procedural bloating and pain. In computed tomographic colonography, automated insufflators deliver the gas at controlled pressure through a small rectal catheter to ensure adequate distension of the bowel for imaging.

The term also describes a route of drug administration in which a powder, vapour, or aerosol is drawn or blown into the nasal passages. The nasal mucosa has a rich blood supply, and substances absorbed there avoid first-pass metabolism in the liver, often producing a rapid onset of action. Licensed preparations given in this way include naloxone for opioid overdose, midazolam for seizures, and desmopressin. Recreational drugs such as cocaine are frequently taken by the same route. Chronic use may damage the mucosa and, in severe cases, lead to perforation of the nasal septum.

The iAUDIO line was introduced in 2000 by the South Korean company Cowon Systems, which had previously been known chiefly for its JetAudio media software for personal computers. The first model, the CW100, was a compact flash-memory MP3 player, and it was followed by a succession of small devices such as the CW200, CW300 and iAUDIO 4. These established the brand's reputation in its home market and, increasingly, among audio enthusiasts abroad.

In 2004 Cowon entered the hard-drive player market with the iAUDIO M3, a 20-gigabyte unit unusual for having no display on its body; it relied instead on a wired remote control with its own screen. Its successor, the iAUDIO X5, appeared in 2005 with a colour screen, video playback and USB On-The-Go support, allowing photographs to be copied directly from a digital camera. Flash-based models continued alongside these, including the pendant-style iAUDIO U2 and U3, the AA-battery-powered G3, and the later iAUDIO 7, which was noted for its long battery life and touch-sensitive controls. The iAUDIO 6 was built around a miniature 0.85-inch hard disk.

Reviewers and users generally praised the players for sound quality and for broad format support. In addition to MP3 and WMA, many models could play Ogg Vorbis and FLAC files, a feature rarely offered by larger competitors at the time. Most also included an FM radio tuner, voice and line-in recording, and a suite of BBE audio enhancement effects. Many operated as standard USB mass storage devices, so files could be transferred without proprietary software, which made the players popular with users of Linux and other non-Windows operating systems. The open-source Rockbox firmware was later ported to several of the hard-drive models.

From the mid-2000s Cowon began marketing its flagship products, such as the A2 and D2, under the company name rather than the iAUDIO label, although the brand persisted on models including the iAUDIO 9 and iAUDIO 10.

The syndicate led by Oliver Phelps and Nathaniel Gorham contracted with the Commonwealth of Massachusetts in April 1788 to buy the preemptive right to some six million acres in what is now western New York. The agreed price was $1,000,000, payable in three annual installments. Payment could be made in Massachusetts consolidated securities, which were then trading at a fraction of their face value, a provision that made the terms far more favorable than the nominal sum suggested. Massachusetts held the right to sell under the Treaty of Hartford of 1786, which had settled the two states' competing colonial claims by granting New York sovereignty over the territory while reserving to Massachusetts the exclusive right to purchase the land from its Native inhabitants.

Because the contract conveyed only preemption, Phelps still had to extinguish Iroquois title. In July 1788 he met with leaders of the Seneca and other nations of the Haudenosaunee at Buffalo Creek. There he secured a cession of roughly 2.25 million acres lying between the Preemption Line on the east and the Genesee River on the west, together with a smaller parcel on the river's western bank known as the Mill Yard Tract. The Seneca received $5,000 and a perpetual annuity of $500, and they declined to part with the remaining lands west of the Genesee.

Phelps then had the tract surveyed into ranges and townships and opened a land office at Canandaigua in 1789, often described as one of the first of its kind in the United States. Sales to settlers and speculators proceeded briskly, but the syndicate's finances soon collapsed. The federal assumption of state debts caused Massachusetts securities to rise sharply in value, greatly increasing the real cost of the outstanding installments. Unable to meet their obligations, Phelps and Gorham surrendered their claim to the lands west of the Genesee, which reverted to Massachusetts, and in 1790 they sold most of their unsold eastern holdings to the financier Robert Morris.

Federal Route 1 runs for roughly 826 kilometres along the western side of Peninsular Malaysia, from Johor Bahru in the south to the Thai border at Bukit Kayu Hitam in Kedah. It is the oldest and longest federal road in the country, and its Kilometre Zero is located in the centre of Johor Bahru. From there the road heads north-west through Kulai, Ayer Hitam, Yong Peng and Segamat before crossing into Negeri Sembilan at Gemas. It then continues through Tampin and Seremban, enters Selangor near Kajang, and passes directly through Kuala Lumpur, where sections of it are known locally as Jalan Cheras and Jalan Ipoh.

North of the capital, the route passes through Rawang and crosses into Perak at Tanjung Malim. It then serves a string of towns including Slim River, Bidor, Tapah, Kampar and Gopeng before reaching Ipoh. Beyond Ipoh it winds through Kuala Kangsar and Taiping, enters the mainland portion of Penang at Seberang Perai, and passes through Butterworth. The final stretch runs through Kedah via Sungai Petani, Alor Setar, Jitra and Changlun, ending at the border checkpoint, where it connects with Thailand's Phetkasem Road.

The road was built in stages during the British colonial period, beginning in the late nineteenth century, by linking existing cart tracks and trunk roads between the tin-mining and plantation centres of the Malay states. For much of the twentieth century it was the main north–south artery of the peninsula, carrying most long-distance passenger and freight traffic. Growing congestion and a high accident rate eventually led to the construction of the North–South Expressway, which was completed in 1994 and runs largely parallel to the older road.

Although it has lost most of its through traffic to the expressway, Federal Route 1 remains an important toll-free alternative and a key local link for the towns along its length. Many sections have been widened to dual carriageways, particularly in urban areas.

The by-election was triggered by the resignation of Barry McElduff, who had been elected as the Sinn Féin Member of Parliament for West Tyrone at the general election of June 2017. On 5 January 2018, the anniversary of the 1976 Kingsmill massacre in which ten Protestant workmen were shot dead by republican paramilitaries, McElduff posted a video on social media showing himself with a loaf of Kingsmill-branded bread balanced on his head. The video provoked widespread condemnation, including from relatives of the victims and from Alan Black, the sole survivor of the attack. McElduff apologised and insisted that he had not intended any reference to the killings. Sinn Féin initially suspended him from party activity for three months, a sanction which critics described as inadequate, and on 15 January he announced his resignation from the seat.

Polling took place on 3 May 2018, the same day as local elections in England. Sinn Féin selected Órfhlaith Begley, a 26-year-old solicitor from Carrickmore, to defend the seat, which the party had held since 2001. She was opposed by Thomas Buchanan of the Democratic Unionist Party, Daniel McCrossan of the Social Democratic and Labour Party, Chris Smyth of the Ulster Unionist Party and Stephen Donnelly of the Alliance Party. Efforts to agree on a single cross-community candidate, an idea raised in the aftermath of the controversy, came to nothing.

Begley retained the seat for Sinn Féin with 16,346 votes, a share of just under 47 per cent, giving her a majority of nearly 8,000 over Buchanan. The party's share of the vote fell by several percentage points compared with the previous general election, and turnout declined to about 55 per cent. Begley became the first woman to represent the constituency. In keeping with Sinn Féin's long-standing policy of abstentionism, she did not take her seat in the House of Commons.

In the episode, Liz Lemon prepares to tape the pilot of *Dealbreakers*, a talk show spun off from the relationship-advice sketch and book that made her catchphrase popular. Jack Donaghy, who has championed the project as a potential hit for the network, grows nervous about its prospects and begins to micromanage every element of the production, from the set design to the opening titles. His interference, combined with the unfamiliar pressure of appearing on camera, sends Liz into a spiral of insecurity. Jenna Maroney, quietly resentful that Liz is being given a starring vehicle, offers her backhanded advice about performing, and this only deepens Liz's anxiety. Liz starts to adopt the vain and erratic habits of the actors she ordinarily supervises, and eventually locks herself in her dressing room and refuses to come out.

A recurring visual joke concerns the high-definition cameras installed for the new show. Seen through the lens, Liz appears haggard and aged, while Jack looks like a younger version of himself and Kenneth Parcell is rendered as a felt puppet. Pete Hornberger, left to run *TGS* in Liz's absence, struggles to keep the writers and the production on track without her.

In a parallel storyline, Tracy Jordan acquires a diamond-encrusted necklace bearing the letters "EGOT" and learns that the acronym stands for the Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony awards. He resolves to make winning all four his new life goal, and seeks counsel from Whoopi Goldberg, who appears as herself and is one of the few performers to have completed the set.

The episode ends with Jack conceding that Liz's talents lie behind the camera rather than in front of it, and the pilot is abandoned before it can be broadcast. Critics singled out the high-definition sequence and the introduction of the "EGOT" concept, which went on to become a running thread in later episodes and entered wider popular usage.

Elegar played four seasons of college basketball at Drexel University in Philadelphia, where he developed from a lightly recruited prospect into one of the leading frontcourt players in the Colonial Athletic Association. A 6 ft 9 in forward-center, he was noted for his shot-blocking and rebounding as well as an efficient scoring touch around the basket. In his junior season he was a central figure on the Drexel team that won several notable non-conference road games and earned a berth in the National Invitation Tournament, and he received all-conference recognition for his play. He finished his collegiate career in 2008 ranked among the program's leaders in points, rebounds and blocked shots.

After going unselected in the 2008 NBA draft, Elegar began a professional career overseas, spending his early seasons with clubs in Turkey. He later moved to Estonia, first with Rakvere Tarvas and then with Kalev/Cramo of Tallinn, where he enjoyed the most successful period of his career. With Kalev he won Estonian league championships and competed in the VTB United League against leading clubs from Russia and Eastern Europe. His mobility and timing as a defender earned him recognition as one of that competition's best defensive players, and he was regularly among its leaders in blocked shots and rebounds. His performances in Tallinn raised his profile across Europe and led to further contracts abroad, including a return to the Turkish league, where he played for several teams in subsequent seasons.

Born in the United States Virgin Islands, Elegar has also represented the territory in international competition. He became a regular member of the Virgin Islands national team, appearing in regional tournaments such as the Centrobasket and in the FIBA AmeriCup, where he served as one of the side's principal interior players alongside other professionals based in Europe and the Americas.

Work on the album began after Ken Jordan and Scott Kirkland of The Crystal Method left the converted garage known as the Bomb Shelter, where they had made their earlier records, and built a larger, purpose-designed studio in North Hollywood that they named Crystalwerks. The move delayed the sessions considerably, but the duo later described the new facility as central to the record's sound, since it gave them room to track live instruments and to host visiting musicians rather than relying chiefly on samples and file exchanges. The album was issued in May 2009 through their own imprint, Tiny e Records, five years after its predecessor, *Legion of Boom*.

More than any previous Crystal Method release, *Divided by Night* is built around collaboration. Matisyahu contributes vocals to the lead single "Drown in the Now", and Peter Hook of New Order supplies his distinctive high-register bass on "Dirty Thirty". Emily Haines of Metric sings on "Come Back Clean", Justin Warfield of She Wants Revenge appears on "Kling to the Wreckage", and Jason Lytle of Grandaddy fronts the closing stretch of the record with "Slipstream". The Los Angeles electro-hop duo LMFAO feature on "Sine Language", and singer-songwriter Meiko lends a softer presence to "Falling Hard". Drummer Samantha Maloney also performs on several tracks, reinforcing the album's partly live character.

Critics were divided on the result. Some reviewers praised the broadened palette and the stronger emphasis on song structure, while others felt that the parade of guests diluted the aggressive big beat identity established on *Vegas*. Even so, the album performed respectably on the American charts and earned a nomination for the Grammy Award for Best Electronic/Dance Album at the 52nd ceremony. "Sine Language" was later remixed and issued as a single, and several of the album's instrumental pieces were licensed for use in television, film trailers and video games.

A thyristor-switched capacitor consists of a power capacitor bank connected in series with a bidirectional thyristor valve and, usually, a small current-limiting reactor. Unlike the thyristor-controlled reactor, which can be varied continuously by phase control, the capacitor branch is operated only fully on or fully off. To obtain a stepwise variable output, several branches are commonly connected in parallel, and in a static VAR compensator the steps are combined with a controlled reactor so that the net reactive power can be adjusted smoothly. In three-phase installations the branches are normally arranged in delta, although star connections are sometimes used.

Because the current through a capacitor leads the voltage by ninety degrees, the thyristors cease conducting at a current zero that coincides with a voltage peak. The capacitor is therefore left charged to approximately the peak system voltage when the valve blocks, and this trapped charge decays only slowly through discharge resistors. As the supply voltage continues to alternate, the blocked valve must withstand a voltage that reaches roughly twice the peak value half a cycle later. For this reason the valve of a thyristor-switched capacitor generally requires more series-connected thyristors than that of a comparable thyristor-controlled reactor.

Turn-on must be timed with care. Ideally the valve is fired at the instant when the voltage across it is at a minimum, preferably zero, so that the capacitor is reconnected without a transient. Firing at any other instant produces a large oscillatory inrush current, whose amplitude and rate of rise are limited by the series reactor. The reactor also serves to detune the branch, preventing resonance with the system impedance at characteristic harmonic frequencies.

Since the branch conducts full sinusoidal current when on and none when off, it produces no harmonic currents in steady-state operation and so requires no filters of its own. This is an advantage over mechanically switched capacitors, which cannot be switched as rapidly or as frequently.

On June 16, 1943, Zeamer and his crew volunteered for an unescorted photographic mapping mission over Bougainville in the Solomon Islands, flying a salvaged Boeing B-17E Flying Fortress, serial number 41-2666, known as "Old 666". The crew had rebuilt the aircraft and fitted it with additional machine guns, including a fixed nose gun that Zeamer could fire from the pilot's seat. The flight was meant to chart the island's western coast around Empress Augusta Bay ahead of the Allied landings planned for later that year. The crew had also been asked to reconnoiter the Japanese airfield on nearby Buka.

As the bomber neared the end of its mapping run, it was intercepted by a force of Japanese fighters. Zeamer held the aircraft steady so the photography could be completed, and the fighters then pressed a series of frontal attacks. Cannon fire shattered the nose and mortally wounded the bombardier, Second Lieutenant Joseph Sarnoski, who crawled back to his gun and kept firing until he collapsed. Zeamer was struck in both arms and legs, and one leg was broken, but he refused medical aid and continued to maneuver the damaged bomber through an engagement that lasted about forty minutes. During the fight he was credited with shooting down at least one enemy aircraft himself. With the oxygen system destroyed, he dived to a lower altitude, and only when the attackers withdrew did he hand over the controls. Drifting in and out of consciousness, he went on directing the flight until the bomber made an emergency landing at Dobodura, New Guinea.

Zeamer had lost so much blood that he was at first believed dead, and he spent some fifteen months recovering in hospitals. He and Sarnoski each received the Medal of Honor, and every other member of the crew was awarded the Distinguished Service Cross, making it one of the most highly decorated aircrews in American history.

Uchima was born in Stockton, California, in 1921 to parents who had emigrated from Okinawa, and he grew up in Los Angeles. In 1940 he traveled to Japan to study architecture at Waseda University in Tokyo, in keeping with his father's wishes. The outbreak of the Pacific War left him stranded there, and during these years he abandoned architecture in favor of painting, studying oil technique privately with established Japanese artists.

His turn toward printmaking came in the postwar period, when his fluency in both English and Japanese made him a valuable interpreter. He assisted the American writer and collector Oliver Statler, who was then interviewing artists for his study *Modern Japanese Prints: An Art Reborn*. Through this work Uchima met the leading figures of the sōsaku-hanga, or "creative print," movement, among them Onchi Kōshirō, whose abstract approach left a lasting impression on him. Unlike traditional ukiyo-e, which divided labor among designer, carver, and printer, sōsaku-hanga artists insisted on performing every stage themselves, and Uchima embraced this principle. Largely self-taught in the medium, he began exhibiting woodcuts in Japan in the mid-1950s.

Around 1960 he returned to the United States with his wife, the artist Toshiko Uchima, and their family, settling in New York City. There he taught printmaking for two decades at Sarah Lawrence College and also at Columbia University, introducing a generation of American students to Japanese water-based woodblock methods. He received fellowships from the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation in 1962 and 1970.

Uchima's mature prints combined the lyrical abstraction of postwar American painting with the delicate gradations made possible by hand-printing on Japanese paper. His late *Forest Byobu* series, built up from dozens of separate impressions, evoked shimmering screens of light and color. A stroke in 1982 ended his artistic career, and he died in New York in 2000.

*Asterias amurensis* is native to the coastal waters of northern China, the Korean Peninsula, Japan and far eastern Russia, with its range extending across the northern Pacific to the Bering Sea and Alaska. It favours sheltered, shallow environments such as bays and estuaries, where it lives on mud, sand and rocky substrates from the intertidal zone to depths of about 200 metres. The species prefers cool water, generally between 7 and 10 °C, although established populations have adapted to temperatures as high as 22 °C. It tolerates a wide range of salinities, which enables it to colonise estuaries.

The species was first recorded outside its native range in the Derwent Estuary of Tasmania in 1986, and a second population became established in Port Phillip Bay, Victoria, during the 1990s. It was probably introduced as larvae carried in the ballast water of ships arriving from Japan, though transport on fouled hulls may also have contributed. Its high fecundity has aided its spread: a single female can release between 10 and 25 million eggs in a year, and the planktonic larvae may drift for up to 120 days before settling. Within a few years of its discovery in Australia, the Derwent population was estimated to number in the millions.

The seastar is a voracious, opportunistic predator that feeds mainly on bivalve molluscs such as mussels, scallops and clams. It also eats gastropods, crabs, barnacles, ascidians and other echinoderms. In its introduced range it has been linked to declines in native shellfish and causes losses in aquaculture by preying on stock and settling on lines and cages. It is also considered a threat to the critically endangered spotted handfish, because it eats the stalked ascidians on which the fish attaches its eggs. The species is listed among the world's hundred worst invasive alien species, and control efforts, including diver removal and trapping, have had limited success.

Cooper spent most of his professional life in the public schools of Mississippi, where he rose from classroom teaching to become one of the state's best-known school administrators of the first half of the twentieth century. After early appointments as a teacher and principal in smaller communities, he served as superintendent of the Kosciusko schools before accepting the superintendency of the Vicksburg city schools, the post with which his name remains most closely associated. He held that office for several decades, guiding the district through the financial hardships of the Great Depression, the disruptions of the Second World War, and the rapid growth in enrollment that followed.

As superintendent, Cooper was regarded as a careful manager and a persistent advocate for improved facilities, higher teacher qualifications, and a broader secondary curriculum. He pressed local officials and voters to support bond issues for new construction, arguing that the city's aging buildings could no longer accommodate its student population. He was also active in state and regional professional circles, taking part in the work of the Mississippi Education Association and in efforts to standardize accreditation requirements for high schools across the state. Like other Southern administrators of his generation, he presided over a racially segregated system, and the resources he secured were distributed unequally between white and Black schools.

His long tenure was commemorated when the city named a new high school in his honor. H. V. Cooper High School opened in Vicksburg in the late 1950s and served as the city's principal white high school until the reorganization that accompanied desegregation, after which its campus was absorbed into the consolidated Vicksburg school system. Former students and colleagues remembered him as a formal, exacting figure who nonetheless took a close personal interest in the progress of individual pupils and teachers. Although the school that bore his name no longer operates as a separate institution, alumni associations have continued to preserve its history and his memory.

Organised competition on the Gold Coast dates from 1961, when the Gold Coast Australian Football League was established with a small group of foundation clubs, among them Southport, Surfers Paradise and Palm Beach-Currumbin. The code grew in step with the region's rapid population growth, much of it driven by migration from the southern states, where the game was the dominant winter sport. Southport emerged as the strongest local club, winning a string of premierships before leaving for the Brisbane-based Queensland Australian Football League in 1983, where it won the premiership in its first season.

The region gained national exposure in 1987, when the Brisbane Bears entered the Victorian Football League and, despite their name, were based at Carrara Oval. Backed initially by businessman Christopher Skase, the club struggled both on the field and at the gate, and the collapse of Skase's business interests at the end of the decade left it in serious financial difficulty. The Bears began shifting matches to the Gabba in 1991 and relocated permanently to Brisbane in 1993, leaving the Gold Coast without an elite-level team for nearly two decades.

Interest from the Australian Football League revived in the mid-2000s, when the league began scheduling matches at Carrara and North Melbourne sold several of its home games to the venue. After North Melbourne declined a proposal to relocate at the end of 2007, the AFL pursued a new licence instead, and a local consortium known as GC17 was granted provisional entry. The new team competed in the under-18 TAC Cup in 2009 and the Victorian Football League in 2010 before making its AFL debut in 2011 as the Gold Coast Suns, with Gary Ablett Jr. as inaugural captain. Carrara Stadium was substantially rebuilt for the club's arrival, reopening in mid-2011 with a capacity of about 25,000.

The dispute arose from the Texas legislature's creation of the Railroad Commission in 1891, a body empowered to set freight and passenger rates for carriers operating within the state. John H. Reagan, a former United States senator, resigned his seat to serve as its first chairman. The Farmers' Loan and Trust Company of New York, acting as trustee for bondholders of the International and Great Northern Railroad, filed suit in federal circuit court against the commissioners and the state attorney general. It alleged that the schedule of rates the commission had imposed was so low as to deprive the railroad of any reasonable return and thereby threatened the security of the bonds.

Writing for a unanimous Court in 1894, Justice David J. Brewer rejected the argument that the action was in substance a suit against the State of Texas barred by the Eleventh Amendment. He reasoned that a suit to restrain state officers from enforcing an unconstitutional measure was directed at individuals acting beyond lawful authority, not at the sovereign itself. Brewer also dismissed the contention that the Texas statute confined challenges to rates to the state courts in Travis County, holding that a state could not by its own legislation curtail the jurisdiction of the federal courts.

On the merits, the Court upheld the validity of the act establishing the commission, affirming that a state may regulate railroad charges through an administrative body. It nonetheless held that the judiciary retained the power to inquire whether particular rates were unjust and unreasonable to the point of taking property without due process of law. Finding the challenged tariff confiscatory, the Court sustained the injunction against its enforcement, while reversing the part of the lower court's decree that had restrained the commission from exercising its statutory powers altogether.

The decision built upon Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railway Co. v. Minnesota and anticipated the fuller doctrines later announced in Smyth v. Ames and Ex parte Young.

Within the Italian Communist Party, the current known as migliorismo took shape during the 1970s and 1980s around the political legacy of Giorgio Amendola, who had long argued for a pragmatic, reformist course and for closer cooperation with the other forces of the Italian left. Its most prominent exponents were Giorgio Napolitano, Gerardo Chiaromonte and Emanuele Macaluso, and it found sympathy among figures such as Paolo Bufalini and the trade union leader Luciano Lama. The tendency was particularly well rooted in Milan, where Gianni Cervetti and a group of local leaders gave it an organisational base and, from the mid-1980s, a voice in the magazine *Il Moderno*.

The name, generally attributed to the philosopher Salvatore Veca, derived from the conviction that capitalism could be progressively improved through gradual reforms rather than overthrown. It was initially used with a polemical edge by opponents on the party's left, especially those close to Pietro Ingrao, who saw in the miglioristi an abandonment of any transformative ambition. The miglioristi themselves looked to the experience of European social democracy, especially the German SPD. They favoured the party's full acceptance of the Western alliance and of European integration, and regarded the market economy as a framework to be governed rather than abolished.

In domestic politics the current pressed for dialogue with the Italian Socialist Party of Bettino Craxi, a stance that set it at odds with Enrico Berlinguer's later emphasis on the "moral question" and on communist distinctiveness. It was also sceptical of the party's confrontational line during the 1984–85 dispute over the wage indexation mechanism known as the scala mobile.

After 1989 the miglioristi supported Achille Occhetto's decision to dissolve the party and found the Democratic Party of the Left, within which they formed the reformist wing. Their closeness to the Socialists exposed some Milanese members to criticism during the Tangentopoli investigations.

Jacob returned to India in 1857, having commanded the native light battalion under Sir James Outram in the Persian expedition, and arrived at Bombay just as news of the outbreak in Bengal was spreading through the western presidency. Lord Elphinstone, the governor, sent him at once to Kolhapur, where the 27th Bombay Native Infantry had mutinied and plundered the treasury. With only a small force at his disposal, Jacob disarmed the regiment, brought the ringleaders to trial, and restored order in the town. When a second rising was attempted in December, he acted with equal speed, securing the gates and dispersing the insurgents before the disturbance could spread to the neighbouring states. He was afterwards appointed special commissioner for the Southern Maratha Country, with wide political and military powers, and he held that charge until the region was considered quiet.

His conduct during these months was marked by a readiness to inquire into the causes of discontent as well as to punish it. Jacob had long argued that the government's policy of annexation, and its handling of land tenures and adoptions among the chiefs, had alienated classes whose loyalty might otherwise have been relied upon. He pressed these views on his superiors with a frankness that did not always help his advancement.

Failing health and deteriorating eyesight obliged him to leave India in 1859, and he retired from the service with the rank of major-general in 1861. He was made a Companion of the Bath in 1859 and a Knight Commander of the Star of India in 1869. In retirement he continued to write on Indian affairs, and in 1871 he published *Western India before and during the Mutinies*, an account drawn largely from his own experience. Though nearly blind in his last years, he remained an active correspondent, assisted by his adopted niece, Gertrude Le Grand Jacob. He died in London on 27 January 1881.

Uberti rose to national prominence during the presidency of Néstor Kirchner, when he was appointed head of the Órgano de Control de Concesiones Viales (OCCOVI), the agency that supervised Argentina's toll road concessions. The post placed him within the orbit of the Ministry of Federal Planning, led by Julio de Vido. Beyond his formal duties, he became an informal intermediary in the growing commercial relationship between Argentina and Venezuela, and the Argentine press came to describe him as a "parallel ambassador" to the government of Hugo Chávez.

His public career ended abruptly in August 2007. In the early hours of 4 August, a chartered jet hired by the state energy company Enarsa landed at Aeroparque Jorge Newbery in Buenos Aires, carrying Argentine and Venezuelan officials, among them Uberti. Customs officers found nearly 800,000 US dollars in undeclared cash in a suitcase belonging to another passenger, the Venezuelan-American businessman Guido Antonini Wilson. The episode, known as the "maletinazo" or suitcase scandal, prompted allegations that the money was meant for Cristina Fernández de Kirchner's presidential campaign, a claim the government firmly denied. Uberti was dismissed within days, and he spent the following years facing judicial proceedings over the attempted smuggling of the funds.

He returned to the headlines in 2018, when the so-called "notebooks" investigation into bribes allegedly paid by public works contractors led to a wave of arrests. Uberti presented himself to the courts and agreed to testify as a cooperating defendant. In his statements he said that he had collected payments from highway concessionaires and delivered them to senior officials, and he described large quantities of cash that he claimed to have seen in the Kirchners' residence in Buenos Aires. The former president and her allies rejected his account as a fabrication obtained under pressure. His testimony nonetheless became one of the more widely cited elements of the case.

Brewster's only known book, *Poems on Divers Subjects*, was printed in New London, Connecticut, in 1757 and reissued in Boston the following year. The slim volume gathers verse and a small amount of prose composed over roughly two decades. It includes occasional pieces, among them elegies, epitaphs, acrostics, verse letters to relatives and friends, scriptural paraphrases, and an account of a dream. Much of the collection is domestic in orientation. Several poems are addressed to her husband, Oliver Brewster, and to her two children, Ruby and Wadsworth, and they include farewell verses written on the occasion of her daughter's marriage and removal from the family home in Lebanon.

Alongside these conventional subjects, Brewster wrote on public affairs to a degree unusual for a colonial woman of her generation. Her poems on the wars with France, including verses prompted by Braddock's defeat in 1755, dwell on military losses and the fear of invasion, which she interprets through the lens of Protestant providentialism. In them she calls her readers to repentance while lamenting the human costs of the conflict. Scholars have noted that this willingness to treat warfare and politics set her apart from the few other women then appearing in print in the colonies. She was also among the first American-born women to publish verse under her own name.

Her authorship did not go unquestioned. According to a note within the collection, Brewster was challenged to demonstrate that she had written her own poems and answered by turning a psalm into verse in the presence of witnesses. This episode anticipates the better-known examination of Phillis Wheatley some years later. In her prefatory address to the reader, Brewster acknowledges the rarity of a woman venturing into print and offers the customary apologies for doing so. Even so, she presents her work as a legitimate offering to the public and to her descendants. Little is recorded of her life after the book appeared, and the date of her death remains uncertain.

The holotype of *Ziapelta sanjuanensis*, catalogued as NMMNH P-64484, was discovered in 2011 by Robert Sullivan in the Hunter Wash area of the Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness in northwestern New Mexico. It was recovered from the De-na-zin Member of the Kirtland Formation, in rocks dating to the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, about 73 million years ago. The specimen consists of a nearly complete skull lacking the lower jaws, together with parts of the first and second cervical half rings and a number of isolated osteoderms. A second specimen, an isolated first cervical half ring, was designated as a paratype. The genus was named and described in 2014 by Victoria Arbour and colleagues. The generic name combines a reference to the Zia sun symbol, which appears on the state flag of New Mexico, with the Latin *pelta*, meaning a small shield. The specific name honours San Juan County and the San Juan Basin.

*Ziapelta* was a medium-sized ankylosaurid, with a body length estimated at roughly 4.5 to 6 metres. It is distinguished from its relatives chiefly by the ornamentation of the skull and neck armour. The snout bears a large, roughly triangular median nasal caputegulum, an arrangement that differs from the pattern of bony plates seen in other ankylosaurines. The squamosal horns at the rear corners of the skull are thick and curve strongly downward. The cervical half rings carry tall, keeled osteoderms, the outermost of which are notably prominent.
