Phylogenetic analysis placed *Ziapelta* within Ankylosaurinae, in a group of derived North American forms that includes *Ankylosaurus*, *Euoplocephalus* and *Scolosaurus*. This result was somewhat unexpected, as the describers had anticipated a close relationship with *Nodocephalosaurus*, another ankylosaurid from the Kirtland Formation. Instead, *Ziapelta* appeared more closely allied to taxa from Alberta and Montana. Its discovery adds to the evidence that Late Cretaceous dinosaur faunas of southern Laramidia were distinct from those farther north.

Spottiswood was appointed a privy councillor by James VI on his return to Scotland, and in 1622 he became an Extraordinary Lord of Session, taking the title Lord Newabbey from lands in Kirkcudbrightshire that his father had made over to him. Charles I made him an Ordinary Lord in 1626, and on the death of Sir James Skene in 1633 he was chosen President of the Court of Session. He later sold the lands of New Abbey to the king, who used them to endow the newly created bishopric of Edinburgh, and he was thereafter styled Lord Dunipace, after an estate he had bought in Stirlingshire.

As the son of the Archbishop of St Andrews and a firm supporter of episcopacy, Spottiswood was detested by the Covenanters. When the troubles began in 1638 he withdrew to England and remained with the king. He returned to Scotland with Charles in 1641, but was arrested and held in Edinburgh Castle as one of the "incendiaries" blamed for the breach between the king and his subjects. He was released after some months and rejoined the court. At Oxford, following the disgrace of the Earl of Lanark, the king appointed him Secretary of State for Scotland. In this capacity he sealed the commission naming the Marquess of Montrose as the king's lieutenant in Scotland, and in 1645 he made the hazardous journey north to deliver it in person.

Spottiswood was with the royalist army when it was surprised and routed at Philiphaugh on 13 September 1645, and he was taken prisoner. He was tried before the Parliament sitting at St Andrews on a charge of treason. He argued that he had never borne arms against the state and that he had surrendered on a promise of quarter, but the plea was rejected. He was beheaded by the Maiden at the market cross of St Andrews in January 1646, having been denied leave to address the crowd.

Road transport forms the backbone of movement within Saskatchewan, which maintains more kilometres of road than any other Canadian province. The provincial highway network extends roughly 26,000 kilometres and is supplemented by a vast grid of municipal gravel roads laid out along the survey lines of the Dominion Land Survey. The Trans-Canada Highway crosses the southern part of the province through Swift Current, Moose Jaw and Regina, while the Yellowhead Highway runs northwest through Yorkton, Saskatoon and the Battlefords toward Edmonton. Highway 11, designated the Louis Riel Trail, links Regina, Saskatoon and Prince Albert and serves as the principal corridor between the province's two largest cities. In the north, where permanent roads are sparse, seasonal ice roads and winter trails provide access to remote communities.

Rail transport played a decisive role in the settlement of the province. The arrival of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the early 1880s determined the location of many towns, and branch lines later spread across the grain belt to serve country elevators. Today the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Kansas City main lines carry grain, potash and other bulk commodities to ports on the Pacific coast and the Great Lakes. Numerous short line railways, some of them owned by local farmers, operate on former branch lines. Passenger rail is limited to Via Rail's transcontinental service, which stops at Saskatoon and several smaller communities.

Air travel is centred on Saskatoon John G. Diefenbaker International Airport and Regina International Airport, with smaller airports and aerodromes serving northern mining operations and isolated settlements. The provincial government also operates about a dozen seasonal ferries, most of them cable ferries, across the North and South Saskatchewan Rivers; these are free of charge. Intercity bus service was provided for decades by the Saskatchewan Transportation Company, a Crown corporation that ceased operations in 2017, leaving private carriers to serve a reduced number of routes.
